Poem: 北野どの御すきものや梅の花
Romaji:
kitano-dono                
onsuki no mono ya        
ume no hana
My translation:
What the Lord of Kitano
most enjoys
are plum blossoms.
Kigo: 梅 【うめ】 ume, （sometimes むめ mume）, plum (blossoms) [technically, the "Japanese apricot", Prunus mume; but this has almost always been translated "plum" for literary purposes] (early spring).
Ueda Haiku: test

Poem: かめにさす柳のさけやつくりばな
Romaji:
kame ni sasu
yanagi no sake ya
tsukuribana
My translation:
a willow branch thrust
into the vase—is it sake
or a paper flower?
Kigo: 柳 【やなぎ】 yanagi, willow(s) / weeping willow(s) (late spring).

Poem: 春雨にあらいてけづれ柳がみ
Romaji:
harusame ni 
araite kezure
yanagi gami
My translation:
Spring rain
washing, combing
the willow hair.
Kigo: 春雨 【はるさめ】 harusame, spring rain (all spring).

Poem: 気力なしと誰かは見ましこぶ柳
Romaji:
kiryoku nashi to
dare kawa mimashi
kobu yanagi
My translation:
No power—
who would see that in
a swelling willow?
Kigo: 柳 【やなぎ】 yanagi, willow(s) / weeping willow(s) (late spring).

Poem: 世にふるも更に時雨の宿りかな
Romaji:
yo ni furu mo
sara ni shigure no
yadori kana
My translation:
enduring this world
while all along the winter rain
falls on my shelter
Kigo: 春雨 【はるさめ】 harusame, spring rain (all spring).

Poem: 雪ながら山本かすむ夕べかな
Romaji:
yuki nagara
yama moto kasumu 
yube kana
My translation:
still bearing snow
the foothills of the mountain
wrap in evening haze
Kigo: 雪 【ゆき】 yuki, snow. / 霞 【かすみ】 kasumi, (spring) mist [frequently translated "haze"; see note "On Haze, Mist, Fog"] (all spring).
Notes: Snow lingering while the foothills haze over—classic late-spring juxtaposition.

Poem: 菫咲く野はいくすじの春の水
Romaji:
sumire saku
no wa ikusuji no
haru no mizu
My translation:
violet fields—
how many streamlets run
through the spring water
Kigo: 菫 【すみれ】 sumire, violet(s) [Viola mandshurica] (all spring).

Poem: にがにがしいつ迄嵐ふきのたう
Romaji:
niganigashi
itsu made arashi fuki no tō  
fuki no tō
My translation:
till when will
the bitter winds blow 
butterbur pot
Kigo: ふきのたう (butterbur)
Notes: ふきのたう (fuki no tō) is the butterbur shoot, a spring kigo. Bitterness of wind plays against the bitterness of the shoot.

Poem: 手をついて歌申しあぐる蛙かな
Romaji:
te wo tsuite 
uta mōshi aguru 
kawazu kana
My translation:
with hands supplicated
reciting a song
a frog:
Kigo: 蛙 【かわず】 kawazu, （かはづ）, frog(s) [note that this is a literary word] (all spring).
Notes: his poem is also included in 『歴代滑稽伝』『温故集』『俳諧古選』『俳家奇人談』, but we can not be should that it is in fact Sokan’s poem.  However, it is considered to be on of his masterpieces.  Arano was published in 1689, the year that Bashō left on his journey to the deep north.  This collection was published with the idea of opposing Teimon haikai which had wildly broken all of the traditions of haikai, so this poem by the founder of haikai fit perfectly with the ideal of the editors.

Poem: すゞしさや水に柳のかげ法師
Romaji:
suzushisa ya 
mizu ni yanagi no
kage-bōshi
My translation:
how cool-
on the water, the willows’
silhouettes
Kigo: 柳 【やなぎ】 yanagi, willow(s) / weeping willow(s) (late spring).
Notes: Willow is a spring kigo, but 涼しさ suzushisa (coolness) is a summer kigo; this is classified as summer.
Other translation: Willow is a spring season word, but in this case coolness, a summer word, is the main season word, so this is considered to be a summer poem.

Poem: うづきゝてねぶとに鳴けや郭公
Romaji:
uzuki kite 
nebuto ni nake ya 
Hototogisu
My translation:
the deutzia moon has come
sing in a loud voice 
hototogisu
Kigo: 郭公 【ほととぎす】 hototogisu, little cuckoo (all summer).
Notes: 卯月 (uzuki) is the fourth lunar month (early summer). ねぶと (nebuto) = boil/carbuncle.
Other translation:
acheing
carbuncle cry
hototogisu

Poem: きえにけりこれぞまことの雪ぼとけ
Romaji:
kie ni keri
kore zo makoto no
yuki botoke
My translation:
it has vanished—
this was the true form
of the snow Buddha
Kigo: 雪仏 【ゆきぼとけ】 yuki botoke, snow Buddha (winter).
Notes: A snow effigy of the Buddha that melts away—Buddhist impermanence (無常 mujō).

Poem: 月にえをさしたらばよき団哉
Romaji:
tsuki ni 
e wo sasitaraba yoki
utiwa kana
My translation:
if this moon
had a handle 
a fine fan!
Kigo: 団扇 【うちわ】 uchiwa, （うちは）, (round) fan [usually made of lightly framed paper glued to a handle] (all summer).
Notes: Playful conceit: if the full moon had a handle it would make a perfect fan.

Poem: 風寒し破れ障子の神無月
Romaji:
kaze samushi 
yabure shōji no 
kaminazuki
My translation:
cold wind
ripped shoji screen
godless month
Kigo: 神無月 【かんなづき】 kannazuki, 10th lunar month [literally "gods-absent month"; approximately November] (early winter).
Notes: 神無月 refers to the tenth lunar month when the gods leave for Izumo; broken shoji screens add to the chill.

Poem: 満丸に出でてもながき春日かな
Romaji:
manmaru ni 
idetemo nagaki
haru-bi kana
My translation:
thou rising roundly
the sun elongates 
on long spring days:
Kigo: 春日 【はるひ】 haruhi, a day in spring / spring day / spring sun [either or both meanings simultaneously, depending on context] (all spring).
Notes: 満丸に (manmaru ni) = roundly, perfectly round—the sun rising full and round on a long spring day.

Poem: さむくともひになあたりそ雪仏
Romaji:
samuku tomo
hi ni na atari so
yuki hotoke
My translation:
even if you’re cold
don’t warm yourself by the fire
snowman
Kigo: 雪仏 【ゆきぼとけ】 yuki botoke, snow Buddha (winter).
Notes: Companion piece to Row 13. Comic warning: do not warm yourself by the fire or the snow Buddha will melt.

Poem: 飛梅やかろがろしくも神の春
Romaji:
tobi ume ya  
karogaroshiku mo  
kami no haru
My translation:
Flying plum—
lightly, lightly,
the god’s spring.
Kigo: 梅 【うめ】 ume, （sometimes むめ mume）, plum (blossoms) [technically, the "Japanese apricot", Prunus mume; but this has almost always been translated "plum" for literary purposes] (early spring).
Other translation: flying plum and spring (spring)

Poem: 元朝や神代のことも思はるゝ
Romaji:
ganchō ya
kamiyo no koto mo
Omowaruru
My translation:
New year's morning—
the age of the gods
are in my thoughts
Kigo: 元朝 【がんちょう】 ganchō, New Year's morning (New Year).
Notes: The age of the gods (神代 kamiyo) brought to mind on New Year's morning.
Other translation: cold plum (winter)

Poem: 青柳まゆかくきしのひたひかな
Romaji:
aoyanagi
mayukakukishi no
hitai kana
My translation:
emerald willow
the bank is the forehead
on which eyebrows are drawn
Kigo: 柳 【やなぎ】 yanagi, willow(s) / weeping willow(s) (late spring).

Poem: 落花枝にかへると見れば胡蝶哉
Romaji:
rakuka eda ni
kaeru to mireba
kochō kana
My translation:
falling blossoms 
appear to return to the boughs
butterflies
Kigo: 落花 【らっか】 rakka, （らくくわ）, falling (cherry) blossoms (late spring).
Notes: Famous conceit: falling petals appear to return to the branch—only to reveal themselves as butterflies.

Poem: 夏の夜は明くれどあかぬまぶた哉
Romaji:
natsu no yo ha
akuredo akanu
mabuta kana
My translation:
summer nights
dawn but eyelids
can't open
Kigo: 夏の夜 【なつのよ】 natsu no yo, summer night (all summer).
Notes: Comic poem playing on 花 hana (blossom) and 鼻 hana (nose)—the nose has fragrance surpassing flowers.

Poem: かささぎや今日久かたの雨の川
Romaji:
kasasagi ya
kyō hisakata no
ama no kawa
My translation:
magpie bridge—
today the sky's long river
rains down upon it
Kigo: 天の川 【あまのがわ】 ama-no-gawa, Milky Way (mid autumn).
Notes: Tanabata imagery: the magpie bridge (鵲橋) of Chinese legend that spans the Milky Way.

Poem: 花よりも鼻ありけるにほひかな
Romaji:
hana yori mo
hana ari keru
niohi kana
My translation:
more than blossoms—
it was here all along,
this fragrant nose
Kigo: 花 【はな】 hana, (cherry) blossoms [in haiku and haikai the simple word hana 花 refers to cherry blossoms, as do all kigo listed here; but note that in Manyōshū and some other early poetry hana was understood as referring to ume 梅【うめ】plum blossoms, an early spring topic] (late spring).
Notes: Comic wordplay on 花 (blossom) and 鼻 (nose). The nose wins out over blossoms in the fragrance contest.

Poem: 春立つやにほんめでたき門の松
Romaji:
haru tatsu ya
nihon medetaki
kado no matsu
My translation:
twin pines stand auspiciously
as Japan celebrates
the dawning of spring
Kigo: 春立つ 【はるたつ】 haru tatsu, spring begins.

Poem: 足もとのよきをぞとらんよめが萩
Romaji:
ashi moto no
yoki wo zo toran
yome ha hagi
My translation:
you oughta pick 
supple limbed bride clover
right underfoot
Kigo: bride clover

Poem: しし舞もせよやぼたんの花見酒
Romaji:
shishi mai mo
se you ya botan no
hanami-zake
My translation:
dance that lion 
dance— among peony blossoms
sipping blossom-viewing sake
Kigo: 牡丹 【ぼたん】 botan, tree peony (early summer).

Poem: あきなひか空ねも高き杜宇
Romaji:
akinai ka
sora ne mo takaki
hototogisu
My translation:
that’s business, I guess 
inflating the asking price
the cuckoo

will I ever tire
of your sharp call high in the sky
cuckoo
Kigo: 子規 【ほととぎす】 hototogisu, little cuckoo.

Poem: 身にしむや香炉の煙秋の風
Romaji:
mi ni shimu ya
karō no kemuri
aki no kaze
My translation:
piercing into me— 
smoke from the incense burner blown 
by the autumn wind
Kigo: 秋風 【あきかぜ】 akikaze, autumn breeze / autumn wind [carries with it the sound of rustling leaves] (all autumn).

Poem: 一はつの 花や夏野の きのうけふ
Romaji:
ichi hatsu no
hana ya natsuno no
kinō kyō
My translation:
first iris blooms—
yesterday and today
the summer meadow
Kigo: 一初 【いちはつ】 ichi-hatsu, iris [Iris tectorum] (early summer).
Notes: 一初 (ichihatsū) is the first iris to bloom, marking the transition into summer. 夏野 (natsuno) = summer field.

Poem: 鮎膾藍より青き蓼酢かな
Romaji:
ayu namasu
ai yori aoki 
tade zu kana
My translation:
sweet fish salad
bluer than indigo
nettle vinegar
Kigo: 鮎 【あゆ】 ayu, sweet fish / ayu (all summer).
Notes: 蓼酢 (tadezu) = smartweed vinegar sauce for ayu. 蓼 (tade) also a summer kigo.

Poem: 今まではいきたはごとを月夜かな
Romaji:
ima made wa
ikita wa goto wo
tsukiyo kana
My translation:
until just now
everything felt like a dream—
a moonlit night
Kigo: 月 【つき】 tsuki, moon (mid autumn).
Notes: The moon as metaphor for dreamlike existence. まで (made) = until now, suggesting a sudden awakening.

Poem: 唐人も渡るや霜の日本橋
Romaji:
toujin mo
wataru ya shimo no
nihonbashi
My translation:
even the foreign merchants
cross it—Nihonbashi
in the frost
Kigo: 霜 【しも】 shimo, frost (mid winter).
Notes: Nihonbashi in frost. 唐人 (tōjin) = Chinese/foreign merchant; the bridge as cosmopolitan meeting point.

Poem: 口切に時雨を知らぬ青茶かな
Romaji:
kuchikiri ni
shigure wo shiranu
aojya kana
My translation:
the season's first tea—
this pale green, ignorant
of the winter rain
Kigo: 口切 【くちきり】 kuchikiri, opening of the tea jar (early winter).
Notes: 口切 (kuchikiri) is the ceremony of opening the new year's tea jar—an early winter tea-ceremony kigo. 時雨 shigure = winter drizzle.

Poem: 煙にもすすけず白し富士の雪
Romaji:
kemuri ni mo
susukenu shiroshi
Fuji no yuki
My translation:
not even smoke
can darken it—white
snow on Fuji
Kigo: 雪 【ゆき】 yuki, snow (all winter).
Notes: 富士 (Fuji) snow so pure even smoke cannot stain it.

Poem: 五月雨の晴れて犬なく日和かな
Romaji:
samidare no
harete inu naku
hiyori kana
My translation:
the long rains clear—
a dog barks into
the fine weather
Kigo: 五月雨 【さみだれ】 samidare, early summer rains / monsoon (mid summer).
Notes: 五月雨 (samidare) = the prolonged early summer rains. A dog barks when they finally clear.

Poem: 諸行無常聞くや林鐘の声
Romaji:
shogyo mujo
kiku ya rinsho no
koe
My translation:
all things must pass—
so I hear in the tolling
of the summer bell
Kigo: 林鐘 【りんしょう】 rinshō, sixth-month bell tone (mid summer).
Notes: 林鐘 is the musical note associated with the sixth lunar month (midsummer). 諸行無常 (shōgyō mujō) = Buddhist "all things are impermanent."

Poem: たぎりてや湯玉たばしる霰釜
Romaji:
tagiri te ya
tama tobashiru
arare kama
My translation:
how it boils—
hail beads scatter and fly
from the kettle
Kigo: 霰 【あられ】 arare, snow pellets [often given in dictionaries, and therefore mistranslated, as "hail"--which is 雹【ひょう】 hyō--a summer phenomenon] (all winter).
Notes: 霰釜 (arare-gama) = a hail-patterned tea kettle. 湯玉 (tama) = water beads from boiling—pun on hail.

Poem: 人魂か魂祭る野に飛ぶ蛍
Romaji:
hitodama ka
tamamatsuru no ni
tobu hotaru
My translation:
a wandering soul?
in the fields of the bon festival
a firefly drifts
Kigo: 蛍 【ほたる】 hotaru, firefly / fireflies (mid summer).
Notes: 人魂 (hitodama) = will-o'-the-wisp / wandering soul. Bon festival association; fireflies as the souls of the dead.

Poem: 武蔵野の雪ころばしか富士の山
Romaji:
musashino no
yuki korobashi ka
Fuji no yama
My translation:
Musashino's snow
rolling down, is it?
Mount Fuji
Kigo: 雪 【ゆき】 yuki, snow (all winter).
Notes: Musashino plain snow rolling toward Fuji—playful image of snow sliding off the plain to gather on the peak.

Poem: 槍梅の散らしかかるこだちかな
Romaji:
yari ume no
chirashi kakaru
kodachi kana
My translation:
scattered plum blossoms
drop upon the thrusting grove
of young trees
Kigo: 梅 【うめ】 ume, （sometimes むめ mume）, plum (blossoms) [technically, the "Japanese apricot", Prunus mume; but this has almost always been translated "plum" for literary purposes] (early spring).
Notes: 槍梅 (yari ume) = spear-shaped plum branch variety. Petals scattering over a grove of young trees.

Poem: 霞さへまだらにたつやとらの年
Romaji:
kasumi sae
madara ni tatsu ya
tora no toshi
My translation:
even the mist
is decked in stripes
year of the tiger
Kigo: 霞 【かすみ】 kasumi, (spring) mist [frequently translated "haze"; see note "On Haze, Mist, Fog"] (all spring).

Poem: 鳳凰も出でよのどけきとりの年
Romaji:
hōō mo ide 
nodokeki 
tori no toshi
My translation:
may even phoenixes
come out this calm
year of the bird
Kigo: 【のどけし】 nodokeshi, tranquil.

Poem: 花よりも団子やありて帰る雁
Romaji:
hana yori mo
dango ya arite
kaeru kari
My translation:
It is said, dumplings
are better than blossoms-
returning geese.
Kigo: 帰る雁
Other translation: 帰る雁 (Returning geese) spring

Poem: けさたるるつららやよだれうしの年
Romaji:
kesa taruru
tsurara ya yodare
ushi no toshi
Kigo: 丑の年 【うしのとし】 ushi no toshi, Year of the Ox (New Year).
Notes: つらら (tsurara) = icicles; よだれ (yodare) = drool—comic image of ox drooling icicles at New Year.

Poem: 紅梅やかの銀公がからごろも
Romaji:
kōbai ya 
kano ginkō no 
Karakoromo
My translation:
crimson plum—
renowned Empress Ginko’s
Chinese robe
Kigo: 紅梅

Poem: 烏には似ぬうの花ぞ鷺の色
Romaji:
karasu niwa
ninu unohana zo
sagi no iro
My translation:
resembling a crow
not in the least, the cormorant flower
color of egret
Kigo: 卯の花 【うのはな】 u-no-hana, deutzia flowers [Deutzia crenata] (early summer).

Poem: 比翼かやはねをならべて帰雁
Romaji:
hiyoku kaya
hane wo narabete
kaeru kari
My translation:
be as two birds! 
flying wingtip to wingtip
returning geese
Kigo: 帰る雁
Notes: 帰雁 (kaeru kari) = returning geese, a classic spring kigo. 比翼 (hiyoku) = paired birds flying wing to wing—symbol of conjugal love.
Other translation: 帰る雁 (Returning geese) spring

Poem: 松ならび穴へ餅ひき子のひ哉
Romaji:
matsu narabi
ana e mochi hiki
ko no hi kana
My translation:
rows of pine trees—
into the hole they pull the mochi
this Children's Day
Kigo: 子の日 【ねのひ】 ne no hi, Day of the Rat (New Year).
Notes: 子の日 is the first Day of the Rat in the new year, traditionally spent pulling up young pines. Mochi is pulled into holes.

Poem: 正月の礼者とながむいぬの年
Romaji:
shogatsu no
reija to nagamu
inu no toshi
My translation:
New Year's visitors—
I watch them come and go
in the Year of the Dog
Kigo: 礼者 【れいしゃ】 reisha, New Year's callers (New Year).
Notes: 戌 (inu) = Year of the Dog. New Year's visitors observed while watching the year cycle.

Poem: 野寺あれて跡にやはゆる仏の座
Romaji:
nodera arete
ato ni ya wa yuru
hotoke no za
My translation:
the country temple decays—
and in its place a lotus
burns warmly on
Kigo: 梅 【うめ】 ume, （sometimes むめ mume）, plum (blossoms) [technically, the "Japanese apricot", Prunus mume; but this has almost always been translated "plum" for literary purposes] (early spring).
Notes: Alludes to the legend of 飛梅 (tobiume), the plum that flew to Dazaifu to follow Sugawara no Michizane into exile.

Poem: かははがれからきめやみる山椒の木
Romaji:
kawa wa gare
kara ki me ya miru
sansho no ki
My translation:
the river runs dry—
looking at the withered buds
of the pepper tree
Kigo: 花の雨 【はなのあめ】 hana no ame, blossom rain (mid spring).
Notes: pun: ame = rain and candy. Let the blossoms sleep (nursed by the rain / candy). Cf. Row 74 which is a variant.

Poem: 信あれば是も飛梅の奇特かな
Romaji:
shin areba
kore mo tobi ume no
kitoku kana
My translation:
with true faith
even this is a miracle
of the flying plum
Kigo: 土筆 【つくし】 tsukushi, horsetail shoot(s) [the reproductive shoots of Equisetum arvense] (mid spring).
Notes: Horsetail shoots sold by street vendors in the hakama-cloth district.

Poem: ねふらせて養ひ立よ花の雨
Romaji:
nefurasete
yashihai tate yo
hana no ame
My translation:
let it sleep
and nurse it into growth—
the blossom rain
Kigo: 暑き夜 【あつきよ】 atsuki yo, hot night (all summer).
Notes: 天の原 (amano hara) = the plain of heaven / the night sky. Playful: are the stars sweating from the heat?

Poem: つくつくし売るやはかまの町くだり
Romaji:
tsukushi uru ya
hakama no machi
kudari
My translation:
horsetails for sale—
down the street of hakama
shops they go
Kigo: 玉祭 【たままつり】 tama matsuri, spirit festival (New Year).
Notes: 正月 (shōgatsu) = New Year. 玉祭 here likely refers to a New Year game or spirit invocation.

Poem: 暑き夜の星はあせぼかあまの原
Romaji:
atsuki yo no
hoshi wa asebo ka
amano hara
My translation:
on this hot night
are the stars sweating too
up in the sky-plain?
Kigo: 蟋蟀 【こおろぎ】 kōrogi, （こほろぎ）, cricket(s) (all autumn).
Notes: きれぎれす = onomatopoeia for the cricket's cry. "Patch it, patch it" (つづりさせ) mimics the sound.

Poem: 正月にうちしは夢か玉まつり
Romaji:
shogatsu ni
uchi shi wa yume ka
tama matsuri
My translation:
struck at New Year—
was it a dream?
the spirit festival
Kigo: 木の葉 【このは】 ko-no-ha, leaves of trees [noted for drying, falling, blowing in wind] (all winter).
Notes: おもしろく (omoshiroku) = with pleasure/delight. はらはら = leaves scattering lightly—a gentle, pleasing fall.

Poem: つづりさせとちちち鳴くやきれぎれす
Romaji:
tsuzuri sase to
chichichi naku ya
kiregiresu
My translation:
"patch it, patch it"
so chirps the cricket,
over and over
Kigo: 蟋蟀 【こおろぎ】 kōrogi, （こほろぎ）, cricket(s) (all autumn).

Poem: おもしろくはらはら落る木葉哉
Romaji:
omoshiroku
harahara ochiru
konoha kana
My translation:
delightfully
scattering and falling—
the fallen leaves
Kigo: 木の葉 【このは】 ko-no-ha, leaves of trees [noted for drying, falling, blowing in wind] (all winter).

Poem: 門前に市も立花の盛哉
Romaji:
kado mae ni
ichi mo tachibana no
sakari kana
My translation:
a throng of mandarin viewers
gather before my gate 
like a bazaar
Kigo: Tachibana
Notes: based on saying; pun on tachi

Poem: 七夕のなかうどなれや宵の月
Romaji:
tanabata no
nakaudo nare ya
yoi no tsuki
My translation:
be the matchmaker 
for the star festival—
evening moon
Kigo: 七夕 【たなばた】 tanabata, Festival of the Weaver.

Poem: 皆人のひるねのたねや秋のつき
Romaji:
mina hito no
hirune no tane ya
aki no tsuki
My translation:
the seed of 
everyone's naps—
autumn moon
Kigo: 月 【つき】 tsuki, moon.

Poem: かへり点の文字か跡先帰雁
Romaji:
kaeriten no
moji ka ato saki
kaerikari
My translation:
diacritical marked
letters? Switching order
returning geese
Kigo: 帰る雁 (Returning geese) spring

Poem: 酒や時雨のめば紅葉ぬ人もなし
Romaji:
sake ya shigure 
nomeba momijinu
hito mo nashi
My translation:
wine & winter drizzle
drink it up and everyone's face  
reddens like maple leaves
Kigo: 紅葉 【もみじ】 momiji,  red (maple) leaves.

Poem: 在次第うす雪きやせ今日の春
Romaji:
ari shidai
usu yuki kiyase
kyō no haru
My translation:
melt every last bit
of the dappled snow
this day of spring
Kigo: 春【はる】haru, Spring.
Notes: daiusu means Christian. Poem about Christian upraising.

Poem: ありたつたひとりたつたる今年かな
Romaji:
ari tattta  
hitori tattaru  
kotoshi kana
My translation:
Oh! He stood!
He is standing by himself!
This New Year
Kigo: 春立つ 【はるたつ】 haru tatsu, spring begins.

Poem: 歌いづれ小町躍や伊勢躍
Romaji:
uta izure			
komachi odori ya		
ise odori
My translation:
which has the better songs?
the Komachi dance-
or the Ise dance
Kigo: 踊 【おどり】 odori, (Bon Festival) dance/dancing [note that while this is the common word for dancing, in haikai it always means dancing at Obon unless otherwise specified] (early autumn).

Poem: 大服や城を粉になす茶磨山
Romaji:
ōfuku ya
shiro wo ko ni nasu
chausuyama
My translation:
auspicious New Year’s tea—
the castle is ground to powder
from Mt. Tea Mortar
Kigo: 大服
Notes: marks the end of the Osaka campain. Earlest known saitan mitsumono

Poem: しほるるは何かあんずの花の色
Romaji:
shioruru wa
nanka annzu no 
hana no iro
My translation:
withering
with worry, the hue 
of apricot blossoms
Kigo: 杏の花 【あんずのはな】 anzu no hana, apricot blossoms.
Notes: anzu ouns apricot and worry

Poem: すそ野暑く頭寒足熱富士の雪
Romaji:
suso no atsuku
zukan sokunetsu
fuji no yuki
My translation:
these foothills are so hot
cool the head and heat the feet
Mt. Fuji
Kigo: 暑し 【あつし】 atsushi, hot (all summer).
Notes: zukan-sokunetsu is a saying

Poem: 雪月花一度に見する卯木かな
Romaji:
setsu-getsu-ka
ichido ni misuru
utsuki kana
My translation:
snow, moon, and blossoms
viewed all at once
in deutzia flowers
Kigo: 卯木の花 【うつぎのはな】 utsugi-no-hana, deutzia flowers.
Notes: 卯 is a blssom. Utsuki mean moon, and u is white like snow

Poem: つみ綿かぬり桶なりの庭の雪
Romaji:
tsumi wata ka
nuri oke nari no
niwa no yuki
My translation:
is it pulled cotton?
a lacquered bucket covered with snow
in the garden
Kigo: 雪 【ゆき】 yuki, snow.
Notes: Composed for the Kanei 6 haikai meeting at Myomanji. The host was Saimu, who was a cotton

Poem: てん長くち人誉むるや秋の月
Romaji:
ten nagaku
chihito homuru ya
aki no tsuki
My translation:
heavenly marked and
celebrated by the multitudes—
moon of autumn
Kigo: 秋の月 【あきのつき】 aki no tsuki, autumn moon.
Notes:
tennaga 1. 天長eternal, 2. His students will long mark poems, 3. High praise
chihito 1. Many people, 2. 天地人

Poem: ねぶらせて養ひたてよ花のあめ
Romaji:
neburasete
yashinai-tate yo
hana no ame
My translation:
raise them up
by letting them lick
the candy rain of spring
Kigo: 花 【はな】 hana, (cherry) blossoms [in haiku and haikai the simple word hana 花 refers to cherry blossoms, as do all kigo listed here; but note that in Manyōshū and some other early poetry hana was understood as referring to ume 梅【うめ】plum blossoms, an early spring topic] (late spring).
Notes:
pun: ame-rain and candy
maegaki: poem celebrating birth of child

Poem: 春たつは衣の棚の霞かな
Romaji:
haru tatsu wa			
koromo no tana no
kasumi kana
My translation:
spring begins
in the Robe Bureau district 
with bolts cut from mist
Kigo: 春立つ 【はるたつ】 haru tatsu, spring begins.
Notes: pun: tatsu-stand/start and to cut

Poem: 冬籠虫けらまでもあなかしこ
Romaji:
fuyugomori
mushikera made mo
ana kashiko
My translation:
winter seclusion
even down to the lowliest insects, 
how reverent!
Kigo: 冬籠り 【ふゆごもり】 fuyugomori, winter seclusion.

Poem: ゆき尽くす江南の春の光かな
Romaji:
end of the snow journy 
the light of spring in Jiangnan 
how it shines!
My translation:
Yuki tsukusu
Kōnan no haru no
hikari kana
Kigo: 春 【はる】 haru, spring.
Notes: 江南 (Kōnan) = south of the Yangtze (Jiangnan), Chinese literary reference to a land of perpetual spring.

Poem: くくり目を見つつ夜長き枕かな
Kigo: 夜長 【よなが】 yonaga, long night (all autumn).
Notes: 夜長 (yonaga) = long autumn nights. Lying awake staring at the knots of stitching on the pillow.

Poem: けさたるるつららやよだれうしの年
Kigo: 丑の年 【うしのとし】 ushi no toshi, Year of the Ox (New Year).
Notes: つらら (tsurara) = icicles likened to a drooling ox. Comic new-year zodiac poem.

Poem: 梅も先にほひてくるや午の年
Romaji:
ume mo saki 
nioite kuru ya 
ushi no toshi
My translation:
The scent of plum
comes first carried by
the Year of the Ox
Kigo: 午の年 【うまのとし】 uma no toshi, Year of the Horse (New Year).
Notes: 先 (mazu) = first of all. The plum is the first fragrance of the new year in the Year of the Horse.

Poem: もえながら有るや火鼠のかは柳
Romaji:
moe nagara
aru ya hinezumi no
kawa yanagi
My translation:
While burning
the fire rat skin
river willow.
Kigo: 柳 【やなぎ】 yanagi, willow(s) / weeping willow(s) (late spring).
Notes: 火鼠 (hi-nezumi) = fire rat from Chinese legend whose pelt does not burn. The willow burning yet enduring.

Poem: 玉札の飛脚か急ぎ帰雁
Romaji:
tamazusa no
hikyaku ka isogi
kaeru kari
My translation:
a jade-letter courier—
surely it hurries past
the returning wild geese
Kigo: 帰雁 【かえるかり】 kaeru kari, returning geese (mid spring).
Notes: 玉札 (tama-fuda) = jade letter/letter-carrier. The wild geese as messengers rushing home in spring.

Poem: 山の腰にはく夕だちや雲の帯
Romaji:
yama no koshi ni
haku yudachi ya
kumo no obi
My translation:
from mountain hips
hangs an evening storm blade—
belt of clouds
Kigo: 夕立 【ゆうだち】 yūdachi, （ゆふだち）, sudden (summer) shower [literally "evening shower"] (all summer).
Notes: 夕だち (yūdachi) = sudden evening storm. The mountain's flank wrapped in a cloud-sash.

Poem: 先かづく頭はかみなづきんかな
Romaji:
mazu ka zuku
kashira wa kamina
zukin kana
My translation:
first must wear 
on a baldhead in godless month
a hood
Kigo: Godless month, hood (winter)

Poem: しも月のあるに付てやかみな月
Romaji:
shimo tsuki no
aru ni tsukite ya
kaminatsuki
My translation:
the frost month
is below and so above
is the godless month
Kigo: Godless month, hood (winter)
Notes: Wordplay: 霜月 (shimotsuki, Eleventh Month) contains 有る (aru = to exist), so the "godless" tenth month is about to be replaced.

Poem: 春と夏と秋とけふとの四ぐれかな
Romaji:
haru to natsu to
aki to kyō to no
shigure kana
My translation:
spring & summer &
autumn & today’s
makes “four kures”
Kigo: 時雨 【しぐれ】 shigure, (winter) shower/drizzle (early winter).

Poem: 足はやき雲や時雨の先ばしり
Romaji:
ashihayaki
kumo ya shigure no
Sakibashiri
My translation:
the quick-footed
cloud—winter shower's 
forerunner
Kigo: 時雨 【しぐれ】 shigure, (winter) shower/drizzle (early winter).

Poem: きつくふるをやいたやとゆふ時雨
Romaji:
Hard falling sound
on the roof boards, “it hurts!”
says the winter shower
My translation:
kutsuku furu
oto ya itaya to
yuu shigure
Kigo: 時雨 【しぐれ】 shigure, (winter) shower/drizzle (early winter).

Poem: 山姥が尿やしぐれの山めぐり
Romaji:
the mt. Hag
goes around the mt.
Pissing a winter shower
My translation:
yamauba ga
bari ya shigure no
Yamamuguri
Kigo: 時雨 【しぐれ】 shigure, (winter) shower/drizzle (early winter).
Notes:
前書：渋谷紀州興行に
渋谷以重 Shibuya Ijū – noh actor
play on the play Yamauba
冬は萌冴え行く時雨の雲の
Konzanshu- 山姥やしとをしぐれの山めぐり

Poem: 時宗寺の時雨の亭や雨やどり
Romaji:
＠ the winter rain pavilion 
@ Jishū Temple
waiting for the rain to stop
My translation:
Jishūdera no
shigure no chin ya
Ameyadori
Kigo: 時雨 【しぐれ】 shigure, (winter) shower/drizzle (early winter).
Notes: 前書：六条道場にて

Poem: さざれ言もいははふとての試筆哉
Romaji:
sazare goto mo
ihawa futo no
shihitsu kana
My translation:
even small words
casually begun—
the year's first writing
Kigo: 試筆 【しひつ】 shihitsu, first calligraphy of the new year (New Year).
Notes: 試筆 (shihitsu) = first brush practice of the New Year. Even small words begin the year's writing.

Poem: 風ならで誰かあぐべき柳髪
Romaji:
kaze narade
dare ka agubeki
yanagikami
My translation:
who but the wind
could lift and toss
willow hair?
Kigo: 柳 【やなぎ】 yanagi, willow(s) / weeping willow(s) (late spring).
Notes: Willow as flowing hair that only the wind can lift and comb.

Poem: 天は沖地は磯なれや霧の海
Romaji:
ten wa oki
chi wa iso nare ya
kiri no umi
My translation:
the sky is open sea
the earth is rocky shore—
a sea of fog between
Kigo: 霧 【きり】 kiri, autumn mist / fog [see note "On Haze, Mist, Fog"] (all autumn).
Notes: The fog-sea evokes the liminal boundary between sky and earth. Spring sea fog blurs the horizon.

Poem: ながめしは野菊のくきのはじめ哉
Romaji:
nagame shi wa
nogiku no kuki no
hajime kana
My translation:
what I have gazed upon:
the very beginning
of a wild chrysanthemum stalk
Kigo: 野菊 【のぎく】 nogiku, wild chrysanthemum(s)/aster(s) [any of several species of wild chrysanthemums or asters with thin-petalled, single white flowers with yellow centers] (mid autumn).
Notes: ながめし (nagameshi) = that which I have long gazed upon. The first stalk of a wild chrysanthemum observed closely.

Poem: 乗うつる人玉ならし蓮の露(「犬子(えのこ)集
Romaji:
nori utsuru
hitodama narashi
hasu no tsuyu
My translation:
transferring like a soul—
they must be will-o-the-wisps
the dew on the lotus
Kigo: 蓮 【はす】 hasu, lotus (mid summer).
Notes: 人玉 (hitodama) = will-o'-the-wisp. Dew on the lotus transfers like a wandering soul. From 犬子集 (Enokosha).

Poem: 千金をのべたか春の月の弓
Romaji:
senkin wo
nobetaka haru no
tsuki no yuki
My translation:
did it stretch out
a thousand gold coins?
the moon's bow in spring
Kigo: 春の月 【はるのつき】 haru no tsuki, spring moon (all spring).
Notes: 千金 (senkin) = a thousand gold coins. The crescent spring moon shaped like a bow stretched wide.

Poem: 水なしが花の波たつ夕あらし
Romaji:
mizu nashi ga
hana no nami tatsu 
yū arashi
My translation:
waterless place—
waves of blossoms rise
in the evening storm
Kigo: 花 【はな】 hana, (cherry) blossoms [in haiku and haikai the simple word hana 花 refers to cherry blossoms, as do all kigo listed here; but note that in Manyōshū and some other early poetry hana was understood as referring to ume 梅【うめ】plum blossoms, an early spring topic] (late spring).
Notes: Blossom waves rising in an evening storm. Water-misting landscape.

Poem: 定家にて向けむ花やはつか草
Romaji:
sadaie ni
te-mukemu hana ya
Hatsuka-gusa
My translation:
in Teika's style—
do the blossoms lean toward
the ephemeral grass?
Kigo: 花 【はな】 hana, (cherry) blossoms [in haiku and haikai the simple word hana 花 refers to cherry blossoms, as do all kigo listed here; but note that in Manyōshū and some other early poetry hana was understood as referring to ume 梅【うめ】plum blossoms, an early spring topic] (late spring).
Notes: 定家 (Teika) = Fujiwara no Teika, the great waka poet. 初草 (hatsukusa) = first young grasses of spring.

Poem: 水けぶる下にてたくやもみぢ鮒
Romaji:
mizu keburu
shita nite taku ya
Momiji-buna
My translation:
beneath the misty
waters—burning—
the maple carp
Kigo: 紅葉 【もみじ】 momiji, red (maple) leaves (all autumn).
Notes: 水けぶる (mizu keburu) = misty water. もみぢ鮒 (momiji buna) = autumn maple carp, red as autumn leaves.

Poem: ほこ長し天が下照る姫はじめ
Romaji:
hoko nagashi
ten ga shita teru
hime hajime
My translation:
spear shaft long—
the sun shines across the land
on this first day
Kigo: 姫始め 【ひめはじめ】 hime hajime, "Princess Beginning" (New Year).
Notes: 姫始め = the first rice cooking or first of the New Year; erotic/comic new-year poem.

Poem: 雨に声鬼一口か郭公
Romaji:
ame ni koe 
oni hitokuchi ka
hototogisu
My translation:
in the rain a voice—
the demon's one gulp?
the cuckoo calls
Kigo: 郭公 【ほととぎす】 hototogisu, little cuckoo (all summer).
Notes: 鬼一口 (oni hitokuchi) = the demon's single bite. The cuckoo's cry in the rain as a demon swallowing.

Poem: 花に来ぬ人笑ふらし春の山
Romaji:
hana ni konu
hito warau rashi
haru no yama
My translation:
those who don't come
for the blossoms must be laughed at—
the spring mountain
Kigo: 花 【はな】 hana, (cherry) blossoms [in haiku and haikai the simple word hana 花 refers to cherry blossoms, as do all kigo listed here; but note that in Manyōshū and some other early poetry hana was understood as referring to ume 梅【うめ】plum blossoms, an early spring topic] (late spring).
Notes: Those who do not come for the blossoms are to be pitied—the spring mountain blooms regardless.

Poem: 風をさへまねき出したる扇哉
Romaji:
kaze wo sae
maneki dashitaru
oiogi kana
My translation:
even the wind
it has beckoned forth—
a waving fan
Kigo: 扇 【おうぎ】 ōgi, folding fan (summer).
Notes: A fan beckons the wind into existence—playful personification.

Poem: 松笠や花笠となす今朝の雪
Romaji:
matsukasa ya
hanagasa to nasu
kesa no yuki
My translation:
pine cones—
turned into flower hats
by this morning's snow
Kigo: 雪 【ゆき】 yuki, snow (all winter).
Notes: 松笠 (matsukasa) = pine cones. Morning snow transforms pine cones into flower-petal hats.

Poem: 雨の親やそだつる花の子を大じ
Romaji:
ame no oya ya
sodatsuru hana no 
ko wo daiji
My translation:
the rain—a parent
nurturing the blossoms
to be cherished
Kigo: 花 【はな】 hana, (cherry) blossoms [in haiku and haikai the simple word hana 花 refers to cherry blossoms, as do all kigo listed here; but note that in Manyōshū and some other early poetry hana was understood as referring to ume 梅【うめ】plum blossoms, an early spring topic] (late spring).
Notes: Rain as nurturing parent of the blossoms. Combines natural and parental imagery.

Poem: 引きかへて蛇を人やのむ菖蒲ざけ
Romaji:
hikikaete
hebi wo hito ya nomu
shōbu zake
My translation:
transformed entirely—
do people swallow snakes
in the iris wine?
Kigo: 菖蒲酒 【しょうぶざけ】 shōbu-zake, iris-root sake (early summer).
Notes: Tango (Boys' Day, 5th day of 5th month) iris sake. Snake transformed / swallowed—festival custom of drinking medicinal sake.

Poem: おぼえぬや手の舞ひ足の文月よ
Romaji:
oboe nu ya
te no mai ashi no
fumizuki yo
My translation:
unconsciously—
hands dancing, feet moving
on this July night
Kigo: 文月 【ふみづき】 fumizuki, Seventh (Lunar) Month (late summer).
Notes: 七月 (fumizuki) = the seventh lunar month. Hands and feet moving unconsciously in the summer heat.

Poem: あぢはひはからや高麗きくの酒
Romaji:
ajiwai wa
kara ya korai
giku no sake
My translation:
the flavor—
is it bitter? Korean
chrysanthemum sake
Kigo: 菊の酒 【きくのさけ】 kiku no sake, chrysanthemum wine (mid autumn).
Notes: 高麗菊 (Kōrai giku) = Korean chrysanthemum. Chrysanthemum wine drunk at the Double Nine festival (重陽 chōyō).

Poem: 春ながの年の頭や福禄寿
Romaji:
haru-naga no
toshi no kashira ya
fukurokuju
My translation:
spring days are long
head of the year—
God of Wealth, Happiness, Longevity
Kigo: 春なが (spring days are long), 日永 【ひなが】 hinaga, day(s) lengthening (all spring).

Poem: ね入ばなの園や萌黄の蚊やの内
Romaji:
neiribana no
sono ya moegi no
kaya no uchi
My translation:
drifting off, sleep blossoms 
orchard—inside a vernal green
mosquito net
Kigo: 蚊や (), 蚊帳 【かや】 kaya, mosquito net (all summer).

Poem: 花に蝶のまふは神楽ぞいせ桜
Romaji:
hana no chō no 
mau ha kagura zo 
ise-zakura
My translation:
butterflies dance
the Kagura among the blossoms
here on Ise Hill
Kigo: 花 【はな】 hana, (cherry) blossoms [in haiku and haikai the simple word hana 花 refers to cherry blossoms, as do all kigo listed here; but note that in Manyōshū and some other early poetry hana was understood as referring to ume 梅【うめ】plum blossoms, an early spring topic] (late spring).
Notes: Butterflies dancing among blossoms compared to shrine maidens performing kagura. 伊勢桜 = Ise cherry.

Poem: 稲妻の面影見てやよばひ星
Romaji:
inazuma no
omokage mite ya
Yobaiboshi
My translation:
to view his wife's
vestige 
the star wanders
Kigo: 稲妻 【いなずま】 inazuma, lightning (all autumn).
Notes: 稲妻 (inazuma) = lightning; 流れ星 = shooting star. Lightning seen in a shooting star.

Poem: 馬合羽雪打ちはらふ袖もなし
Romaji:
umagappa 
yuki ichi harau
sode mo nashi
My translation:
my riding jacket 
hasn't even sleeves
to brush the snow off of
Kigo: 雪 【ゆき】 yuki, snow (all winter).
Notes: 馬合羽 (uma-kappa) = horse-riding rain cape. Riding through snow with no sleeves to brush it off.

Poem: 帰らずば都の人やうれしかり
Romaji:
kaerazuba
miyako no hito zo
ureshi-kari
My translation:
if you don't return
how glad the capital's people
would be for you
Kigo: 帰雁 【かえるかり】 kaeru kari, returning geese (mid spring).
Notes: If the geese do not return north, the people of the capital might be relieved—playful inversion.

Poem: 柴にまた餅花咲くや二度の春
Romaji:
shiba ni mata
mochibana saku ya
nido no haru
My translation:
on the brushwood again—
mochi flowers bloom
a second spring
Kigo: 餅花 【もちばな】 mochihana, rice-cake flowers (New Year).
Notes: Mochi flowers (rice-cake ornaments on branches) bloom again. "A second spring."

Poem: 花にあふぞ浮木の亀の一万句
Romaji:
hana ni asobu
fuboku no kame no
ichimanku
My translation:
meeting blossoms—
like the turtle on the floating log
at ten thousand verses
Kigo: 花 【はな】 hana, (cherry) blossoms [in haiku and haikai the simple word hana 花 refers to cherry blossoms, as do all kigo listed here; but note that in Manyōshū and some other early poetry hana was understood as referring to ume 梅【うめ】plum blossoms, an early spring topic] (late spring).
Notes: 浮木の亀 (ukigi no kame) = the turtle on a floating log—a Buddhist metaphor for rare encounters. Here at 10,000 verses.

Poem: 福の神を今日乗せ来るや午の年
Romaji:
fuku no kami 
wo kyō nose-kuru ya
uma no toshi
My translation:
the god of fortune—
ride him here today!
the Year of the Horse
Kigo: 午の年 【うまのとし】 uma no toshi, Year of the Horse (New Year).
Notes: 福の神 (fuku no kami) = the god of fortune, associated with New Year celebrations.

Poem: 春永といふやことばのかざり縄
Romaji:
harunaga to  
ufu ya kotoba no
kazari nawa
My translation:
draping the verbal garland  
of “the abiding spring”
like a sacred straw hawser
Kigo: abiding spring

Poem: 餅花をけふや宰府の神のぬさ
Romaji:
ten mo hana ni
weeru ka kumo no
midareashi
My translation:
dumpling blossoms
will be, today, here in Dazai
my Shinto wand
Kigo: dumpling blossoms
Notes: References Hyakunin ishu 24 by Sugawara no Michizane. 餅花 is a decoration/toy made with mochi on a stick that looks like a willow.
NKBZ:
This time around
I couldn’t even bring the sacred streamers
—Offering Hill—
but if this brocade of leaves
is to the gods’ liking….
俳句大観:
Kono tabi wa
Nusa mo toriaezu
Tamukeyama
Momiji no nishiki
Kami no mani mani
名歌名句辞典:
このたびは 
幣もとりあへず 
手向山 
紅葉のにしき 
神のまにまに

Poem: かをり来て目に酢ぞたまる梅の花
Romaji:
kaori kite
me ni su zo tamaru
ume no hana
My translation:
the scent wafts over
and its sour tang irritates my eyes
plum blossoms
Kigo: 梅 【うめ】 ume, （sometimes むめ mume）, plum (blossoms) [technically, the "Japanese apricot", Prunus mume; but this has almost always been translated "plum" for literary purposes] (early spring).
Notes: Based on a a Wakan roei shu poem by Michizane

Poem: 松風の琴の唱歌や蝉のこゑ
Romaji:
matsukaze no
koto no shōga ya
semi no koe
My translation:
pining wind’s
harp notes accompanied by
the cry of cicadas
Kigo: cicadas

Poem: 霧の海の底なる月はくらげ哉
Romaji:
kiri no umi no
sokonaru tsuki wa
kurage naka
My translation:
at the bottom
of an ocean of fog, the moon, darkly 
like a jellyfish
Kigo: Moon
Notes: くらげ is a soft pun on darkly

Poem: あらはれて見えよ芭蕉の雪女
Romaji:
arawarete
mieyo bashō no
Yukionna
My translation:
appear and
show yourself banana
snow woman
Kigo: snow woman
Notes: Banana woman from the Noh play Basho mixed with Yukionna. Saying Banana in the snow, something that should not exist.

Poem: 絵に似たる顔やヘマムシ夜半の月
Romaji:
e ni nitaru
kao ya hemamushi
yowa no tsuki
My translation:
like a portrait  
of a hemamushi face—
midnight moon
Kigo: Moon
Notes: https://www.library.metro.tokyo.jp/collection/features/digital_showcase/057/10/index.html  ヘマムシ入道昔話　山東京伝著　歌川国直画　六巻二冊　文化10年（1813）刊　和泉屋市兵衛　請求記号：函97-2 light pun on hemamushiyo and yowa

Poem: 源氏ならで上下に祝ふ若菜かな
Romaji:
genji narade
jōge ni iwau
wakana kana
My translation:
it ain't Genji
but the halves & have nots are
celebrating “Young Herbs”
Kigo: Young Herbs
Other translation:
Unlike in the Genji Monogatari,
The wakana is eaten felicitously 
     Without “first and last.” Blyth, History

Poem: 声なくて花や梢の高笑ひ
Romaji:
koe nakute
hana ya kozue no
taka-warai
My translation:
without a voice, 
the blossoms boughs ring 
with high laughter
Kigo: Blossoms

Poem: 月影をくみこぼしけり手水鉢
Romaji:
tsukikage wo
kumi-koboshi keri
chōubachi
My translation:
Scooping up the moon
In the wash-basin,
      And spilling it.
Kigo: Moon

Poem: 花ひとつたもとにすがる童かな
Romaji:
hana hitotsu
tamoto ni sugaru
warabe kana
My translation:
one bough of blossoms
clinging to my sleeve sleeve 
a child
Kigo: Blossoms

Poem: ほころぶや尻も結ばぬ糸桜
Romaji:
hokorobu ya
shiri mo musubanu
ito-zakura
My translation:
coming apart at the seems—
like a stitch with its end unfastened 
thread cherry
Kigo: thread cherry
Notes: 尻も結ばぬ is a saying meaning something slovenly
Other translation:
Brusting,
The ends cannot be tied,—
     Thread-like cherry trees in bloom.

Poem: 天も花にゑへるか雲のみだれあし
Romaji:
ten mo hana ni
weeru ka kumo no
midareashi
My translation:
even the sky
drunk on on blossoms? the clouds
stumble on wobbly legs
Kigo: Blossoms
Notes: 天酔于花。桃李盛也 wakan roei shu; 「花時天似酔序」冒頭  菅原道真『和漢朗詠集』39

Poem: 月花の三句めをいま知る世かな
Romaji:
tsuki hana no
sanku-me wa ima
shiru yo kana
My translation:
The moon, and the cherry-blossoms,—
Now I know, in this world,
     What the third verse is!
Kigo: 月 【つき】 tsuki, moon (mid autumn).
Notes: 月花 (tsuki hana) = moon and blossoms, the canonical pair of seasonal beauty. The third verse (三句目) that combines them.

Poem: 颯々のすずしさや此の松の声
Romaji:
satsusatsu no
suzushisa ya kono
matsu no koe
My translation:
murmuring  
coolness— this 
pining voice
Kigo: 涼しさ 【すずしさ】 suzushisa, coolness (all summer).
Notes: 颯々のすずしさ puns cool with bell

Poem: 篝火も蛍もひかる源氏かな
Romaji:
kagaribi mo 
hotaru mo hikaru
genji kana
My translation:
Cresset Fires and
Fireflies shining 
Genji
Kigo: 蛍 【ほたる】 hotaru, firefly / fireflies (mid summer).
Notes: 篝火 (kagaribi) = bonfire/torch; 蛍 = fireflies. Both illuminate Genji scenes. Reference to The Tale of Genji chapters "Fireflies" and "Torchlight."

Poem: 散る音も色もさらさの紅葉哉
Romaji:
chiru oto mo
iro mo sarasa mo
momiji kana
My translation:
sound of scattering
and hue as well, chintz calico
autumn leaves
Kigo: 紅葉 【もみじ】 momiji, red (maple) leaves (all autumn).
Notes: さらさ (sarasa) = a kind of calico/printed cloth. Autumn leaves scatter with the sound and color of printed fabric.

Poem: やあしばらく花に対して鐘撞く事
Romaji:
ya shibara ku
hana ni taishite
kane tsuku koto
My translation:
wait—hold on!
facing the blossoms
strike the bell
Kigo: 花 【はな】 hana, (cherry) blossoms [in haiku and haikai the simple word hana 花 refers to cherry blossoms, as do all kigo listed here; but note that in Manyōshū and some other early poetry hana was understood as referring to ume 梅【うめ】plum blossoms, an early spring topic] (late spring).
Notes: やあしばらく (yā shibaraku) = "Wait! Just a moment!"—a famous Kabuki phrase. Striking the bell while facing the blossoms.

Poem: 秋や今朝一足に知るのごひ縁
Romaji:
aki ya kesa
hito ashi ni shiru
nogoi en
My translation:
autumn this morning—
known in a single step
on the wiped veranda
Kigo: 秋 【あき】 aki, autumn.
Notes: 一足 (hitoashi) = a single step. Autumn known in an instant—the first cool morning felt stepping onto the freshly wiped veranda.

Poem: さほひめやかくる柳の長かもじ
Romaji:
saho hime ya
kakuru yanagi no
naga kamoji
My translation:
The goddess Sao—
hidden in the willow,
her long hair.
Kigo: 柳 【やなぎ】 yanagi, willow(s) / weeping willow(s) (late spring).
Notes: 佐保姫 (Saho-hime) = goddess of spring. The willow trailing long tresses like a woman's hair.

Poem: 鶯が引琴の緒や糸柳
Romaji:
uguisu ga
hiki koto no o ya
itoyanagi
My translation:
The warbler
plays the harp strings
of a thread willow.
Kigo: 柳 【やなぎ】 yanagi, willow(s) / weeping willow(s) (late spring). / 鶯 【うぐいす】 uguisu, bush warbler [Cettia diphone; sometimes translated as "nightingale" (Luscinia megarhynchos), since it is a small songbird and occupies a position in Japanese literature similar to that of the nightingale in European literature] (all spring).
Notes: 糸柳 (ito-yanagi) = thread willow, a variety whose drooping branches resemble koto strings.

Poem: 観音のちからや見するこぶ柳
Romaji:
Kannon no
chikara ya misuru
kobu yanagi
My translation:
Kannon’s
strength seen in
a swelling willow.
Kigo: 柳 【やなぎ】 yanagi, willow(s) / weeping willow(s) (late spring).
Notes: 観音 (Kannon) = Bodhisattva of Compassion. The gnarled willow revealed as a spiritual wonder.

Poem: 春の日の威光をみする雪間哉
Romaji:
haru no hi no
ikō wo misuru
yukima kana
My translation:
the spring sun
shows its authority
in in gaps in snow
Kigo: spring sun

Poem: 料理して今日もくらしつ桜だひ
Romaji:
ryōri shite
kyō mo kurashitsu
sakura-dai
My translation:
cooking
today, again, passing the day
cherry sea bream
Kigo: cherry sea bream
Notes: Are the officials of the hundredfold palace at leisure, then? They stick cherry blossoms in their hair and spend the day, agian, in play. Shinkokin 1:104 Momoshiki no I Omiyahito wa I Itoma are ya I Sakura kazashite I Kyo mo kurashitsu

Poem: 落汐に鳴門やつれて暮の春
Romaji:
ochi shio ni
Naruto yasurete
kure no haru
My translation:
at the ebbing tide
Naruto grows weary—
spring's end
Kigo: 暮の春 【くれのはる】 kure no haru, end of spring / late spring (late spring).
Notes: 鳴門 (Naruto) = the famous whirlpool strait. The ebb tide leaves Naruto diminished at spring's end.

Poem: しばし見む蟻の通路蝉のから
Romaji:
shibashi mimu
ari no kayoiji
semi no kara
Kigo: 蝉の殻 【せみのから】 semi no kara, cicada shell/husk (late summer/early autumn).
Notes: 蟻 (ari) = ants; 蝉のから = empty cicada shell. A moment of quiet observation in the summer-turning-autumn garden.

Poem: 順礼の棒ばかり行く夏野かな
Romaji:
junrei no
bo bakari yuku
natsuno kana
My translation:
nothing but their staffs
going on ahead—
pilgrims through the summer fields
Kigo: 夏野 【なつの】 natsuno, summer field(s) (all summer).
Notes: 順礼 (junrei) = pilgrims. Only their staffs visible above the tall summer grasses—a haiku of absences.

Poem: 野に嬉し虫待宵の小行灯
Romaji:
no ni ureshi
mushi machi yoi no
koandon
My translation:
how glad in the fields—
waiting for insects
the small lantern at dusk
Kigo: 虫 【むし】 mushi, insect(s) [usually plural, for their singing] (all autumn). / 待宵 【まつよい】 matsuyoi, the eve before the full moon (mid autumn).
Notes: 待宵 (matsuyoi) = the night before the harvest moon. Small lantern in the fields waiting for insects' songs.

Poem: 御座舟や霧間もれたる須磨明石
Romaji:
gozabune ya
kiri ma moretaru
Suma Akashi
My translation:
the royal barge—
through gaps in the fog
Suma, Akashi
Kigo: 霧 【きり】 kiri, autumn mist / fog [see note "On Haze, Mist, Fog"] (all autumn).
Notes: 御座舟 (gozabune) = a royal/official barge. Through breaks in the autumn fog, the storied shores of Suma and Akashi appear.

Poem: ふる雪は京おしろいとみやこ哉
Romaji:
furu yuki wa
kyo oshiroi to
miyako kana
My translation:
falling snow
is the capital's face powder—
such a city
Kigo: 雪 【ゆき】 yuki, snow (all winter).
Notes: 京おしろい (kyō oshiroi) = Kyoto face powder, famous for its whiteness. Snow as the capital's cosmetic.

Poem: ながむとて花にもいたし首の骨
Romaji:
nagamu to te  
hana ni mo itashi     
kubi no hone
My translation:
staring at
the blossoms it hurts
my neck bone
Kigo: 花 【はな】 hana, (cherry) blossoms [in haiku and haikai the simple word hana 花 refers to cherry blossoms, as do all kigo listed here; but note that in Manyōshū and some other early poetry hana was understood as referring to ume 梅【うめ】plum blossoms, an early spring topic] (late spring).
Notes: Variant of Row 151. Gazing at blossoms until the neck aches—comic devotion to flower-viewing.

Poem: さればここに談林の木あり梅の花
Romaji:
sareba kokoni     
danrin no ki ari   
ume no hana
My translation:
and here stands
the Danrin tree of haiku—
plum blossoms
Kigo: 梅 【うめ】 ume, （sometimes むめ mume）, plum (blossoms) [technically, the "Japanese apricot", Prunus mume; but this has almost always been translated "plum" for literary purposes] (early spring).
Notes: Danrin school (談林) haiku. Here stands the Danrin plum tree. Sōin's manifesto poem for his school.

Poem: ながむとて花にもいたし頸の骨
My translation:
gazing so long
at the blossoms—
neck bones aching
Kigo: 花 【はな】 hana, (cherry) blossoms [in haiku and haikai the simple word hana 花 refers to cherry blossoms, as do all kigo listed here; but note that in Manyōshū and some other early poetry hana was understood as referring to ume 梅【うめ】plum blossoms, an early spring topic] (late spring).
Notes: Shortened variant of Row 149. 首の骨 (kubi no hone) / 頸の骨 = neck bone.

Poem: 今こんといひしばかりの料理かな
My translation:
"I'll come soon," you said—
and then nothing but that
for dinner
Kigo: 料理 【りょうり】 ryōri, cooking / meal.
Notes: "I'll come right away"—a laconic poem about a guest who never comes, leaving only the meal.

Poem: 里人のわたり候かはしの霜
My translation:
has a villager
crossed the bridge?—frost
covers the river
Kigo: 霜 【しも】 shimo, frost (mid winter).
Notes: Has a villager crossed? The frosted bridge as evidence of passage, or absence of it.

Poem: 若竹の心かけ樋や軒のつま
Romaji:
waka-take no
kokoro-kake hi ya
noki no tsuma
My translation:
a bamboo pipe
for the young shoot—dripping
from the eave's edge
Kigo: 若竹 【わかたけ】 wakatake, young bamboo (mid summer).
Notes: pun: kokorokake = "hanging one's heart on" and 懸樋 (kakehihi) = hanging water pipe; 軒のつま = eave's edge / wife at the eave.

Poem: 鶯の歌や書ぞめ鳥のあと
Romaji:
uguisu no
uta ya kakizome
tori no ato
My translation:
taking the warbler's song
for the first calgraphy of the year
like bird tracks
Kigo: 書初 【かきぞめ】 kakizome, first calligraphy [of the New Year] (New Year).

Poem: 咲くえだの夭々たるや桃の酒
Romaji:
saku eda no
yōyōtaru ya
momo no sake
My translation:
the flowering boughs
pictured so youthfully—
pulm sake
Kigo: 桃の酒 【もものさけ】 momo no sake, peach wine (early spring, 3rd Month).
Notes: 夭夭 (yōyō) = young and flourishing (from the Classic of Poetry). Peach blossom wine at the Dolls Festival.

Poem: さほ姫のかく恋草や土の筆
Romaji:
sahohime no
kaku koe-gusa ya
tsuchi no fude
My translation:
Princes Sao 
expresses her weedy love
with horsetail shoot
Kigo: 土筆 【つくし】 tsukushi, horsetail shoot(s) [the reproductive shoots of Equisetum arvense] (mid spring).

Poem: 若竹の心かけ樋や軒のつま
Romaji:
waka-take no
kokoro-kake hi ya
noki no tsuma
My translation:
the consideration to 
mount a young bamboo gutter—
on the eaves
Kigo: 若竹 【わかたけ】 wakatake, young bamboo (mid summer).
Notes: pun: kokorokake=kakehi; tsu as egde and wife

Poem: そちは何をなげきの森のよるの蝉
Romaji:
sochi wa nani wo
nageki no mori no
yoru no semi
My translation:
what is it you grieve
in the forest of sorrow
cicada of the night?
Kigo: 蝉 【せみ】 semi, cicada (all autumn).
Notes: 嘆きの森 (nageki no mori) = forest of sorrow. The cicada asked what it grieves—addressed as a suffering soul.

Poem: こもよみこ餅煮んとつむ若菜哉
Romaji:
komo yo mi ko
mochi ni n to tsumu
wakana kana
My translation:
"dear child with your basket"—
gathering greens to make
festival mochi
Kigo: 若菜 【わかな】 wakana, young herbs (New Year / early spring).
Notes: こもよみこ (komo yo mi ko) = opening of the Man'yōshū poem no. 1. Young herbs gathered to cook into mochi cakes.

Poem: これはこれはとばかり花の吉野
Romaji:
kore wa kore wa to 
bakari hona no
yoshino yama
My translation:
this is it, this is it!
that's the only thing to say
Mt. Yoshino
Kigo: 花 【はな】 hana, (cherry) blossoms [in haiku and haikai the simple word hana 花 refers to cherry blossoms, as do all kigo listed here; but note that in Manyōshū and some other early poetry hana was understood as referring to ume 梅【うめ】plum blossoms, an early spring topic] (late spring).
Notes: これはこれは (kore wa kore wa) = "Oh my, oh my!"—speechless before the blossoms of Yoshino. Famous exclamatory haiku.

Poem: 歌いくさ文武二道の蛙かな
Romaji:
uta ikusa
bunbu nido no
kawazu kana
My translation:
the poetry war—
a frog of two ways:
pen and sword
Kigo: 蛙 【かわず】 kawazu, （かはづ）, frog(s) [note that this is a literary word] (all spring).
Notes: 歌いくさ (uta ikusa) = poetry battle. 文武二道 (bunbu nidō) = the two paths of letters and arms. The frog masters both.

Poem: 夏迄もとつておきなの氷室哉
Romaji:
natsu made mo
totte oki nao no
himuro kana
My translation:
kept right through
to summer—the old man's
ice-house
Kigo: 氷室 【ひむろ】 himuro, ice house / ice cellar (mid summer).
Notes: 氷室 (himuro) = a pit where winter ice was preserved for summer use. The old man (おきな) keeps ice through the heat.

Poem: 口ばしを雲にかけぬる雲雀かな
Romaji:
kuchibashi wo
kumo ni kake nuru
hibare kana
My translation:
beak stretched up
lodged in the clouds—
the skylark
Kigo: 雲雀 【ひばり】 hibari, skylark [Alauda arvensis] (all spring).
Notes: The skylark's beak seems to reach the clouds. 口ばし (kuchibashi) = beak, literally "mouth chopstick."

Poem: 春立つや人の心をうご霞
Romaji:
haru tatsu ya
hito no kokoro wo
ugo kasumi
My translation:
spring arrives—
moving the human heart
the haze stirs
Kigo: 春立つ 【はるたつ】 haru tatsu, spring begins (early spring).
Notes: 霞 (kasumi) = spring haze. Spring stirs human hearts as the haze stirs in the landscape.

Poem: 月の貌やふけてもわかし十八夜
Romaji:
tsuki no kao ya
fukete mo wakashi
juhachiya
My translation:
the moon's face—
even deep in the night, young
on the eighteenth night
Kigo: 月 【つき】 tsuki, moon (mid autumn).
Notes: 十八夜 (jūhachiya) = the eighteenth night of the lunar month. The moon still young-looking even late in the night.

Poem: 独寝も肌やあはする紙ぶすま
Romaji:
hitori ne mo
hada ya awasuru
kami buton
My translation:
sleeping alone—
even skin touching
the paper coverlet
Kigo: 紙ぶすま 【かみぶすま】 kami-buton, paper coverlet (winter).
Notes: 独寝 (hitori-ne) = sleeping alone. Even a paper coverlet feels like warmth when sleeping alone in the cold.

Poem: 名乗りけり大をんじゃうしほととぎす
My translation:
it proclaimed its name—
what a mighty voice—
the cuckoo
Kigo: 郭公 【ほととぎす】 hototogisu, little cuckoo (all summer).
Notes: 大音声 (daionshō) = a mighty voice. The cuckoo "proclaims its name"—an image from Noh and warrior tales.

Poem: 夏痩と答へてあとは涙かな
My translation:
summer leanness—
I answered and after that
only tears
Kigo: 夏痩せ 【なつやせ】 natsuyase, summer weight loss (all summer).
Notes: Kigin's version of the "summer thinness" motif. Answering honestly leads to tears of sympathy.

Poem: まざまざといますがごとし魂祭
My translation:
so vividly
as if here and present—
the spirit festival
Kigo: 魂祭 【たままつり】 tama-matsuri, spirit / Bon festival (mid autumn).
Notes: 魂祭 = the Bon festival. The spirit appears so vividly it seems still present—ghostly vision at the festival.

Poem: 腰をふる門やかぶきもの
My translation:
hips swaying
at the gate—the dandy
passing by
Kigo: 郭公 【ほととぎす】 hototogisu, little cuckoo (all summer).
Notes: 傾城 (keisei) = a courtesan. The dandy swaying past the gate in summer heat.

Poem: 身がろげに舞ふ羽づかひや趙飛燕
My translation:
light as a feather
her dancing sleeves—
Zhào Fēiyàn
Kigo: 花 【はな】 hana, (cherry) blossoms [in haiku and haikai the simple word hana 花 refers to cherry blossoms, as do all kigo listed here; but note that in Manyōshū and some other early poetry hana was understood as referring to ume 梅【うめ】plum blossoms, an early spring topic] (late spring).
Notes: 趙飛燕 (Zhào Fēiyàn) = a famous Han dynasty dancer, so light she could dance on a palm.

Poem: 桃の酒いつみかはけふ三かのはら
My translation:
the peach blossom wine—
how many cups on
this third-month plain?
Kigo: 桃の酒 【もものさけ】 momo no sake, peach wine (early spring).
Notes: 三かのはら (mika no hara) = the plain of Mika, a famous utamakura. Third-month peach wine festival.

Poem: 匂ひみちぬ天も地もとの花ざかり
My translation:
fragrance fills all—
heaven and earth alike
at full blossom
Kigo: 花 【はな】 hana, (cherry) blossoms [in haiku and haikai the simple word hana 花 refers to cherry blossoms, as do all kigo listed here; but note that in Manyōshū and some other early poetry hana was understood as referring to ume 梅【うめ】plum blossoms, an early spring topic] (late spring).
Notes: 天も地も (ten mo chi mo) = heaven and earth alike. Fragrance completely filling all space at peak blossom.

Poem: 地主からは木の間の花の都哉
My translation:
from Jizhu's grounds—
between the trees, the blossoms
of the capital
Kigo: 花 【はな】 hana, (cherry) blossoms [in haiku and haikai the simple word hana 花 refers to cherry blossoms, as do all kigo listed here; but note that in Manyōshū and some other early poetry hana was understood as referring to ume 梅【うめ】plum blossoms, an early spring topic] (late spring).
Notes: 地主 (jishu) = Jizhu Gongen, tutelary deity of Kiyomizudera, celebrated for cherry blossoms.

Poem: はら筋をよりてや笑ふ絲ざくら
My translation:
drawing out the belly
laughing, twisted—
the weeping cherry
Kigo: 糸桜 【いとざくら】 ito-zakura, weeping cherry (mid spring).
Notes: 腹筋 (hara suji) = belly muscles; よりて (yorite) = twisted/wrung out. The weeping cherry makes one double over laughing.

Poem: めづらしや二四八のほととぎす
My translation:
how rare—
the cuckoo of
the twenty-fourth day
Kigo: 郭公 【ほととぎす】 hototogisu, little cuckoo (all summer).
Notes: 二四八 (ni-shi-hachi) may refer to a particular date or count. The cuckoo appearing on an unusual day.

Poem: 鴈は文字おほふや霧のゐんふたぎ
Kigo: 雁 【かり】 kari, (wild) goose/geese [usually Anser species, though Branta are included] (late autumn).
Notes: 雁 (kari) = wild geese in the autumn sky. Kigin's verse on the geese and writing—霧 (kiri) = fog.

Poem: 年の内へふみこむ春の日足哉
Kigo: 春の日足 【はるのひあし】 haru no hiashi, lengthening spring days (all spring).
Notes: 年の内 (toshi no uchi) = within the old year. Spring's lengthening days arriving before New Year's has officially ended.

Poem: 一僕とぼくぼくあるく花見かな
Romaji:
hitoshimobe to
boku boku aruku
hanami kana
My translation:
just one attendant
and I plod along
blossom viewing
Kigo: 花見 【はなみ】 hanami, (cherry) blossom viewing (late spring).
Notes: One attendant plodding along at a leisurely blossom-viewing pace. Kigin's self-portrait as a humble viewer.

Poem: 夏痩と答へてあとは涙かな
Romaji:
natsuyase to
kotaete ato wa
namida kana
My translation:
summer thinness—
that's my answer, and after
only tears remain
Kigo: 夏痩せ 【なつやせ】 natsuyase, summer thinness (all summer).
Notes: Duplicate of Row 171.

Poem: くず水や花の下ゆく吉野川
Romaji:
kuzumizu ya
hana no shita yuku
Yoshino-gawa
My translation:
arrowroot water—
beneath the blossoms flows
the Yoshino River
Kigo: 花 【はな】 hana, (cherry) blossoms [in haiku and haikai the simple word hana 花 refers to cherry blossoms, as do all kigo listed here; but note that in Manyōshū and some other early poetry hana was understood as referring to ume 梅【うめ】plum blossoms, an early spring topic] (late spring).
Notes: Variant of Row 182. くず水 (kuzumizu) = arrowroot water, clear and cool, flowing under the blossoms of Yoshino.

Poem: 秋風の姿なりけりむらすすき
Romaji:
aki kaze no
sugata nari keri
mura susuki
My translation:
the form of the autumn wind—
that is what it is:
clusters of pampas grass
Kigo: 秋風 【あきかぜ】 akikaze, autumn breeze / autumn wind [carries with it the sound of rustling leaves] (all autumn).
Notes: 村薄 (murasusuki) = clumps of pampas grass. The autumn wind's form made visible through swaying pampas grass.

Poem: 一僕とぼくぼくありく花見哉
Romaji:
hitoshimobe to
boku boku ariku
hanami kana
My translation:
with just one servant
I plod plod along
for blossom viewing
Kigo: 花見 【はなみ】 hanami, (cherry) blossom viewing (late spring).
Notes: Variant of Rows 182/184.

Poem: 地主からは木の間の花の都かな
Romaji:
jishu kara wa
koma no hana no
miyako kana
My translation:
from Jizhu's grounds
between the tree-gap blossoms—
the capital
Kigo: 花 【はな】 hana, (cherry) blossoms [in haiku and haikai the simple word hana 花 refers to cherry blossoms, as do all kigo listed here; but note that in Manyōshū and some other early poetry hana was understood as referring to ume 梅【うめ】plum blossoms, an early spring topic] (late spring).
Notes: Variant of Row 177.

Poem: 腰をふる門の柳やかぶきもの
Romaji:
koshi wo furu
kado no yanagi ya
kabuki mono
My translation:
swaying at the hips
at the gate, the willow—
a dandy strolling
Kigo: 柳 【やなぎ】 yanagi, willow(s) / weeping willow(s) (late spring).
Notes: Variant of Row 173. The gate willow swaying like a kabukimono (dandy) at the hips.

Poem: まざまざといますが如し魂祭
Romaji:
mazamaza to
imasu ga gotoshi
tamamatsuri
My translation:
so vivid and clear
as if still present—
the souls' festival
Kigo: 魂祭 【たままつり】 tama-matsuri, spirit / Bon festival (mid autumn).
Notes: Variant of Row 172. The spirit appearing so vividly at the Bon festival.

Poem: 時雨るるや黒木積む屋の窓あかり
Kigo: 時雨 【しぐれ】 shigure, (winter) shower/drizzle (early winter).
Notes: 黒木 (kuroki) = black/charcoal wood. Window glowing from stacked wood in the drizzle—warmth within the dark.

Original source: 『去来発句集』『貞享三年其角歳旦帖』（
Modern Source: 日本古典文学全集 (256) 蝸牛俳句文庫31 (4)

Poem: 手をはなつ中に落ちけり朧月
Romaji:
te wo hanatu
naka ni ochi keri
oborozuki
My translation:
letting go the hand—
into that space between
falls the hazy moon
Kigo: 朧月 【おぼろづき】 oborozuki, hazy moon (all spring).
Notes: 手をはなつ (te wo hanatu) = releasing the hand. The hazy spring moon falls into the space between parted hands.

Poem: 元日や家に譲りの太刀帯かん
Romaji: ganjitsu ya ie ni yuzuri no tachi hakan
My translation:
first day-
the sword past down in my family
I will wear
Kigo: 元日 【がんじつ】 ganjitsu, New Year's Day (New Year).
Notes: 家に譲りの太刀 (ie ni yuzuri no tachi) = the inherited sword of the house. Wearing the ancestral blade on New Year's morning.

Poem: うめ一輪一りんほどのあたゝかさ
Romaji: ume ichirin chirin hodo no atatakasa
My translation:
one branch of plum
one branch worth of
warmth
Kigo: cold plum

Poem: わびぬれば身は埓もなきもぞくかな
Romaji:
wabi nureba
mi wa rato mo naki
mozoku kana
My translation:
grown so forlorn—
my body unbounded
like mozuku seaweed
Kigo: もぞく mozoku, mozuku seaweed (summer).
Notes: 侘びぬれば (wabi nureba) = having grown forlorn. The self compared to unmoored mozuku seaweed.

Poem: ながながと川一筋や雪の原
Romaji:
naganaga to
kawa hitosuji ya
yuki no hara
My translation:
long and long
the single river flows
across the snowy plain
Kigo: snow

Poem: 軽口にまかせてなけよほととぎす 　　　（任口）
Romaji:
karuguchi ni 
makasete nakeyo 
hototogisu
My translation:
just adlib
your song
cuckoo
Kigo: 郭公 【ほととぎす】 hototogisu, little cuckoo (all summer).
Notes: 軽口 (karukuchi) = light talk / witty banter. Even the cuckoo is allowed to cry as it pleases—lighthearted.

Poem: 何と世に桜も咲かず下戸ならば
Romaji:
nani to yo ni   
sakura sakazu  
geko naraba
My translation:
if only in  this world
the cherry trees did not bloom
and one was a teetotaler
Kigo: 花 【はな】 hana, (cherry) blossoms [in haiku and haikai the simple word hana 花 refers to cherry blossoms, as do all kigo listed here; but note that in Manyōshū and some other early poetry hana was understood as referring to ume 梅【うめ】plum blossoms, an early spring topic] (late spring).
Notes: 下戸 (geko) = a non-drinker. What kind of world if cherry blossoms didn't bloom and no one drank?

Poem: 大晦日定めなき世のさだめ哉
Romaji:
ōmisoka
sadame naki yo no 
sadame kana
My translation:
New Years Eve
in our unsettled world
is the only constant
Kigo: New Years Eve
Notes:
debts are payed on new years
commoner viewpoint

Poem: 春立つや新年ふるき小目五升
Romaji:
haru tasu 
shinnen furuki 
go-shō
My translation:
spring begins―
for the new year, five pints
of old rice
Kigo: Beginning of spring

Poem: 春雨や蜂の巣つたふ屋根の漏
Romaji:
harusame ya
hachi no su tsutau
yane no mori
My translation:
spring rain―
along a bee nest
the roof leak
Kigo: spring rain

Poem: 六月や峯に雲置あらし山
Romaji:
roku-gatsu ya
mine ni kumo oku
arashi yama
My translation:
the sixth month-
a cloud set on its peak
Mt. Storm
Kigo: 六月 【ろくがつ】 rokugatsu, Sixth Month (mid summer).
Notes: 嵐山 (Arashiyama) = Storm Mountain near Kyoto. Summer storm clouds building on the peak.

Romaji:
araumi ya
sado ni yokotau
Amanogawa
My translation:
The rough sea—
Extending toward Sado Isle,
The Milky Way.
Kigo:
Summer
夏 natsu
Other translation:
the sixth month --
with clouds laid on its summit
Mount-Arashi 
Tr. Ueda Makoto

Poem: 甲比丹もくばはせけり君が春
Romaji:
kapitan mo
tsukuba hase keri
kimi ga haru
Kigo: 君が春 【きみがはる】 kimi ga haru, the lord's New Year (New Year).
Notes: 甲比丹 (kapitan) = Dutch East India Company captain in Nagasaki. Even a foreign captain bows to the Japanese New Year.

Poem: よく見ればなづな花咲く垣根哉
Romaji:
yoku mireba
nazuna hanasaku
kakine kana
My translation:
look closely:
the shepherd's purse is
flowering at the hedge
Kigo: 薺 【なずな】 nazuna, shepherd's purse [Capsella bursa-pastoris] (all spring).
Notes: よく見れば (yoku mireba) = if you look closely. Bashō's famous verse on attentiveness.
Other translation:
Looking carefully,—
There is a shepherd's-purse
	Blooming under the hedge.
Blyth, Haiku vol. 4, 981

Poem: 春まくや人さまざまも伊勢まいり
Romaji:
haru-meku ya
hito samazama no
ise-mairi
My translation:
vernal signs―
people on various 
Ise pilgramages
Kigo:
Vernal signs
春めくharu-meku

Poem: 春の日に念仏ゆるき野寺かな
Romaji:
haru no hi ni
nembutsu yuruki
no-dera kana
My translation:
on a spring day
the nembutsu chant grows languid
in a country temple
Kigo:
Spring day
 春の日 haru no hi
Modern Source:
Spring day
春の日 haru no hi

Poem: 石塔もはや苔つくや春の雨
Romaji:
sekitō
mohaya koke tsuku ya
haru no ame
My translation:
on the stone stupa
already moss grows―
spring rain
Kigo: Spring rain

Poem: 元日や家に譲りの太刀帯かん
Romaji: ganjitsu ya ie ni yuzuri no tachi hakan
My translation:
first day-
the sword past down in my family
I will wear
Kigo: 元日 【がんじつ】 ganjitsu, New Year's Day (New Year).
Notes: Variant of Row 193. Wearing the inherited sword on New Year's morning.

Poem: 花守や白き頭をつきあわせて
Romaji:
Hana mori ya   blossom guards-
 Shiroki kashira wo  poking white heads together
 Tsukiawasete   for a chat
My translation:
the blossom keeper—
two white heads
bent together
Kigo: 花 【はな】 hana, (cherry) blossoms [in haiku and haikai the simple word hana 花 refers to cherry blossoms, as do all kigo listed here; but note that in Manyōshū and some other early poetry hana was understood as referring to ume 梅【うめ】plum blossoms, an early spring topic] (late spring).
Notes: Two white-haired blossom guardians knocking heads together—tender humorous image of old age and devotion.

Poem: さほひめやかくる柳の長かもじ
Romaji:
saho hime ya
kakuru yanagi no
naga kamoji
My translation:
Saho-hime!
the willow conceals her
long streaming hair
Kigo: 柳 【やなぎ】 yanagi, willow(s) / weeping willow(s) (late spring).
Notes: Variant of Row 137. Spring rain washing and combing willow hair.

Poem: 鶯が引琴の緒や糸柳
Romaji:
uguisu ga
hiki koto no o ya
itoyanagi
My translation:
the warbler strums
the koto strings—
the thread willow
Kigo: 柳 【やなぎ】 yanagi, willow(s) / weeping willow(s) (late spring).
Notes: Variant of Row 81. Fire-rat pelt and riverside willow.

Poem: 春雨にあらいてけづれ柳がみ
Romaji:
harusame ni
araite kezure
yanagikami
My translation:
washed in spring rain
and combed through—
willow hair
Kigo: 柳 【やなぎ】 yanagi, willow(s) / weeping willow(s) (late spring).
Notes: Variant of Row 5. The gnarled willow seen as lacking power.

Poem: もえながら有るや火鼠のかは柳
Romaji:
moe nagara
aru ya hinezumi no
kawa yanagi
My translation:
burning yet surviving—
the fire-rat pelt
and riverside willow
Kigo: 柳 【やなぎ】 yanagi, willow(s) / weeping willow(s) (late spring).
Notes: Variant of Row 139. The gnarled willow revealed by Kannon's power.

Poem: 気力なしと誰かは見ましこぶ柳
Romaji:
kiryoku nashi to
dare ka wa mimashi
kobu yanagi
My translation:
lacking all vigor—
who would see that
in a gnarled willow?
Kigo: 柳 【やなぎ】 yanagi, willow(s) / weeping willow(s) (late spring).

Poem: 観音のちからや見するこぶ柳
Romaji:
Kannon no
chikara ya misuru
kobu yanagi
My translation:
by Kannon's power—
revealed to us:
the gnarled willow
Kigo: 柳 【やなぎ】 yanagi, willow(s) / weeping willow(s) (late spring).

Poem: 元日や家に譲りの太刀帯（は）かん
Romaji:
ganjitsu ya
ie ni yuzuri no
tachi hakan
My translation:
New Year's morning—
my inherited sword
worn at the waist
Kigo: 元日 【がんじつ】 ganjitsu, New Year's Day (New Year).
Notes: Variant of Row 211. Wearing the inherited sword on New Year's morning.

Poem: 鉢たたき来ぬ夜となれば朧なり
Romaji:
hachi tataki
konu yo to nareba
oboro nari
My translation:
the bowl-beaters gone
and night grown hazy—
the bowl-striking night
Kigo: 朧 【おぼろ】 oboro, misty (night) / hazy (night) [see "On Haze, Mist, Fog"] (all spring).
Notes: 鉢たたき (hachi tataki) = bowl-beaters, Buddhist mendicants. Night turning hazy as they depart.

Poem: うごくとも見えで畑打つ男かな
Romaji:
ugoku to mo
miede hata utsu
otoko kana
My translation:
seeming not to move
yet plowing the fields—
the man at work
Kigo: 畑打ち 【はたうち】 hata uchi, field plowing (spring).
Notes: The man plowing the field appears motionless—though working hard. Zen-like observation.

Poem: 花守や白き頭をつき合せ
Romaji:
hanamori ya
shiroki atama wo
tsuki awase
My translation:
blossom keepers—
their white heads
bumping together
Kigo: 花 【はな】 hana, (cherry) blossoms [in haiku and haikai the simple word hana 花 refers to cherry blossoms, as do all kigo listed here; but note that in Manyōshū and some other early poetry hana was understood as referring to ume 梅【うめ】plum blossoms, an early spring topic] (late spring).
Notes: Variant of Row 212.

Poem: 何事ぞ花見る人の長刀
Romaji:
nanigoto zo
hanami ru hito no
naginata
My translation:
what's this all about?
the long sword
of the blossom-viewer
Kigo: 花 【はな】 hana, (cherry) blossoms [in haiku and haikai the simple word hana 花 refers to cherry blossoms, as do all kigo listed here; but note that in Manyōshū and some other early poetry hana was understood as referring to ume 梅【うめ】plum blossoms, an early spring topic] (late spring).
Notes: なぎなた (naginata) = halberd. An incongruous weapon at a blossom-viewing party.

Poem: 一昨日（おととひ）はあの山こえつ花ざかり
Romaji:
ototoi wa
ano yama koetsu
hanazakari
My translation:
the day before yesterday
I crossed that mountain—
blossoms at their peak
Kigo: 花盛り 【はなざかり】 hanazakari, peak blossom (mid spring).
Notes: The day before yesterday I crossed that mountain—now at peak blossom. Journey to the blossoms.

Poem: 郭公（ほととぎす）なくや雲雀と十文字
Romaji:
hototogisu
naku ya hibari to
jumonji
My translation:
the cuckoo cries—
crossing paths with the lark
in a cross shape
Kigo: 郭公 【ほととぎす】 hototogisu, little cuckoo (all summer).
Notes: The cuckoo's cry crossing paths with the skylark's—their flight paths forming a cross (十文字) in the sky.

Poem: うの花の絶間たゝかん闇の門
Romaji:
uno hana no
tatema tatakan
yami no kado
My translation:
in the gap of deutzia
I shall knock—
the gate in darkness
Kigo: 卯の花 【うのはな】 u-no-hana, deutzia flowers (early summer).
Notes: 闇の門 (yami no kado) = gate in darkness. The deutzia flowers glowing white in the dark.

Poem: 湖の水まさりけり五月雨
Romaji:
mizu no umi
masari keri
samidare
My translation:
the lake water
has risen—
the long summer rains
Kigo: 五月雨 【さみだれ】 samidare, early summer rains (mid summer).
Notes: 湖 (mizuumi) = lake. The lake level rises with the summer rains.

Poem: 手のうへにかなしく消ゆる螢かな
Romaji:
te no ue ni
kanashiku kiyuru
hotaru kana
My translation:
on the palm of my hand
sadly fading out—
a firefly
Kigo: 蛍 【ほたる】 hotaru, firefly / fireflies (mid summer).
Notes: 手のうへ (te no ue) = on the palm. A firefly fading out on the palm—pathos of transient light.

Poem: 螢火や吹きとばされて鳰のやみ
Romaji:
hotaruhi ya
fuki tobasarete
niwa no yami
My translation:
firefly light—
blown away
into the garden's dark
Kigo: 蛍 【ほたる】 hotaru, firefly / fireflies (mid summer).
Notes: 鳰 (nio) = grebe. Firefly blown into the dark waters of the grebe's lake.

Poem: 石も木も眼にひかる暑さかな
Romaji:
ishi mo ki mo
me ni hikaru
atsusa kana
My translation:
stones and trees alike
glittering to the eye—
the heat
Kigo: 暑さ 【あつさ】 atsusa, heat (all summer).
Notes: Stones and trees glittering in the heat. Everything radiant with the summer sun's intensity.

Poem: 魂棚の奥なつかしや親の顔
Romaji:
tamadana no
oku natsukashi ya
ota no kao
My translation:
in the depths of the spirit shelf—
how dear to me:
father's face
Kigo: 魂棚 【たまだな】 tama-dana, spirit shelf (mid autumn).
Notes: 魂棚の奥 (tamadana no oku) = in the depths of the spirit shelf. Father's face seen in the offerings—Bon festival mourning.

Poem: いなづまやどの傾城とかり枕
Romaji:
inazuma ya
dono keisei to
kari makura
My translation:
lightning flash—
which courtesan
borrowed pillow?
Kigo: 稲妻 【いなずま】 inazuma, lightning (all autumn).
Notes: 傾城 (keisei) = a courtesan. Lightning flash—which courtesan shares this borrowed pillow tonight?

Poem: 稲妻のかきまぜて行くやみよかな
Romaji:
inazuma no
kakimazete yuku
yami yo kana
My translation:
the lightning stirs
and stirs as it passes—
the dark night
Kigo: 稲妻 【いなずま】 inazuma, lightning (all autumn).
Notes: 掻き交ぜて (kakimazete) = stirring up. Lightning stirs up the darkness as it passes through.

Poem: 岩端や爰（ここ）にもひとり月の客
Romaji:
iwa hana ya
koko ni mo hitori
tsuki no kyaku
My translation:
ledge of rock—
here too is one
guest of the moon
Kigo: 月 【つき】 tsuki, moon (mid autumn).
Notes: 岩端 (iwa-hana) = rocky ledge. Even here, alone on a rock ledge, one is a guest of the autumn moon.

Poem: あき風やしら木の弓に弦はらん
Romaji:
aki kaze ya
shira ki no yumi ni
tsuru haran
My translation:
autumn wind—
I shall string the bow
of pale birch wood
Kigo: 秋風 【あきかぜ】 akikaze, autumn breeze / autumn wind [carries with it the sound of rustling leaves] (all autumn).
Notes: 白木の弓 (shiraki no yumi) = bow of unfinished/pale wood. Stringing the white-wood bow in the autumn wind.

Poem: 雁がねの竿になる時尚さびし
Romaji:
karigane no
sao to naru toki
nao sabishi
My translation:
when the wild geese
form their pole formation—
still more lonely
Kigo: 雁 【かり】 kari, (wild) goose/geese [usually Anser species, though Branta are included] (late autumn).
Notes: 竿 (sao) = pole. When the geese form a pole-like line, loneliness deepens.

Poem: 故郷も今はかり寝や渡鳥
Romaji:
furusato mo
ima wa kari ne ya
watari dori
My translation:
even home
is now a borrowed sleep—
the migrating bird
Kigo: 渡り鳥 【わたりどり】 wataridori, migrating bird(s) (mid autumn).
Notes: Even one's homeland is now just a temporary resting place—like a migrating bird.

Poem: 鳶の羽もかいつくろひぬ初しぐれ
Romaji:
tobi no hane mo
kaitsu kuroi nu
hatsushigure
My translation:
even the kite's wings
have been preened and smoothed—
the season's first rain
Kigo: 初時雨 【はつしぐれ】 hatsushigure, first winter shower (early winter).
Notes: 鳶 (tobi) = black kite (bird). Even the kite preens its wings in the first winter rain.

Poem: いそがしや沖の時雨の眞帆片帆
Romaji:
isogashi ya
oki no shigure no
maho kataho
My translation:
so busy:
the winter squall at sea
full sail, half sail
Kigo: 時雨 【しぐれ】 shigure, (winter) shower/drizzle (early winter).
Notes: The winter squall at sea—full sail and half sail tacking in the busy storm.

Poem: こがらしの地にも落さぬしぐれかな
Romaji:
kogarashi no
chi ni mo otosanu
shigure kana
My translation:
the wintry blast—
not even letting it fall to earth,
this winter rain
Kigo: 木枯らし 【こがらし】 kogarashi, wintry gust / cold blast (early winter).
Notes: The wintry blast—not even letting leaves reach the ground, carrying them off instead.

Poem: 鴨啼くや弓矢を捨てて十余年
Romaji:
kamo naku ya
yumiya wo sute te
juyo nen
My translation:
ducks are calling—
been ten-odd years
since I laid down bow and arrow
Kigo: 鴨 【かも】 kamo, wild duck(s) (all winter).
Notes: Ducks calling—it has been over ten years since Kyorai abandoned the martial arts. Peaceful acceptance.

Poem: 荒磯やはしり馴れたる友千鳥
Romaji:
araiso ya
hashiri nare taru
tomo chidori
My translation:
the rocky shore—
accustomed to running there,
flocks of plovers
Kigo: 千鳥 【ちどり】 chidori, plover(s) (all winter).
Notes: 荒磯 (araiso) = rocky seashore. Plovers accustomed to running along the rough shore.

Poem: 応々といへどたゝくや雪の門
Romaji:
o-o to
iedo tataku ya
yuki no kado
My translation:
"Yes, yes," I call out—
but they keep knocking
at the snow-covered gate
Kigo: 雪 【ゆき】 yuki, snow (all winter).
Notes: "Yes, yes"—calling out repeatedly while someone keeps knocking at the snow-covered gate.

Poem: 尾頭の心もとなき海鼠かな
Romaji:
odono no
kokoromotonaki
namako kana
My translation:
head and tail
both uncertain—
the sea cucumber
Kigo: 海鼠 【なまこ】 namako, sea cucumber (all winter).
Notes: The sea cucumber with no clear head or tail—complete uncertainty of direction. Comic winter image.

Poem: 浪うつてよせ来る勢子や花薄
My translation:
beating waves
the hunter boy press near
flowering pampas
Kigo: 花薄 【はなすすき】 hana-susuki, pampas grass in bloom (mid autumn).
Notes: 勢子 (seko) = beaters in a hunt. Waves beating in like hunt beaters; pampas grass waving like prey flushed out.

My translation:
hearth coal
placed; spirit good
New Year’s bells

trolling to 
dark Ox Inland
moon viewing boat

light snow
falling also is tea ceremony
flower

basket fire
threading through the reed gaps
cormorant boat:

bright moon-
ant climbing along
a fence next door

quietness-
not stirring the blossoms
the bell voice

the sedge hat’s
shadow even warps
in the heat:

dripping-
even 
small

withering wind-
seeing through to the 
Jyomeiji Temple

Poem: 名月や煙這いゆく水のうへ
Romaji:
meigetsu ya
kemuri hai yuku
mizu no ue
My translation:
harvest moon—
smoke crawls and drifts
along the surface of the water
Kigo: 名月 【めいげつ】 meigetsu, harvest moon [literally "famous moon"; all these kigo refer to the full moon of the eighth lunar month, usually in September] (mid autumn).
Notes: Smoke crawling along the water surface beneath the harvest moon—atmospheric perspective.

Poem: 黄菊白菊其外の名はなくもがな
Romaji:
kigiku shiragiku
sono hoka no na wa
naku mo ga na
My translation:
yellow chrysanthemum, white chrysanthemum—
beyond these names
I wish there were none
Kigo: 菊 【きく】 kiku, chrysanthemums (all autumn).
Notes: A wish to have only yellow and white chrysanthemums—to simplify the world of chrysanthemum names.

Poem: 凩の吹きゆくうしろすがたかな
Romaji:
kogarashi no
fuki yuku ushiro
sugata kana
My translation:
the wintry gust:
blowing along, seen
only from behind
Kigo: 木枯らし 【こがらし】 kogarashi, wintry gust / cold blast (early winter).
Notes: The wintry gust seen only from behind as it blows away—like a retreating figure.

Poem: ふとん着て寐たる姿や東山
Romaji:
futon kite
netaru sugata ya
Higashiyama
My translation:
wrapped in quilts
lying there—the shape of
the Eastern Hills
Kigo: ふとん 【ふとん】 futon, quilts / bedding (winter).
Notes: 東山 (Higashiyama) = Eastern Hills of Kyoto. The rounded hills resemble a sleeping figure under quilts.

Poem: 名月や煙這いゆく水のうへ
Romaji:
meigetsu ya
kemuri hai yuku
mizu no ue
My translation:
harvest moon—
smoke creeps along
over the water
Kigo: 名月 【めいげつ】 meigetsu, harvest moon [literally "famous moon"; all these kigo refer to the full moon of the eighth lunar month, usually in September] (mid autumn).
Notes: Variant of Row 255.

Poem: 元日やはれて雀のものがたり
Romaji:
ganjitsu ya
harete suzume no
monogatari
My translation:
New Year's Day—
the sky clears and sparrows
chattering away
Kigo: 元日 【がんじつ】 ganjitsu, New Year's Day (New Year).
Notes: New Year's sky clears; sparrows chattering—a lively, auspicious opening to the year.

Poem: 出替りや幼な心に物あはれ
Romaji:
degawari ya
osana kokoro ni
mono aware
My translation:
the servants change posts—
in a child's heart
a sudden sadness
Kigo: 出替り 【でがわり】 degawari, servants' change of employment (all spring).
Notes: 出替り = the biannual servant-change season in Edo. A child's heart moved by the servant leaving—物哀れ.

Poem: うまず女の雛かしづくぞ哀れなる
Romaji:
umazu onna no
hina kashizuku zo
aware naru
My translation:
a childless woman
tending her doll with care—
how moving
Kigo: 雛 【ひな】 hina, （ひいな）, (ceremonial) doll(s) [specifically, dolls representing the Heian court, typically displayed in homes with female children during the "Doll Festival", 3 March (formerly observed on the third day of third lunar month, late spring)] (mid spring).
Notes: A childless woman tending her hina doll—pathos of maternal longing at the Dolls' Festival.

Poem: 竹の子や兒（ちご）の歯ぐきのうつくしき
Romaji:
take no ko ya
chigo no haguki no
utsukushiki
My translation:
bamboo shoots—
like the gums of a young child,
so beautiful
Kigo: 竹の子 【たけのこ】 takenoko, bamboo shoots (mid summer).
Notes: Bamboo shoots likened to a baby's pink gums—innocent and beautiful.

Poem: 角力とり並ぶや秋のから錦
Romaji:
sumo tori
narabu ya aki no
kara nishiki
My translation:
sumo wrestlers
standing in rows—autumn
Chinese brocade
Kigo: 相撲 【すもう】 sumō, sumo wrestling (all autumn).
Notes: 唐錦 (kara nishiki) = Chinese/foreign brocade. Sumo wrestlers lined up like the rich patterns of autumn brocade.

Poem: 真夜中やふりかはりたる天の川
Romaji:
mayonaka ya
furi kawari taru
amano gawa
My translation:
midnight—
and the Milky Way
has shifted overhead
Kigo: 天の川 【あまのがわ】 ama-no-gawa, Milky Way (mid autumn).
Notes: At midnight the Milky Way has shifted position overhead—subtle observation of the night sky's movement.

Poem: 名月や烟這ひゆく水のうへ
Romaji:
meigetsu ya
kemuri hoi yuku
mizu no ue
My translation:
bright harvest moon—
smoke drifting and crawling
across the water
Kigo: 名月 【めいげつ】 meigetsu, harvest moon [literally "famous moon"; all these kigo refer to the full moon of the eighth lunar month, usually in September] (mid autumn).
Notes: Variant of Rows 255/259. Different kigo spelling (烟 vs 煙).

Poem: 黄菊白菊その外はなくもがな
Romaji:
kigiku shiragiku
sono hoka wa
naku mo ga na
My translation:
yellow and white chrysanthemums—
beyond these names
I wish for none other
Kigo: 菊 【きく】 kiku, chrysanthemums (all autumn).
Notes: Variant of Row 256.

Poem: はぜ釣るや水村山廓酒旗の風
Romaji:
haze tsuru ya
suison sankaku
shuki no kaze
My translation:
fishing for goby—
water village, mountain pass,
flag wine in the wind
Kigo: 鯊 【はぜ】 haze, goby [Acanthogobius flavimanus] (all autumn).
Notes: 水村山廓 (suison sankaku) = water village, mountain fortress—a Chinese literary landscape formula.

Poem: 凩の吹きゆくうしろすがたかな
Romaji:
kogarashi no
fukiyuku ushiro
sugata kana
My translation:
the cold winter blast:
blowing past, leaving only
a retreating figure
Kigo: 木枯らし 【こがらし】 kogarashi, wintry gust (early winter).
Notes: Variant of Row 257.

Poem: ふとん着て寐たる姿や東山
Romaji:
futon kite
netaru sugata ya
Higashiyama
My translation:
quilts pulled over—
sleeping in that shape:
the Eastern Hills
Kigo: ふとん 【ふとん】 futon, quilts / bedding (winter).
Notes: Variant of Row 258.

Poem: うめ一輪一りんほどのあたたかさ
Romaji:
ume ichi rin
ichirin hodo no
atatakasa
My translation:
one plum blossom—
one blossom's worth
of warmth
Kigo: 梅 【うめ】 ume, （sometimes むめ mume）, plum (blossoms) [technically, the "Japanese apricot", Prunus mume; but this has almost always been translated "plum" for literary purposes] (early spring).
Notes: 梅一輪 (ume ichi rin) = one plum blossom. Even a single blossom brings exactly one blossom's worth of warmth.

Poem: 布団着て寝たる姿や東山
Romaji:
futon kite   shape of a man 
netaru sugata  ya  sleeping covered with a blanket—
higashiyama   Mt. East
Kigo: ふとん 【ふとん】 futon, quilts / bedding (winter).
Notes: Variant of Rows 258/270.

Poem: うめ一輪一輪ほどのあたたかさ
Romaji:
ume ichirin   a blanch of plum
 ichirin hodo no  one branch worth of
 atatakasa   warmth
Kigo: 梅 【うめ】 ume, （sometimes むめ mume）, plum (blossoms) [technically, the "Japanese apricot", Prunus mume; but this has almost always been translated "plum" for literary purposes] (early spring).
Notes: Variant of Row 271.

Poem: 十団子も小粒になり秋の風
Romaji:
tōdango mo   the Tōdango dumplings too
kotsubu ni nari  have goten smaller
aki no kaze   autumn wind
Kigo: 秋の風 【あきのかぜ】 aki no kaze, autumn wind (all autumn).
Notes: 十団子 (tōdango) = ten-dango, rice dumplings sold at Satta Pass on the Tōkaidō. Growing small as autumn passes.

Poem: それも応これも応なり老の春
Romaji: sore mo ō/ kore mo ō nari/ oi no haru
My translation:
