“yes” to this,
   “ Fine” to that question,
  old man's spring
Kigo: 老の春 【おいのはる】 oi no haru, spring of old age / an elder's spring (New Year).
Notes: それも応これも応 = "yes to that, yes to this"—the acceptance and contentment of old age at New Year.

Poem: 鐘ひとつ賣れぬ日はなし江戸の春
Romaji:
kane hitotsu 
urenu hi wa nashi 
Edo no haru
My translation:
Springtime in Edo,
Not a day passes without
A temple bell sold.
Kigo: 江戸の春 【えどのはる】 Edo no haru, Edo's spring / New Year in Edo (New Year).
Modern Source: ＮKBZ 近世俳句俳文集, p. 124
Notes: 鐘一つ (kane hitotsu) = a single bell. Not one day passes without a bell being sold in Edo's bustling spring commerce.
Other translation:
Springtime in Edo,
Not a day passes without
A temple bell sold.

Poem: 鴬の身をさかさまに初音かな
Romaji:
uguisu no
mi wo sakasama ni
hatsune kana
My translation:
the warbler—
turning itself upside down
for its first song
Kigo: 初音 【はつね】 hatsune, first song (of the bush warbler) (New Year / early spring).
Notes: The warbler upside-down for its first song of the year—a contortionist of joy at the New Year.

Poem: 鷹の目の枯野にすわる嵐かな
Romaji:
taka no me no   
kareno ni suwaru
arashi kana
My translation:
the falcon’s eyes
perched in the withered field 
a storm
Kigo: 鷹 【たか】 taka, hawk / falcon (all autumn).
Notes: The hawk's fierce gaze in the withered fields; the storm seated in the desolation—fierce autumn landscape.

Poem: 草の戸に我は蓼食う蛍かな
Romaji:
kusa no to ni   I’m a firefly
ware wa tada kuu  who chumps on nettles 
hotaru kana   in a grass hut
My translation:
in a brushwood cottage
I too eat smartweed—
the firefly
Kigo: 蛍 【ほたる】 hotaru, firefly (mid summer).
Notes: 蓼 (tade) = water pepper/smartweed. Reference to the proverb: even worms that eat smartweed have their preferences.

Poem: 声かれて猿の歯白し峰の月
Romaji:
koe karete   with wizen voice
 saru no ha shiroshi  the monkey’s white teeth
 mine no tsuki   moon of the peak
My translation:
voice gone hoarse
the monkey's teeth flash white—
the peak in moonlight
Kigo: 月 【つき】 tsuki, moon (mid autumn).
Notes: The monkey's voice gone hoarse, its white teeth gleaming in the moonlight of the peak.

Poem: 手を延べて折り行く春の草木かな
Romaji: te wo nobete/ ori-yuku haru no/ kusaki kana
My translation:
reach out,
    go along picking the grasses
  and boughs of spring
Kigo: 春の草木 【はるのくさき】 haru no kusaki, spring vegetation (all spring).
Notes: 手を延べて (te wo nobete) = extending one's hand. Reaching out as one walks through the spring vegetation.

Poem: 春雨や枕崩るるうたひ本
Romaji:
harusame ya   spring rains—
 makura kuzururu  the pillow of song books
 utaihon    collapses
My translation:
spring rain—
the pillow dissolves
into the chant book
Kigo: 春雨 【はるさめ】 harusame, spring rain (all spring).
Notes: 枕崩るる (makura kuzururu) = the pillow crumbles. Spring rain causing the paper pillow to soften while chanting from a songbook.

Poem: 船頭の耳の遠さよ桃の花
Romaji:
sendo no
mimi no tosa ya
momo no hana
My translation:
the boatman's
hearing so dull—
peach blossoms
Kigo: 桃の花 【もものはな】 momo no hana, peach blossoms (early spring).
Notes: The boatman's deafness contrasted with the delicate peach blossoms.

Poem: 馬の耳すぼめて寒し梨の花
Romaji:
uma no mimi
subomete samushi
nashi no hana
My translation:
the horse tucks in
its ears in the cold—
pear blossoms
Kigo: 梨の花 【なしのはな】 nashi no hana, pear blossoms (mid spring).
Notes: The horse tucks in its ears in the cold beside the pale pear blossoms. Coolness of early spring.

Poem: 食堂（じきだう）に雀啼くなり夕時雨
Romaji:
jikido ni
suzume naku nari
yushigure
My translation:
in the refectory
a sparrow is crying—
evening winter rain
Kigo: 夕時雨 【ゆうしぐれ】 yūshigure, evening winter drizzle (early winter).
Notes: 食堂 (jikidō) = a Buddhist refectory. A sparrow crying in the refectory in the evening drizzle—desolate quiet.

Poem: 呵（しか）られて次の間へ出る寒さかな
Romaji:
shikarare te
tsugi no ma e deru
samusa kana
My translation:
scolded out—
shuffling to the next room
in the cold
Kigo: 寒さ 【さむさ】 samusa, coldness of weather (all winter).
Notes: Scolded out of the main room, shuffling in the cold to the next room—domestic comedy of winter discomfort.

Poem: 歌書よりも軍書にかなし吉野山
Romaji:
utasho yori mo
gunsho ni kanashi
Yoshino yama
My translation:
more than poetry books
the war chronicles sadden:
Mount Yoshino
Kigo: 花 【はな】 hana, (cherry) blossoms [in haiku and haikai the simple word hana 花 refers to cherry blossoms, as do all kigo listed here; but note that in Manyōshū and some other early poetry hana was understood as referring to ume 梅【うめ】plum blossoms, an early spring topic] (late spring).
Notes: 吉野山 (Yoshino-yama) = famous cherry-blossom mountain. War chronicles sadden more than poetry books.

Poem: 夏立つや衣桁にかはる風の色
Romaji:
natsu tatsu ya
iko ni kawaru
kaze no iro
My translation:
summer begins-
on the clothes rack, changing
the wind's color
Kigo: 立夏  Rikka  [Summer / Season]

Poem: 漏る雨を人と語るや春の宵
Romaji:
moru ame wo
hito to kataru ya
haru no yoi
My translation:
talking about 
the leaking rain with someone
on a spring evening
Kigo:
Spring evening
春の宵 haru no yoi

Poem: 東風吹くと語りもぞ行く主と従者
Romaji:
kochi fuku to
katari mo zo yuku
nushi to jūsha
My translation:
“the east wind blows,”
lord and retainer
say on their way
Kigo:
East wind
東風 kochi

Poem: 公達に狐化けたり宵の春
Romaji:
kindachi ni
kitsune bake tari
yoi no haru
My translation:
into a young nobleman,
the fox has transformed himself
on a spring evening
Kigo:
Spring evening
春の宵 haru no yoi

Poem: 筋違にふとん敷きたり宵の春
Romaji:
sujikai ni
futon shiki tari
yoi no haru
My translation:
at a slant,
the bedding is laid out
on a spring evening
Kigo:
Spring evening
春の宵 haru no yoi

Poem: にほひある衣も畳まず春の暮
Romaji:
nioi aru
kinu mo tatamazu
haru no kure
Kigo:
Spring dusk 
春の暮 haru no kure

Poem: のうれんに東風吹くいせの出店かな
Romaji:
nōren ni
kochi fuku ise no
dedana kana
My translation:
through the curtains
the east wind blows, Ise
shop-stalls
Kigo: 東風 【こち】 kochi, east wind (all spring).
Notes: のれん (noren) = shop curtain. The east wind blowing the curtain of an Ise shop—branch-store atmosphere.

Poem: 春雨や小磯の小貝ぬるるほど
Romaji:
harusame ya
koiso no kogai
nururu hodo
My translation:
spring rain―
until little shells on the beach
are moist
Kigo: 春雨 【はるさめ】 harusame, spring rain (all spring).
Notes: Spring rain just enough to wet the small shells on the small beach—delicate, precise sensory detail.

Poem: 折り釘に烏帽子かけたり春の宿
Romaji:
ori kugi ni e
boshi kake tari
haru no yado
Kigo: 春の宿 【はるのやど】 haru no yado, spring lodging (all spring).
Notes: 折り釘 (orikugi) = a bent nail-hook. An eboshi (court cap) hanging on the nail—a visitor's spring lodging.

Poem: 指南車を胡地に引去る霞かな
Romaji:
shinansha o 
kochi ni hikisaru 
kasumi kana
My translation:
the guide-cart of heaven
dragged off to the northern lands
beyond the haze
Kigo: 霞 【かすみ】 kasumi, (spring) mist [frequently translated "haze"; see note "On Haze, Mist, Fog"] (all spring).
Other translation:
a guided coach
withdrawn into an old place--
this mistiness (UVA)

Poem: 春の日や門ゆく梵論の影法師
Romaji:
haru no hi ya
 kado yuku bonro no
kage-boshi
My translation:
a spring dayー
the shadow of a lay priest
pases by the gate
Kigo:
Spring day
春の日 haru no hi

Poem: 痩馬のあはれ機嫌や秋高し
My translation:
the lean horse—
what wistful good spirits!
the sky is high
Kigo: 秋高し 【あきたかし】 aki takashi, the sky is high in autumn (all autumn).
Notes: 痩馬 (yasuma) = lean horse. The horse in wistful good spirits despite its thinness—autumn sky expansive.

Poem: 花散るや耳ふつて馬のおとなしき
My translation:
blossoms scatter—
twitching its ears
the docile horse
Kigo: 花 【はな】 hana, (cherry) blossoms [in haiku and haikai the simple word hana 花 refers to cherry blossoms, as do all kigo listed here; but note that in Manyōshū and some other early poetry hana was understood as referring to ume 梅【うめ】plum blossoms, an early spring topic] (late spring).
Notes: 花散る (hana chiru) = blossoms scattering. The horse twitching its ears at the falling blossoms—docile and gentle.

Poem: 蛤に雀の斑あり哀れかな
My translation:
on the clamshell
a sparrow's dappled spots—
how touching
Kigo: 蛤 【はまぐり】 hamaguri, cherrystone clam (all spring).
Notes: 雀の斑 (suzume no madara) = sparrow-spotted dappling on the shell. Pathos of the small sparrow-marked clamshell.

Poem: 己が影を慕うて這へる
My translation:
following its own shadow
crawling forward—
the snail
Kigo: 蝸牛 【かたつむり】 katatsumuri, snail / land snail (all summer).
Notes: The snail following its own shadow as it crawls forward. Philosophical self-pursuit.

Poem: 野を焼くやぽつん╲/雨到る
My translation:
burning the fields—
plip-plop the rain
arrives
Kigo: 野焼き 【のやき】 noyaki, burning the fields (early spring).
Notes: 野を焼く (no wo yaku) = burning the fields. Suddenly rain comes, plopping down—the field-burning interrupted.

Poem: 冬蜂の死にどころなく歩きけり
My translation:
a winter bee
with nowhere to die
still walking
Kigo: 冬蜂 【ふゆばち】 fuyubachi, winter bee (all winter).
Notes: 死にどころなく (shini dokoro naku) = with no place to die. The winter bee wandering without finding its death-place.

Poem: ゆさ╲/と大枝ゆるゝ桜かな
My translation:
swaying and swaying—
the great bough shakes
under the cherry blossoms
Kigo: 桜 【さくら】 sakura, cherry blossom(s) (mid spring).
Notes: ゆさゆさ (yusa yusa) = swaying back and forth. A heavy branch swaying under the weight of blossoms.

Poem: 鷹のつらきびしく老いて哀れなり
Kigo: 鷹 【たか】 taka, hawk / falcon (all autumn).
Notes: 老いて哀れ (oite aware) = aged and pitiable. The hawk's fierce face grown old—pathos in the diminishment of a once-proud bird.

Poem: 今朝秋や見入る鏡に親の顔
Kigo: 今朝の秋 【けさのあき】 kesa no aki, first morning of autumn (early autumn).
Notes: 親の顔 (oya no kao) = parent's face. Looking in the mirror on the first morning of autumn—seeing one's parent's face.

Poem: 獅子舞や花の下影濃きところ
Kigo: 花 【はな】 hana, (cherry) blossoms [in haiku and haikai the simple word hana 花 refers to cherry blossoms, as do all kigo listed here; but note that in Manyōshū and some other early poetry hana was understood as referring to ume 梅【うめ】plum blossoms, an early spring topic] (late spring).
Notes: 獅子舞 (shishi-mai) = lion dance. The lion dance in the deep shadow of the cherry blossoms.

Poem: 夏草に這上りたる捨蚕かな
Kigo: 夏草 【なつくさ】 natsukusa, summer grasses (all summer).
Notes: 捨蚕 (sutekaiko) = discarded silkworm cocoon. A silkworm cast aside, crawling up into the summer grass.

Poem: あら野行く我が影もなき暑さ哉
My translation:
crossing a withered moor
I have no shadow
in the heat:
Kigo: 暑さ 【あつさ】 atsusa, heat (all summer).
Notes: 荒野 (ara no) = rough plain. Walking across the desolate plain in such heat that even one's own shadow disappears.

Poem: 永き日や絵馬をみてゐる旅の人
Romaji: nagaki│hi│ya│ema│wo│miteiru│tabi│no│hito
My translation:
on a long day-
viewing the horse-pictures
the traveling man
Kigo: 永き日 【ながきひ】 nagaki hi, long day(s) (all spring).
Notes: 絵馬 (ema) = votive picture tablet. A traveler gazing at the ema on a long spring day—slow time at a shrine.

Poem: あさ風やかもの川原の洗ひ葱
Romaji:
asakaze ya
kamo kawara no 
arai negi
My translation:
a morning breezeー
at the Kamo Riverbed 
washing Welsh onions
Kigo:
Welsh onion
negi 葱

Poem: 春の宵寝ぬ鳥あらば月に鳴け
Romaji:
haru no yoi
nenu tori araba
tsuki ni nake
Kigo:
Spring evening
春の宵 haru no yoi

Poem: 夏の夕吹き倒さるる風もがな
Romaji:
natsu no yu
fuki taosaruru
kaze mo ga na
My translation:
summer dusk
O, for a breeze
to blow me over
Kigo: 夏  Natsu  [Summer / Season]

Poem: 行きとどく春の日影や虫の穴
Romaji:
yuki-todoku
haru no hikage ya
mushi no ana
My translation:
snow melting,
spring sun shadow―
holes of insects
Kigo:
Insects awake
啓蟄 keichitsu
Notes: also listed in eiyaku saijiki under spring day
Other translation:
the light of a 
        spring day reaches even to
        the holes of insects

Poem: 橋守の銭かぞへけり春夕
Romaji:
hashi-mori no
zeni kazoe keri
haru yūbe
My translation:
the bridge keeper
counts up the coins,
spring dusk
Kigo:
Spring dusk 
春の暮 haru no kure

Poem: 春立つや静かに鶴の一歩より
Romaji:
haru tatsu ya
shizukani tsuru no
ippo yori
My translation:
spring begins―
quietly with a single step
of a crane
Kigo: Beginning of spring

Poem: 海は帆に埋もれて春の夕かな
Romaji:
umi wa ho ni
umorete haru no
yūbe kana
My translation:
the ocean…
covered in sails,
spring dusk
Kigo:
Spring dusk 
春の暮 haru no kure

Poem: 来て見れば霞の松に日暮れたり
Romaji:
kite mireba 
kasumi no matsu ni 
hi kuretari
My translation:
coming to look:
the pines wrapped in haze
and day has ended
Kigo: 霞 【かすみ】 kasumi, (spring) mist [frequently translated "haze"; see note "On Haze, Mist, Fog"] (all spring).
Other translation:
when I come to look:
the misty pine the sun
is setting in (UVA)

Poem: 夏はただ昼寝むしろに夜の月
Romaji:
natsu wa tada
hiru ne mushiro ni
yoru no tsuki
My translation:
summer is just
a mat to nap on &
moon at night
Kigo: 夏  Natsu  [Summer / Season]

Poem: 夏めきて人顔見ゆるゆふべかな
Romaji:
atsu mekite
hito-gao miyuru
yube kana
My translation:
the summer-like 
faces of the people
in the evening.
Kigo:
夏めくnatsu meku 
Summery or summer-like

Poem: 閑さを我が相手なり冬ごもり
Romaji:
shizukasa wo
waga aite nari
Fuyugomori
My translation:
stillness itself
is my companion—
winter confinement
Kigo: 冬籠り 【ふゆごもり】 fuyugomori, winter seclusion (all winter).
Notes: Included in a haiga
Other translation:
Making quietude
My only companion:
Winter seclusion.
Blyth, Haiku vol. 4 intro

Poem: 菜の花にくるりくるりと入る日哉
Romaji:
na no hana ni
kururi kururi to
iru hi kana
My translation:
into the rape blossoms
roundly, roundly
the sun enters
Kigo: 菜の花 【なのはな】 na-no-hana, rape flowers / mustard flowers [technically, Brassica rapa, the plant from which canola oil derives; one may prefer to translate with the closely related "mustard" in English; the image is of a field covered with the yellow flowers] (late spring).
Notes: The sun rolling down into the rape blossoms roundly—vivid image of sunset into a field of yellow flowers.

Poem: 時鳥啼くや夜汐のひたひたと
Romaji:
hototogisu
naku ya yoshio no
hitahita to
My translation:
the cuckoo calls—
the night tide
laps and laps
Kigo: 時鳥 【ほととぎす】 hototogisu, little cuckoo (all summer).
Notes: 夜汐 (yoshi-o) = night tide. The cuckoo's cry over the lapping night tide—sound and water combined.

Poem: すずしさや根笹に牛もとながれて
Romaji:
suzushisa ya
ne zasa ni ushi mo
moto nagarete
My translation:
coolness—
even the ox by the root-bamboo
drifts along
Kigo: 涼しさ 【すずしさ】 suzushisa, coolness (all summer).
Notes: 根笹 (ne-zasa) = root bamboo. Coolness: even the ox drifts along by the root bamboo in the stream.

Poem: 江のひかり柱に来たりけさのあき
Romaji:
e no hikari
hashira ni kitari
kesa no aki
My translation:
the river's light
coming to the pillar—
autumn this morning
Kigo: 秋 【あき】 aki, autumn.
Notes: 柱 (hashira) = pillar. The river's light on the pillar—autumn arriving this morning seen in the quality of the light.

Poem: 我たつるけむりは人の秋の暮
Romaji:
ware tatsu ru
kemuri wa hito no
aki no kure
My translation:
the smoke I raise
is another person's
autumn dusk
Kigo: 秋の暮 【あきのくれ】 aki no kure, autumn dusk (all autumn).
Notes: 我たつる煙 = the smoke I raise. My smoke is another person's autumn dusk—shared atmosphere across distance.

Poem: 鈴鴨の虚空に消ゆる日和哉
Romaji:
suzugamo no
koku ni kiyuru
hiyori kana
My translation:
the goldeneye ducks
disappearing into the void—
fine weather
Kigo: 鈴鴨 【すずがも】 suzugamo, goldeneye duck (all winter).
Notes: 虚空 (kokū) = the void / empty sky. Goldeneye ducks vanishing into the void—fine winter weather.

Poem: 春の雨鳥の足に泡のつく
Romaji:
haru no ame
karasu no ashi ni
awa no tsuku
My translation:
spring rain…
on the crow’s feet,
some bubbles
Kigo: 春の雨 【はるのあめ】 haru no ame, spring rain (all spring).
Notes: 鳥の足 (tori no ashi) = bird's feet. Spring rain forming bubbles on a bird's feet—delicate observation.

Poem: 初夏や木屋が掃除の行きわたる
Romaji:
hatsu natsu ya
kiya ga soji no
yuki watari
My translation:
early summer-
the wood shed is cleaned
thorough
Kigo: 初夏 shoka Early summer

Poem: 長閑さにおさへ歩行や膝の皿
Romaji:
nodokasa ni
osae ariku ya
hiza no sara
My translation:
in the tranquil
bracing to walking  
kneecaps
Kigo: 長閑 【のどか】 nodoka, calm/tranquil/serene [of weather] (all spring).

Poem: 暮遅き加茂の川添下りけり
Romaji:
kure osoki
Kamo no kawazoe
kudari keri
My translation:
slow to darken—
along the Kamo riverbank
descending
Kigo: 暮遅き
Notes: 加茂の川添 (Kamo no kawazoe) = along the Kamo River in Kyoto. Walking alongside the Kamo on a slow-darkening spring evening.

Poem: うぐひすに踏まれてうくや竹江杓
Romaji:
uguisu ni
fumarete uku ya
takejaku
My translation:
trodden by the warbler
and floating up—
the bamboo ladle
Kigo: 鶯 【うぐいす】 uguisu, bush warbler [Cettia diphone; sometimes translated as "nightingale" (Luscinia megarhynchos), since it is a small songbird and occupies a position in Japanese literature similar to that of the nightingale in European literature] (all spring).

Poem: 深山木の底に水澄む五月かな
Romaji:
miyama ki no
soko ni mizu sumu
satsuki kana
My translation:
at the foot of deep mountain trees
water runs clear—
the fifth month
Kigo: 皐月 【さつき】 satsuki, Fifth (lunar) Month [approximately June, Gregorian; note: in haikai, in compounds this prounciation is often given to 五月, referring to events that normally take place in June, as in 五月雨【さつきあめ】 satsukiame (= samidare), midsummer rain, while in others 五月【ごがつ】 gogatsu retains its modern pronunciation and meaning, May, Gregorian; see note on months] (mid summer).

Poem: 日の前の雲すわりけり花樗
Romaji:
hi no mae no
kumo suwari keri
hana afochi
My translation:
before the sun
clouds have settled—
the chinaberry blossoms
Kigo: 花樗

Poem: きらきらと音に日のさす鳴子哉
Romaji:
kirakira to
oto ni hi no sasu
naru ko kana
My translation:
glittering and bright
the sun shines through the sound—
bird-scarer rattles
Kigo: 鳴子

Poem: 物しばし匂うて止みぬ枯野原
Romaji:
mono shibashi
niou te yami nu
kare no hara
My translation:
something briefly
fragrant, then still—
the withered moor
Kigo: 枯野 【かれの】 kareno, withered field (all winter).

Poem: 下駄の歯を蹴欠いて戻る師走かな
Romaji:
geta no ha wo
kekake te modoru
shiwasu kana
My translation:
kicking loose a clog tooth
and heading home—
year's end
Kigo: 師走

Poem: 元日や人の妻子の美しき
Romaji:
ganjitsu ya
hito no tsumako no
utsukushiki
My translation:
New Year’s Day—
the neighborhood wives 
looks so lovely
Kigo: #ERROR!

Poem: 寝勝手のよさに又見る柳かな
Romaji:
nekatte no
yoki ni mata miru 
yanagi kana
My translation:
turning to get comfortable 
for my nap, again I see 
the willow:
Kigo: 柳 【やなぎ】 yanagi, willow(s) / weeping willow(s) (late spring).

Poem: けしの散る光ひまなし枕元
Romaji:
keshi no chiru
hikaru hima nashi
makura moto
My translation:
the scattering poppy—
its light so busy
at my pillow
Kigo: 芥子の花 【けしのはな】 keshi no hana, poppy/poppies.

Poem: 桐の木や雨のながるる蝉の腹
Romaji:
kiri no ki ya
ame no ngaruru
semi no hara
My translation:
paulownia tree—
the flowing rainwater 
on the cicada's belly
Kigo: 蝉 【せみ】 semi, cicada / locust (late summer).

Poem: 名月や草木に劣る人のかげ
Romaji:
meigetsu ya
kusa ki ni otoru
hito no kage
My translation:
harvest moon—
the shadows of people
inferior to grass and trees
Kigo: 名月 【めいげつ】 meigetsu, harvest moon [literally "famous moon"; all these kigo refer to the full moon of the eighth lunar month, usually in September] (mid autumn).

Poem: 門ありて国分寺はなし草の花
Romaji:
mon arite
kokubun ji wa nashi
kusa no hana
My translation:
the gate remains
but the temple is gone—
grass flowers
Kigo: 草の花 【くさのはな】 kusa no hana, (autumn) wildflowers [note: "grass flowers" is not a good translation, as 草 includes forbs and herbs] (all autumn).

Poem: 糊の干ぬ行灯ともす寒さかな
Romaji:
nori no hinu
andon tomosu
samusa kana
My translation:
the paste not yet dry
and lighting the paper lamp—
the cold
Kigo: 寒さ 【さむさ】 samusa, coldness [of weather, air, and the like].

Poem: ふゆの夜や針うしなうておそろしき
Romaji:
fuyu no yo ya
hari ushinaute
Osoroshiki
My translation:
on a winter's night
how frightful it is
to drop a sewing needle
Kigo: ふゆの夜

Poem: 大蛇や恐れながらと穴を出る
Romaji:
ōhebi ya
osore nagara to
ana wo deru
My translation:
a large snake―
says, “pardon me” and
exists his hole
Kigo:
Insects awake
啓蟄 keichitsu

Poem: 春の日や水さへあれば暮れ残り
Romaji:
haru no hi ya
mizu sae areba
kure-nokori
My translation:
a spring dayー
where there’s water
dusk lingers on
Kigo:
Spring day
春の日 haru no hi

Poem: 小酒屋の出現したり春の山
Romaji:
ko-zakeya no
shutsugen shitari
haru no yama
My translation:
a small sake stall
has appeared on
the spring mountain
Kigo: 春の山 【はるのやま】 haru no yama, spring mountain (all spring).
Notes: 小酒屋 (ko-sakaya) = small sake shop. A small tavern suddenly appearing on the spring mountain.

Poem: 子らや子ら子等が手をとる躑躅かな
Romaji:
ko ra ya ko ra
kora ga te wo toru
tsutsuji kana
My translation:
children, oh children—
children clasping hands
among the azaleas
Kigo: 躑躅 【つつじ】 tsutsuji, azalea(s) (late spring).
Notes: 子らや子ら (ko ra ya ko ra) = children, oh children! Ryōkan's famous poem of play and joy, children hand-in-hand among the azaleas.

Poem: 夏浅し水を離るる蓮巻葉
Romaji:
natsu asashi
mizu wo hanaruru
hasu maki-ba
My translation:
shallow summer
leaving the water
furled lotus leaves
Kigo: 夏浅し 【なつあさし】 natsu asashi, early summer / shallow summer (early summer).
Notes: 蓮巻葉 (hasu no makiba) = the furled leaf of the lotus. Water leaving the tightly furled lotus leaf—early summer.

Romaji:
mimi tojite
hana wo kokoro ni
hirune kana
My translation:
I will shut my ears
And, thinking only of blossoms,
Enjoy my nap.

Poem: 啓蟄や光り流るる厨水
Romaji:
keichitsu no
ari ga hayahiku
jimushi kana
My translation:
insects awake
ants already dragging
a grub
Kigo:
Insects awake
啓蟄 keichitsu

Poem: はるののゆき扇ではらふ　衣紋かな
Romaji:
harunono yuki
ōgi de harau
eimon kana
My translation:
spring-field snow —
brushing it off with a fan:
straightening the robe
Kigo: 春の雪 【はるのゆき】 haru no yuki, spring snow (spring).

Poem: 薫の梅が香ふく　板戸ころかな
Romaji:
kaoru ume ga ka
fuku itado
koro kana
My translation:
the fragrant plum's scent blowing —
a wooden shutter
rolling
Kigo: 梅 【うめ】 ume, plum blossoms (spring).

Poem: 宿々は皆新茶なり麦の秋
Romaji:
shukushuku wa
mina shin cha nari
mugi no aki
My translation:
all the inns
serve new tea
wheat's autumn
Kigo: 麦の秋 mugi no aki

Poem: 病人の駕も過けり麥の秋
Romaji:
byonin no
kago mo sugi keri
mugi no aki
My translation:
a sick man's
palanquin also pass by
wheat's autumn
Kigo: 麦の秋 mugi no aki

Poem: 麦秋や 子を負いながら いわし売り
Romaji:
mugi aki ya
ko wo oi nagara
iwashi uri
My translation:
autumn of wheat-
with a child on her back
sardine peddler
Kigo: 麦の秋 mugi no aki

Poem: 夏の日や広葉柏に移りそめ
Romaji:
natsu no hi ya
hiro-ba kashiwa ni
utsuri some
My translation:
the summer sunー
tingeing the broad leaves
of the oak
Kigo: 夏の日　natsu no hi

Poem: 夏の夜や崩れて明けしひやし物
Romaji:
natsu no yo ya
kazurete akeshi
hiyashi mono
My translation:
a summer nightー
light breaks over
chilled dishes
Kigo: 夏の夜 natsu no yo

Poem: なつの夜やまだ舌にある唐がらし
Romaji:
natsu no yo ya
mada shita ni aru
to garashi
My translation:
a summer night
still on my tongue
taste of red pepper
Kigo: 夏の夜 natsu no yo

Poem: 人声に子を引きかくす女鹿かな
Romaji:
Hito goe ni
ko wo hiki kakusu
mejika kana
My translation:
At people’s voices
mother deer draws fawn to her
and hides it.
Kigo: 鹿の子 Kanoko — Fawn [Summer Dobutsu]

Poem: かはぼりやむかひの女房こちを見る
Romaji:
Kawahori ya
mukai no nyobo
kochi wo miru
My translation:
Bats —
the wife across the street
looks this way.
Kigo: 蝙蝠 Komori — Bat [Summer Dobutsu]
Notes: They may both have been watching the bats on this warm evening and by chance, their eyes met in a charming moment.

Poem: かはぼりや月のほとりを立ちさらず
Romaji:
Kawahori ya
tsuki no hotori wo
tachi sarazu
My translation:
Bats —
they don’t leave the vicinity
of the moon.
Kigo: 蝙蝠 Komori — Bat [Summer Dobutsu]

Poem: 我が宿に一夜たのむぞ蚊喰鳥
Romaji:
Waga yado ni
hitoyo tanomu zo
kakuidori
My translation:
To my house,
please come a night!
Bird that eats mosquitoes.
Kigo: 蝙蝠 Komori — Bat [Summer Dobutsu]

Poem: 雨蛙芭蕉にのりてそよぎけり
Romaji:
Amagaeru
basho ni norite
soyogi keri
My translation:
A rain frog
got onto a plantain leaf,
and swayed.
Kigo: 雨蛙 Amagaeru — Rain Frog [Summer Dobutsu]

Poem: 麦藁の家してやらん雨蛙
Romaji:
Mugewara no
ie shite yaran
amagaeru
My translation:
Let me make you
a wheat-straw house,
oh rain frog.
Kigo: 雨蛙 Amagaeru — Rain Frog [Summer Dobutsu]

Poem: 鳴きて知りぬ石蕗の若葉の雨蛙
Romaji:
Nakite shirinu
tsuwano wakaba no
amagaeru
My translation:
Crying, it was known —
the rain frog on
young silver-leaf.
Kigo: 雨蛙 Amagaeru — Rain Frog [Summer Dobutsu]

Poem: 這いでよ飼屋が下の蟾の響
Romaji:
Hai ideyo
kaiya ga shita no
hiki no koe
My translation:
Come on out!
From under the coop
a toad’s voice.
Kigo: 蟇 Hikigaeru — Toad [Summer Dobutsu]

Poem: 思ふことだまってるか蟇
Romaji:
Omou koto
damatte iru ka
hikigaeru
My translation:
Will you not say
what you’re thinking?
Oh, toad.
Kigo: 蟇 Hikigaeru — Toad [Summer Dobutsu]

Poem: 月の句を吐いてへらさん蟾の腹
Romaji:
Tsuki no ku wo
haite herasan
hiki no hara
My translation:
If he’d spit out
a ku on the moon, the toad’s belly
might shrink.
Kigo: 蟇 Hikigaeru — Toad [Summer Dobutsu]

Poem: 蟾どのの妻や待つらん子鳴らん
Romaji:
Hiki dono no
tsuma ya matsuran
ko nakuran
My translation:
Mr. Toad’s
wife must be waiting,
his child, crying.
Kigo: 蟇 Hikigaeru — Toad [Summer Dobutsu]

Poem: はつ声を聞かまほしきに時鳥
Romaji:
Hatsu koe wo
kikama hoshiki ni
hototogisu
My translation: Wishing to hear / your first song, / little cuckoo —
Kigo: 時鳥 Hototogisu — Little Cuckoo [Summer Dobutsu]

Poem: 夜深く目をもさましつるかな
Romaji:
Yo fukaku me wo mo
samashitsuru kana
My translation: How late I’ve stayed / up till, tonight!  —  Poet unknown, Tai waka collection
Kigo: 時鳥 Hototogisu — Little Cuckoo [Summer Dobutsu]

Poem: ほととぎす大竹藪を漏る月夜
Romaji:
Hototogisu
o takeyabu wo
moru tsukiyo
My translation: Little cuckoo — / through a large bamboo grove, / the moonnight.
Kigo: 時鳥 Hototogisu — Little Cuckoo [Summer Dobutsu]

Poem: ほととぎす鳴いて行方や島一つ
Romaji:
Hototogisu
naite yukue ya
shima hitotsu
My translation: Little cuckoo — / in the direction it faces, / an island.
Kigo: 時鳥 Hototogisu — Little Cuckoo [Summer Dobutsu]

Poem: ほととぎす鳴くや五月の雨の中
Romaji:
Hototogisu
naku ya gogatsu no
ame no naka
My translation: The little cuckoo / cries — in the fifth month / rain.
Kigo: 時鳥 Hototogisu — Little Cuckoo [Summer Dobutsu]

Poem: ほととぎすまたぬ方より初音かり
Romaji:
Hototogisu
matanu kata yori
hatsune kari
My translation: Little cuckoo — / from an unexpected direction, / the first song.
Kigo: 時鳥 Hototogisu — Little Cuckoo [Summer Dobutsu]

Poem: 鶯や竹の子藪に老を鳴く
Romaji:
Uguisu ya
take no ko yabu ni
oi wo naku
My translation:
The bush warbler —
in a grove of bamboo shoots,
sings of old age.
Kigo: 老鶯 Oi uguisu — Old Bush Warbler [Summer Dobutsu]

Poem: 能なしの寝むたし我をぎやうぎやうし
Romaji:
No nashi no
nemutashi ware wo
gyogyoshi
My translation:
To sleepy me,
with no abilities, it sings —
reed warbler.
Kigo: 葦切 Yoshikiri — Reed Warbler [Summer Dobutsu]

Poem: かはせみや絵の具を流すおのが影
Romaji:
Kawasemi ya
enogu wo nagasu
onoga kage
My translation:
The kingfisher —
making watercolours flow,
his reflection.
Kigo: 翡翠 Kawasemi — Kingfisher [Summer Dobutsu]

Poem: かはせみや羽をよそほふ水鏡
Romaji:
Kawasemi ya
hane wo yosohou
mizu kagami
My translation:
The kingfisher —
it dresses its feathers
in a water mirror.
Kigo: 翡翠 Kawasemi — Kingfisher [Summer Dobutsu]

Poem: 翡翠やぬれ羽にうつる夕日影
Romaji:
Kawasemi ya
nureba ni utsuru
yu hikage
My translation:
Kingfisher —
on its wet feathers
the dusk sunlight.
Kigo: 翡翠 Kawasemi — Kingfisher [Summer Dobutsu]

Poem: 水鶏啼くと人へいへばや佐屋泊り
Romaji:
Kuina naku to
hito no ie baya
Saya domari
My translation:
“A water-rail sings,”
as someone said,
stop at Saya.
Kigo: 水鶏 Kuina — Water-Rail [Summer Dobutsu]
Notes: Although he hadn’t planned to stop at Saya, because a disciple invited him, saying he could hear a water-rail, he did. Saya is in Amagun, Aichi prefecture.

Poem: 馬洗ふ川すそ闇き水鶏かな
Romaji:
Uma arau
kawa suso kuraki
kuina kana
My translation:
Washing the horse
at a dark river-mouth,
a water-rail.
Kigo: 水鶏 Kuina — Water-Rail [Summer Dobutsu]

Poem: 聞くうちにすゑまぼろしの水鶏かな
Romaji:
Kiku uchi ni
sue maboroshi no
kuina kana
My translation:
While listening,
it ended like a phantom —
the water-rail.
Kigo: 水鶏 Kuina — Water-Rail [Summer Dobutsu]

Poem: 水鶏啼いて星うく草のはやまかな
Romaji:
Kuina naite
hoshi uku kusa no
hayama kana
My translation:
A water-rail calls,
and stars float —
grassy hill.
Kigo: 水鶏 Kuina — Water-Rail [Summer Dobutsu]

Poem: 釣竿に鮎のあはれや水はなれ
Romaji:
Tsuri zao ni
ayu no aware ya
mizu banare
My translation:
On the pole,
the ayu pathetic —
leaving the water.
Kigo: 鮎 Ayu — Sweet-Fish [Summer Dobutsu]

Poem: 滝水の中をながるる蜩の声
Romaji:
Takimizu no
naka yo nagaruru
semi no koe
My translation: In the waterfall
Kigo: 滝 Taki
Notes:
the cicada voices
seem to flow

Poem: くつさめのあとしづかなり夏の山
Romaji:
Kutsusame no
ato shizuka nari
natsu no yama
Kigo: 夏の山 Natsu no yama — Summer Mountain [Summer Kigo]

Poem: 夏山や一足づつに海見ゆる
Romaji:
Natsu yama ya
hito ashi zutsu ni
umi miyuru
My translation:
Summer mountain —
with each step
the ocean in view
Kigo: 夏の山 Natsu no yama — Summer Mountain [Summer Kigo]

Poem: 馬ぼくぼく我を絵に見る夏野かな
Romaji:
Uma bokuboku
ware wo e ni miru
natsu no kana
My translation:
The horse, clop... clop...
I see myself in a picture,
summer fields.
A ku of 1682. As the country horse walks slowly in the hot weather, the writer imagines they must appear like a picture.
Kigo: 夏野  Natsuno  [Summer / Chiri]

Poem: 月の頃は寝に行く夏の川辺かな
Romaji:
Tsuki no koro wa
ne ni yuku natsu no
kawabe kana
My translation:
When there's a moon,
I go to sleep by a summer
riverside.
Kigo: 夏の川  Natsu no kawa  [Summer / Chiri]

Poem: 夏川の音に宿かる木曽路かな
Romaji:
Natsu gawa no
oto ni yadokaru
Kisoji kana
My translation:
Where a summer river
murmurs, take an inn.
Kiso road.
Kigo: 夏の川  Natsu no kawa  [Summer / Chiri]

Poem: 夏川を越すうれしさよ手に草履
Romaji:
Natsu gawa wo
kosu ureshisa yo
te ni zori
My translation:
How joyful to cross
a summer river!
Sandals in hand.
Kigo: 夏の川  Natsu no kawa  [Summer / Chiri]

Poem: 島々や千々に砕けて夏の海
Romaji:
Shimajima ya
chijini kudakete
natsu no umi
My translation:
Island after island —
into a myriad, crumbled,
the summer ocean.
A ku about Matsushima, a series of numberless small islands, which Basho described as amazing, and a wondrous work of heaven's creation. Pine trees grow on each little island.
Kigo: 夏の海  Natsu no umi  [Summer / Chiri]

Poem: 夏海や碁盤の石のかいつぶり
Romaji:
Natsu umi ya
goban no ishi no
kaitsubari
My translation:
The summer ocean —
like 'go' stones on a board,
the grebes.
Kigo: 夏の海  Natsu no umi  [Summer / Chiri]

Poem: 松風を中に青田のそよぎかな
Romaji:
Matsu kaze wo
naka ni aota no
soyogi kana
My translation:
The wind of pine trees in them,
green ricefields rustle.
Kigo: 青田  Aota  [Summer / Chiri]

Poem: 山々を低く覚ゆる青田かな
Romaji:
Yama yama wo
hikuku oboyuru
aota kana
My translation:
All the mountains
seem lower, by
green ricefields.
Kigo: 青田  Aota  [Summer / Chiri]

Poem: 傘さしてふかれに出でし青田かな
Romaji:
Kasa sashite
fukare ni ideshi
aota kana
My translation:
With a parasol,
I went out to be blown —
green ricefields.
Kigo: 青田  Aota  [Summer / Chiri]

Poem: 掬ぶよりはや歯にひびく泉かな
Romaji:
Musubu yori
haya ha ni hibiku
izumi kana
My translation:
Just by scooping,
a sting to the teeth —
the spring.
Kigo: 泉  Izumi  [Summer / Chiri]

Poem: 緑わく夏山陰の泉かな
Romaji:
Midori waku
natsu yama kage no
izumi kana
My translation:
Green wells up —
the spring of a summer
mountain shade.
Kigo: 泉  Izumi  [Summer / Chiri]

Poem: さざれ蟹足這いのぼる清水かな
Romaji:
Sazare gani
ashi hai noboru
shimizu kana
My translation:
A little crab
crawls up my foot —
pure water.
Kigo: 清水  Shimizu  [Summer / Chiri]

Poem: 源は氷か雪か苔清水
Romaji:
Minamoto wa
kori ka yuki ka
koke shimizu
My translation:
Is its source
ice, or snow?
Moss pure water.
Kigo: 清水  Shimizu  [Summer / Chiri]

Poem: 出て見せつ隠れつ雲の皐月不二
Romaji:
Dete mesetsu
kakuretsu kumo no
Satsuki Fuji
My translation:
It shows itself,
then hides — Fifth month Fuji
in clouds.
Kigo: 五月富士  Satsuki Fuji  [Summer / Chiri]

Poem: 胴亀や昨日植ゑたる田の濁り
Romaji:
Dogame ya
kino uetaru
ta no nigori
My translation:
A salt-marsh turtle —
the muddiness of a paddy
planted yesterday.
Kigo: 植田  Ueta  [Summer / Chiri]

Poem: 我かものに植田の蛙鳴つのる
Romaji:
Waga mono ni
ueta no kawazu
naki tsunoru
My translation:
As if their own
planted ricefields, frogs'
loud songs.
Kigo: 植田  Ueta  [Summer / Chiri]

Poem: 植ゑつけし夜は三日月の門田かな
Romaji:
Uetsukeshi
yo wa mikazuki no
kakota kana
My translation:
The night they were planted,
a crescent moon —
gate ricefields.
Kigo: 植田  Ueta  [Summer / Chiri]

Poem: ひとつ脱でうしろに負いぬ更衣
Romaji:
Hitetsu nuide
ushiro ni oi nu
koromogae
My translation:
Took off a layer,
flung it on my back —
change of garment.
During a journey, not having a summer garment, he merely took off a layer of the clothes he was wearing.
Kigo: 更衣  Koromogae  [Summer / Jinji]

Poem: 更衣野路の人はつかに白し
Romaji:
Koromogae
noji no hito wazu
kani shireshi
My translation:
Change of garments —
on field paths people
look whiter.
Kigo: 更衣  Koromogae  [Summer / Jinji]

Poem: 羅に遮る蓮のにほひかな
Romaji:
Usumono ni
saegiru hasu no
nioi kana
My translation:
By a thin silk
kimono screened, the
scent of lotus.
Kigo: 羅  Usumono  [Summer / Jinji]

Poem: 山を庭に動き入るるや夏座敷
Romaji:
Yama mo niwa ni
ugoki iruruya
natsu zashiki
My translation:
Even the mountain
seems to move into the garden —
summer parlour.
Kigo: 夏座敷  Natsuzashiki  [Summer / Jinji]

Poem: 行く雲を寝ておゐて見るや夏座敷
Romaji:
Yuku kumo wo
niteite miru ya
natsu zashiki
My translation:
Lie down, and
watch the clouds roll by —
summer parlour.
Kigo: 夏座敷  Natsuzashiki  [Summer / Jinji]

Poem: 松陰や寝茣蓙一つの夏座敷
Romaji:
Matsu kage ya
negoza hitotsu no
natsu zashiki
My translation:
The shade of pine trees —
one rush mat to sleep on,
summer parlour.
Kigo: 夏座敷  Natsuzashiki  [Summer / Jinji]

Poem: 水紋を織得て清し簟
Romaji:
Suimon wo
oriete kiyoshi
takamushiro
My translation:
Water patterns
woven into it, a pure
bamboo mat.
Kigo: 簟  Takamushiro  [Summer / Jinji]

Poem: 細脛に夕風さはるたかむしろ
Romaji:
Hoso hagi ni
yu kaze sawaru
takamushiro
My translation:
On the thin legs
a dusk breeze —
bamboo mat.
Kigo: 簟  Takamushiro  [Summer / Jinji]

Poem: 昼寝して手のうごきやむうちは哉
Romaji:
Hirune shite
te no ugoki yamu
uchiwa kana
My translation:
Dozing off,
the hand stops moving —
round fan.
Kigo: 団扇  Uchiwa  [Summer / Jinji]

Poem: 後家の君たそがれ顔のうちはかな
Romaji:
Goke no kimi
tasogare gao no
uchiwa kana
My translation:
The widow —
her face at dusk, behind
a round fan.
Kigo: 団扇  Uchiwa  [Summer / Jinji]

Poem: 大猫のどさりと寝たる団かな
Romaji:
O neko no
dosari to netaru
uchiwa kana
My translation:
The big cat,
with a thud, lay on it,
round fan.
Kigo: 団扇  Uchiwa  [Summer / Jinji]

Poem: 風鈴や花にはつらき風ながら
Romaji:
Furin ya
hana seiun tsuraki
kaze nagare
My translation:
Windbells —
though for flowers the
wind was cruel.
Kigo: 風鈴  Furin  [Summer / Jinji]

Poem: 見る人も廻り灯籠に廻りけり
Romaji:
Miru hito mo
mawari-toro ni
mawari keri
My translation:
The man looking at
revolving lamps also
went round.
Kigo: 走馬灯  Somato  [Summer / Jinji]

Poem: 山を見る二階なりけり土用ぼし
Romaji:
Yama wo miru
nikai nari keri
doyo boshi
My translation:
On the second floor,
where you can see mountains —
hot day's airing.
Kigo: 虫干  Mushiboshi  [Summer / Jinji]

Poem: 虫干に猫も干されて居たりけり
Romaji:
Mushiboshi ni
neko mo hosarete
itari keri
My translation:
For insect airing
the cat, too,
being aired.
Kigo: 虫干  Mushiboshi  [Summer / Jinji]

Poem: 風流の初やおくの田植うた
Romaji:
Furyu no
hajime ya oku no
taue uta
My translation:
The source of sweet simplicity —
a north province's
rice-plant song.
Kigo: 田植  Taue  [Summer / Jinji]

Poem: 遠里や二筋三すぢ田うゑ笠
Romaji:
To zato ya
futasuji misuji
taue gasa
My translation:
A remote village —
two, three lines of
rice-plant hats.
Kigo: 田植  Taue  [Summer / Jinji]

Poem: 蕗の葉にいわしを配る田植かな
Romaji:
Fuki no ha ni
iwashi wo kubaru
taue kana
My translation:
In butterbur leaves,
sardines passed around —
rice-planting.
Kigo: 田植  Taue  [Summer / Jinji]

Poem: 皿鉢もほのかに闇の宵涼み
Romaji:
Sara hachi mo
honoka ni yami no
yoi suzumi
My translation:
Plates and bowls
faint, feel cool on
a dark evening.
Kigo: 納涼  Suzumi  [Summer / Jinji]

Poem: 夕涼みあぶなき石にのぼりけり
Romaji:
Yu suzumi
abunaki ishi ni
nobori keri
My translation:
Seeking dusk coolness,
a dangerous rock
was climbed.
Kigo: 納涼  Suzumi  [Summer / Jinji]

Poem: つつ立て帆になる袖や涼みぶね
Romaji:
Tsutsu tatete
ho ni naru sode ya
suzumi-bune
My translation:
Stand up suddenly,
the sleeves turn into sails!
Boat for cooling.
Kigo: 納涼  Suzumi  [Summer / Jinji]

Poem: 花火尽て美人は酒に身投げけむ
Romaji:
Hanabi tsukite
bijin wa sake ni
minagekemu
My translation:
The fireworks done,
the beautiful lady,
sunk in drinking.
While watching the display of fireworks, the beautiful lady had sat by his side, pouring rice wine for him, but when the display ended, she disappeared. Worried, on looking around the boat, he discovered she was herself drinking now.
Kigo: 花火  Hanabi  [Summer / Jinji]

Poem: 川面や花火のあとの楫の音
Romaji:
Kawa omo ya
hanabi no ato no
kaji no oto
My translation:
On the river —
after the fireworks,
rudder sounds.
Kigo: 花火  Hanabi  [Summer / Jinji]

Poem: 星一つ残して落つる花火かな
Romaji:
Hoshi hitotsu
nokoshite otsuru
hanabi kana
My translation:
One star
was left, after
the fireworks fell.
Kigo: 花火  Hanabi  [Summer / Jinji]

Poem: 夏痩のわが骨探る寝覚かな
Romaji:
Natsu yase no
waga hone saguru
nezame kana
My translation:
The summer thin
pries his bones,
awakening.
Kigo: 夏痩  Natsu yase  [Summer / Jinji]

Poem: 夏痩や西日さし込む竹格子
Romaji:
Natsu yase ya
nishibi sashikomu
take koshi
My translation:
Summer thinness —
the western sun comes through
a bamboo lattice.
Kigo: 夏痩  Natsu yase  [Summer / Jinji]

Poem: 四辻や匂ひ吹きみつあやめの日
Romaji:
Yotsu tsuji ya
nioi fukimitsu
ayame no hi
My translation:
A crossroad —
the wind brings their fragrance,
blue flags day.
Kigo: 端午  Tango  [Summer / Jinji]

Poem: 鱠にも響くまつりの太鼓かな
Romaji:
Namasu ni mo
hibiku matsuri no
taiko kana
My translation:
Even to the salad
vibrates the festival
big drum.
Kigo: 祭  Matsuri  [Summer / Jinji]

Poem: 鉾処にに夕風そよぐ囃子かな
Romaji:
Hoko shosho ni
yu kaze soyogu
hayashi kana
My translation:
Halberds here and there,
sway in the dusk breeze —
festival music.
Kigo: 祇園会  Gione  [Summer / Jinji]

Poem: 祇園会や京は日傘の下を行く
Romaji:
Gion e ya
kyo wa higasa no
shita wo yuku
My translation:
Gion festival —
in the capital they go
under parasols.
Kigo: 祇園会  Gione  [Summer / Jinji]

Poem: 吹く風の中を魚飛ぶ御祓かな
Romaji:
Fuku kaze no
naka wo uo tobu
misogi kana
My translation:
In the breeze
fish are jumping,
purification.
Kigo: 夏越  Nagoshi  [Summer / Jinji]

Poem: 一番に乙鳥のくぐるちのわ哉
Romaji:
Ichiban ni
tsubame no kuguru
chinowa kana
My translation:
First of all,
a swallow went through,
lalong wreath.
Kigo: 夏越  Nagoshi  [Summer / Jinji]

Poem: 僧達の袂を染むる新茶かな
Romaji:
So tachi no
tameto wo somuru
shincha kana
My translation:
The monks
get their sleeves dyed again,
new tea.
A monk's garment of black was referred to as being dyed with Chinese ink.
Kigo: 新茶  Shincha  [Summer / Jinji]

Poem: 新茶の香真昼の眠気転じたり
Romaji:
Shincha no ka
ma hiru no nemuke
tenji tari
My translation:
The scent of new tea —
noon-time sleepiness
has gone away.
Kigo: 新茶  Shincha  [Summer / Jinji]

Poem: 道ばたに繭干すかぜのあつさかな
Romaji:
Michibata ni
mayu hosu kaze no
atsusa kana
My translation:
By a roadside
cocoons dry, the wind
is hot.
Kigo: 繭  Mayu  [Summer / Jinji]

Poem: 鵜のつらに篝こぼれて憐れなり
Romaji:
U no tsura ni
kagari koborete
aware nari
My translation:
On a cormorant's face
a torch flame spills,
pathetic.
Kigo: 鵜飼  Ukai  [Summer / Jinji]

Poem: つかれ鵜の腮に月のしづくかな
Romaji:
Tsukare u no
agito ni tsuki no
shizuku kana
My translation:
On a tired cormorant's
chin, moonlit
waterdrops.
Kigo: 鵜飼  Ukai  [Summer / Jinji]

Poem: 蚊やりして師の坊を待つ端居かな
Romaji:
Kayari shite
shino bo wo matsu
hashi-i kana
My translation:
With mosquito punk,
I wait for a monk,
sitting on the veranda.
Kigo: 端居  Hashi-i  [Summer / Jinji]

Poem: さをとめや汚れぬ顔は朝ばかり
Romaji:
Saotome ya
yogorenu kao wa
asa bakari
My translation:
Rice-planting girls —
unsoiled faces, only
in the morning.
Kigo: 早乙女  Saotome  [Summer / Jinji]

Poem: 早乙女の祭りのやうに揃ひ出る
Romaji:
Saotome no
matsuri no yo ni
soroi deru
My translation:
Rice-planting girls —
like a festival parade,
come out in a row.
Kigo: 早乙女  Saotome  [Summer / Jinji]

Poem: 早乙女の下りたつあの田この田かな
Romaji:
Saotome no
oritatsu ano ta
kono ta kana
My translation:
Rice-planting girls
step down, stand in that
field and this.
Kigo: 早乙女  Saotome  [Summer / Jinji]

Poem: 貝吹いて雪踏み分けよ花の跡
Romaji:
Kai fuite
yuki fumi wake yo
hana no ato
My translation:
Blow the conch shell,
make way through snow!
After the flowers.
Kigo: 峯入  Mine iri  [Summer / Shukyo]

Poem: 峯入やおもへば深き芳野山
Romaji:
Mine iri ya
omoeba fukaki
Yoshino yama
My translation:
Entering the peak —
when you think of it, Yoshino
mountain is deep.
Kigo: 峯入  Mine iri  [Summer / Shukyo]

Poem: 峯入や鳥さへ知らぬ花を今日
Romaji:
Mine iri ya
tori sae shiranu
hana wo kyo
My translation:
Entering the peak —
today, flowers even birds
don't know of.
Kigo: 峯入  Mine iri  [Summer / Shukyo]

Poem: 灌仏の皺手合はする数珠の音
Romaji:
Kanbutsu no
shiwa te awasuru
juzu no oto
My translation:
Bathed the Buddha —
wrinkled hands together,
rub the rosary.
Kigo: 仏生会  Busshoe  [Spring / Shukyo]

Poem: 山寺や五色にあまる花み堂
Romaji:
Yamadera ya
goshiki ni amaru
hana mido
My translation:
Mountain temple —
more than five colours,
the flowery pavilion.
Kigo: 仏生会  Busshoe  [Spring / Shukyo]

Poem: 灌仏の御指の先や暮の月
Romaji:
Kanbutsu no
oyubi no saki ya
kure no tsuki
My translation:
At the bathed
Buddha's august finger-tip,
the dusk moon.
Kigo: 仏生会  Busshoe  [Spring / Shukyo]

Poem: 目には青葉山郭公初鰹
Romaji:
Me ni wa aoba
yama hototogisu
hatsugatsuo
My translation:
Green leaves to see,
the mountain little cuckoo,
and first bonito.
Kigo: 初鰹 Hatsugatsuo — First Bonito
Notes: This ku was made in Kamakura, famous for bonito; it was also the seat of the first shogunate. The senses of sight, sound and taste are amply satisfied.

Poem: 鎌倉を生きて出でけん　初鰹
Romaji:
Kamakura wo
ikite ideken
hatsugatsuo
My translation:
They must have
left Kamakura alive,
the first bonito.
Kigo: 初鰹 Hatsugatsuo — First Bonito

Poem: くれなゐは　花にかぎらじ　初鰹
Romaji:
Kurenai wa
hana ni kagiraji
hatsugatsuo
My translation:
Scarlet is
not limited to flowers —
the first bonito.
Kigo: 初鰹 Hatsugatsuo — First Bonito

Poem: 夏虫の　碁にこがれたる　命かな
Romaji:
Natsu mushi no
go ni kogaretaru
inochi kana
My translation:
Summer insects —
by "go" being scorched,
their lives.
Kigo: 夏の虫 Natsu no mushi — Summer Insects [Summer / Dobutsu]

Poem: 夏虫も　火を守る　宇治の　網代かな
Romaji:
Natsu mushi mo
hi wo moru Uji no
ajiro kana
My translation:
Summer insects, too,
guard the fires — Uji's
fish weirs.
Kigo: 夏の虫 Natsu no mushi — Summer Insects [Summer / Dobutsu]

Poem: 片羽もえて　這ひ歩きけり　夏の虫
Romaji:
Kata ha moete
hai aruki keri
natsu no mushi
My translation:
A wing scorched,
it crawled on —
summer insect.
Kigo: 夏の虫 Natsu no mushi — Summer Insects [Summer / Dobutsu]

Poem: 筆とめて　打ち払ひけり　火取虫
Romaji:
Fude tomete
uchi harai keri
hitori mushi
My translation:
Stop writing,
to wave them away —
light-drawn insects.
Kigo: 火取虫 Hitori mushi — Light-Drawn Insects, Moths [Summer / Dobutsu]

Poem: 行灯に　はかなき影や　火取虫
Romaji:
Andon ni
hakanaki kage ya
hitori mushi
My translation:
By the paper lamp
their fleeting shadows —
light-drawn insects.
Kigo: 火取虫 Hitori mushi — Light-Drawn Insects, Moths [Summer / Dobutsu]

Poem: 朝風に　毛を吹かれ居る　毛虫かな
Romaji:
Asa kaze ni
ke wo fukare iru
kemushi kana
My translation:
In the morning breeze
its fur being blown —
caterpillar.
Kigo: 毛虫 Kemushi — Caterpillar [Summer / Dobutsu]

Poem: 祭り見に　ぶらぶら下がる　毛虫かな
Romaji:
Matsuri mi ni
burabura sagaru
kemushi kana
My translation:
To see the festival,
it strolls down —
caterpillar.
Kigo: 毛虫 Kemushi — Caterpillar [Summer / Dobutsu]

Poem: 頓て死ぬ　けしきは見えず　蝉の声
Romaji:
Yagate shinu
keshiki wa miezu
semi no koe
My translation:
Soon to die,
it does not seem —
the cicada's voice.
Kigo: 蝉 Semi — Cicada [Summer / Dobutsu]

Poem: 閑さや　岩にしみ入る　蝉の声
Romaji:
Shizukasa ya
iwa ni shimi iru
semi no koe
My translation:
The stillness —
into boulders sink
cicada voices.
Kigo: 蝉 Semi — Cicada [Summer / Dobutsu]

Poem: 蝉鳴いて　杉にも脂の　流れけり
Romaji:
Semi naite
sugi ni mo yani no
nagare keri
My translation:
Cicadas singing,
even from cedars,
resin flowed.
Kigo: 蝉 Semi — Cicada [Summer / Dobutsu]

Poem: 梢より　あだに落ちけり　蝉のから
Romaji:
Kozue yori
ada ni ochikeri
semi no kara
My translation:
From tree-top
in vain it fell,
a cicada shell.
Kigo: 空蝉 Utsusemi — Cicada Shell [Summer / Dobutsu]

Poem: わくらばに　取り付いて　蝉の　もぬけかな
Romaji:
Wakuraba ni
tori tsuite semi no
monuke kana
My translation:
Clinging to a
worm-eaten leaf, a cicada's
discarded shell.
Kigo: 空蝉 Utsusemi — Cicada Shell [Summer / Dobutsu]

Poem: 蓋すれば　出て行く　蠅の羽音かな
Romaji:
Futa sureba
dite yuku hae no
haoto kana
My translation:
Putting on the cover,
it left —
the fly's wing sounds.
Kigo: 蠅 Hae — Flies [Summer / Dobutsu]

Poem: 蠅散って　且う　白しや　盆の糊
Romaji:
Hae chitte
katsu shiroshi ya
bon no nori
My translation:
The flies scatter,
for a moment white —
the tray's starch.
Kigo: 蠅 Hae — Flies [Summer / Dobutsu]

Poem: やれうつな　蠅は手をする　足をする
Romaji:
Yare utsuna
hae wa te wo suru
ashi wo suru
My translation:
Don't swat it!
The fly rubs its hands,
its feet.
Kigo: 蠅 Hae — Flies [Summer / Dobutsu]
Notes: To put the hands together and rub them is a sign of reverence and prayers. When the fly does this, we should feel pity for it. Issa shows his deep sympathy for all living things.

Poem: わが宿は　蚊のちいさきを　馳走也
Romaji:
Waga yado wa
ka no chiisaki wo
chiso nari
My translation:
My house —
tiny mosquitoes
are the treat.
Kigo: 蚊 Ka — Mosquito [Summer / Dobutsu]

Poem: 蚊ばしらの　際ほのぼのと　三日の月
Romaji:
Kabashira no
kiwa honobono to
mika no tsuki
My translation:
A swarm of mosquitoes —
at their edge, dimly,
a crescent moon.
Kigo: 蚊 Ka — Mosquito [Summer / Dobutsu]

Poem: 昼の蚊を　後にかくす　仏かな
Romaji:
Hiru no ka wo
ushiro ni kakusu
hotoke kana
My translation:
A daytime mosquito,
the Buddha hides it
behind him.
Kigo: 蚊 Ka — Mosquito [Summer / Dobutsu]

Poem: 蟻の道　雲の峰より　つづきけん
Romaji:
Ari no michi
kumo no mine yori
tsuzukiken
Kigo: 蟻 Ari — Ants [Summer / Dobutsu]

Poem: なめくぢり　這ひて光るや　古具足
Romaji:
Namekujiri
haite hikaru ya
furu gusoku
My translation:
The slug
crawling, its old
armour shines.
Kigo: 蛞蝓 Namekuji — Slug [Summer / Dobutsu]

Poem: 何事を　壁に書きてや　蛞蝓
Romaji:
Nanigoto wo
kabe ni kakite ya
namekujiri
My translation:
It's written
something on the wall —
the slug.
Kigo: 蛞蝓 Namekuji — Slug [Summer / Dobutsu]

Poem: かたつぶり　角ふりわけよ　須磨明石
Romaji:
Katatsuburi
tsuno furiwake yo
Suma Akashi
My translation:
Oh, snail,
wave your horns apart,
Suma, Akashi.
Kigo: 蝸牛 Katatsumuri — Snail [Summer / Dobutsu]
Notes: Suma and Akashi are two townships west of Kobe City. In the Genji Monogatari, chapter on Suma, it says, "Akashi bay is at a distance to which one can crawl," meaning very near. The word relates the snail to Suma and Akashi.

Poem: 今朝見れば　夜の歩や　かたつぶり
Romaji:
Kesa mireba
yoru no ayumi ya
katatsubari
My translation:
In the morning see
its walk of last night —
the snail.
Kigo: 蝸牛 Katatsumuri — Snail [Summer / Dobutsu]

Poem: 点滴に　うたれて籠る　蝸牛
Romaji:
Tenteki ni
utarete komoru
katatsumuri
My translation:
Hit by a drop
of water, the snail withdraws
from the world.
Kigo: 蝸牛 Katatsumuri — Snail [Summer / Dobutsu]

Poem: なつかしや　若葉に残る　花の蕊
Romaji:
Natsukashi ya
wakaba ni nokoru
hana no shibe
My translation:
How endearing!
Among young leaves, remnants of
flower pistils.
Kigo: 余花 Yoka — Remnants of Flowers [Summer / Shokubutsu]

Poem: 古庭に　蟻　来たりたる　牡丹哉
Romaji:
Furu niwa ni
ari kitaritaru
botan kana
My translation:
To an old garden
the ants have come —
peonies in bloom.
Kigo: 牡丹 Botan — Peony [Summer / Shokubutsu]

Poem: 牡丹散りて　うちかさなりぬ　二三片
Romaji:
Botan chirite
uchi kasanarinu
ni san ben
My translation:
A peony scatters —
one on another, two,
three petals.
Kigo: 牡丹 Botan — Peony [Summer / Shokubutsu]

Poem: 飛ぶ蝶を　喰はんとしたる　牡丹哉
Romaji:
Tobu cho wo
kuwan to shitaru
botan kana
My translation:
A flitting butterfly
it's about to swallow —
the peony.
Kigo: 牡丹 Botan — Peony [Summer / Shokubutsu]

Poem: 白牡丹　崩れんとして　二日見る
Romaji:
Shiro botan
kuzuren to shite
futsuka miru
My translation:
A white peony,
about to crumble,
for two days.
Kigo: 牡丹 Botan — Peony [Summer / Shokubutsu]

Poem: 針ありと　蝶に知らせん　花薔薇
Romaji:
Hari ari to
cho ni shirasen
hana sobi
Kigo: 薔薇 Bara — Rose [Summer / Shokubutsu]

Poem: 駿河路や　花橘も　茶の匂ひ
Romaji:
Suruga-ji ya
Hana tachibana mo
cha no nioi
My translation:
The road through Suruga —
even the citrus flowers
have the scent of tea.
Kigo: 花橘 Hana tachibana — Citrus Flower [Summer / Shokubutsu]
Notes: Suruga is the old name for Shizuoka prefecture, famous for both citrus flowers and tea bushes, which flourish around the same time.

Poem: 橘や　下に落ちたる　鳥の糞
Romaji:
Tachibana ya
shita ni ochitaru
tori no fun
My translation:
Citrus flowers —
under them has fallen
bird dung.
Kigo: 花橘 Hana tachibana — Citrus Flower [Summer / Shokubutsu]

Poem: 世に薫る　花橘やちる跡も
Romaji:
Yo ni kaoru
hana tachibana ya
chiru ato mo
My translation:
A citrus flower
perfumes the world,
even after scattering.
Kigo: 花橘 Hana tachibana — Citrus Flower [Summer / Shokubutsu]

Poem: あぢさゐの　花や手鞠の　染めかへし
Romaji:
Ajisai no
hana ya temari no
some kaeshi
My translation:
Hydrangea
flowers — like hand-balls
re-dyed.
Kigo: 紫陽花 Ajisai — Hydrangea [Summer / Shokubutsu]

Poem: 紫陽花や　寄れば　蚊の鳴く　花の裏
Romaji:
Ajisai ya
yoreba ka no naku
hana no ura
My translation:
Hydrangeas —
if you get close, mosquitoes hum
behind the flowers.
Kigo: 紫陽花 Ajisai — Hydrangea [Summer / Shokubutsu]

Poem: 紫陽花の　末　一色と　なりにけり
Romaji:
Ajisai no
sue iashoku to
nari ni keri
My translation:
The end of
hydrangeas — all became
one colour.
Kigo: 紫陽花 Ajisai — Hydrangea [Summer / Shokubutsu]

Poem: うれしさは　葉がくれ　梅の　ひとつかな
Romaji:
Ureshisa wa
hagakure ume no
hitotsu kana
My translation:
The joy —
to find a plum
hidden in leaves!
Kigo: 青梅 Ao ume — Green Plums [Summer / Shokubutsu]

Poem: 青梅に　眉　あつめたる　美人哉
Romaji:
Ao ume ni
mayei atsume taru
bijin kana
My translation:
At the green plum
her eyebrows gathered,
a beautiful woman.
Kigo: 青梅 Ao ume — Green Plums [Summer / Shokubutsu]

Poem: 青梅や　酸い顔もせず　男の童
Romaji:
Ao ume ya
sui gao mo sezu
o no warawa
My translation:
Green plums —
the little boy doesn't make
a sour face.
Kigo: 青梅 Ao ume — Green Plums [Summer / Shokubutsu]

Poem: 青梅に　手をかけて寝る　蛙かな
Romaji:
Ao ume ni
te wo kakete neru
kawazu kana
My translation:
On a green plum
its hand placed,
the frog asleep.
Kigo: 青梅 Ao ume — Green Plums [Summer / Shokubutsu]

Poem: 先づ頼む　椎の木もあり　夏木立
Romaji:
Mazu tanomu
shii no ki mo ari
natsu kodachi
My translation:
First, a pasania
tree to rely on,
summer grove.
Kigo: 夏木立 Natsu kodachi — Summer Grove [Summer / Shokubutsu]
Notes: A ku of 1690, made on settling briefly in a hut called Genjuan (Abide in Transience Hut), after a long journey. The pasania is a solid evergreen that can grow to 20 meters in height.

Poem: 甘き香は　何の花ぞも　夏木立
Romaji:
Amaki ka wa
nan no hana zo mo
natsu kodachi
My translation:
The sweet scent —
what flower could it be?
Summer grove.
Kigo: 夏木立 Natsu kodachi — Summer Grove [Summer / Shokubutsu]

Poem: 塔ばかり　見えて東寺は　夏木立
Romaji:
To bakari
miete Toji wa
natsu kodachi
My translation:
Only a pagoda
can be seen, the East Temple,
a summer grove.
Kigo: 夏木立 Natsu kodachi — Summer Grove [Summer / Shokubutsu]

Poem: 嵐山　薮の茂りや　風の筋
Romaji:
Arashiyama
yabu no shigeri ya
kaze no suji
My translation:
Arashi mountain —
through the luxuriance of groves
a line of the wind.
Kigo: 茂 Shigeri — Luxuriant Growth [Summer / Shokubutsu]

Poem: 光り合ふ　二つの山の　茂りかな
Romaji:
Hikari au
futatsu no yama no
shigeri kana
My translation:
Reflecting their lustre:
the luxuriant growth of
two mountains.
Kigo: 茂 Shigeri — Luxuriant Growth [Summer / Shokubutsu]

Poem: 山深く　しげりに入りぬ　夕がらす
Romaji:
Yama fukaku
shigeri ni irimu
yu garasu
My translation:
Deep into a mountain's
luxuriant growth,
a dusk crow.
Kigo: 茂 Shigeri — Luxuriant Growth [Summer / Shokubutsu]

Poem: 須磨寺や　吹かぬ笛聞く　木下闇
Romaji:
Suma dera ya
fukanu fue kiku
Koshita yami
My translation:
Suma temple —
an unblown flute heard,
under-trees darkness.
Kigo: 木下闇 Ko no shita yami — Under-Trees Darkness [Summer / Shokubutsu]
Notes: Suma temple has among its treasures a flute called Aoba (Green Leaf) that belonged to Taira Atsumori (1169–84). He was beheaded in the battle of Ichi no Tani by Kumagaya Naozane, an episode reproduced in Kabuki and Noh drama. Basho felt as though he heard the flute in the wind through the lonely, deep grove.

Poem: 霧雨に　木の下闇の　紙帳かな
Romaji:
Kirisame ni
ko no shita yami no
shicho kana
My translation:
In misty rain
the under-trees darkness
mosquito net.
Kigo: 木下闇 Ko no shita yami — Under-Trees Darkness [Summer / Shokubutsu]

Poem: 下闇に　乾かぬ　関伽の　しづくかな
Romaji:
Shita yami ni
kawakanu aka no
shizuku kana
My translation:
In under-trees darkness
lustral water doesn't dry,
water drops.
Kigo: 木下闇 Ko no shita yami — Under-Trees Darkness [Summer / Shokubutsu]

Poem: 不二ひとつ　うづみ残して　わかばかな
Romaji:
Fuji hitotsu
uzumi nokoshite
wakaba kana
My translation:
Only Mt. Fuji
left uncovered —
young leaves.
Kigo: 若葉・青葉 Wakaba, Aoba — Young Leaves / Green Leaves [Summer / Shokubutsu]

Poem: 里の灯を　ふくみて　雨の若葉かな
Romaji:
Sato no hi wo
fukumite ame no
wakaba kana
My translation:
The village lamps
shine in them,
young leaves in the rain.
Kigo: 若葉・青葉 Wakaba, Aoba — Young Leaves / Green Leaves [Summer / Shokubutsu]

Poem: 三井寺や　日は午にせまる　若楓
Romaji:
Miidera ya
hi wa go ni semaru
waka kaede
My translation:
Mii temple —
the sun presses on to noon,
young maple leaves.
Kigo: 若楓 Waka kaede — Young Maple Leaves [Summer / Shokubutsu]

Poem: 清滝や　波に散り込む　青松葉
Romaji:
Kiyotaki ya
nami ni chiri komu
ao matsuba
My translation:
Kiyotaki —
into its waves scatter
green pine needles.
Kigo: 常緑木落葉 Tokiwagi ochiba — Evergreens' Fallen Leaves [Summer / Shokubutsu]
Notes: Kiyotaki river is the upper stream of Arashiyama in Kyoto, and runs into Oi river.

Poem: 卯の花をかざしに　関の晴着かな
Romaji:
Uno hana wo
kazashi ni seki no
haregi kana
My translation:
Deutzia flowers
in the hair, our fine dress
at the barrier.
Kigo: 卯の花 Unohana — Deutzia Flowers [Summer / Shokubutsu]
Notes: A ku of 1689, on a journey to the northern provinces with Basho, at Shirakawa barrier. Old poets wrote of this custom and of the deutzia at this barrier. The writers, being poor pilgrims, could only wear deutzia boughs as hair ornaments.

Poem: うの花に　芦毛の馬の　夜明かな
Romaji:
Uno hana ni
ashige no uma no
yo ake kana
My translation:
Among deutzia flowers,
on a chestnut horse
dawn comes.
Kigo: 卯の花 Unohana — Deutzia Flowers [Summer / Shokubutsu]
Notes: He started his journey before the sun rose. As the light of daybreak broadened, the deutzia along the road increasingly added their whiteness.

Poem: 卯の花の中に崩れし　庵かな
Romaji:
Uno hana no
naka ni kuzure shi
iori kana
My translation:
Among deutzia
flowers, a tumbled-down
hut.
Kigo: 卯の花 Unohana — Deutzia Flowers [Summer / Shokubutsu]
Notes: The remains of a broken down hut where deutzia bloom in confusion makes the writer wonder who might have lived there before.

Poem: 花と針の　心問ひたき　茨かな
Romaji:
Hana to hari no
kokoro toitaki
ibara kana
My translation:
Would like to ask,
why thorns with these flowers?
field roses.
Kigo: 茨の花 Ibara no hana — Field Rose [Summer / Shokubutsu]

Poem: 茨さくや　茶碗の欠けも　散りまじり
Romaji:
Ibara saku ya
chawan no kake mo
chiri majiri
My translation:
Field roses bloom —
chips of a tea cup
also scattered.
Kigo: 茨の花 Ibara no hana — Field Rose [Summer / Shokubutsu]

Poem: 花茨　灯かげに　針の　かくれけり
Romaji:
Hana ibara
hikage ni
hari no
kakuru ken
My translation:
Field rose flowers —
by lamplight the thorns
were hidden.
Kigo: 茨の花 Ibara no hana — Field Rose [Summer / Shokubutsu]

Poem: 若竹や　竹より出でて　青き事
Romaji:
Wakatake ya
take yori idete
aoki koto
My translation:
Young bamboo —
coming out from bamboo,
so green!
Kigo: 若竹 Waketake — Young Bamboo [Summer / Shokubutsu]

Poem: 若竹や　煙のいづる　庫裏の窓
Romaji:
Wake take ya
kemuri no izuru
kuri no mado
My translation:
Young bamboo —
the smoke from the temple
kitchen window.
Kigo: 若竹 Waketake — Young Bamboo [Summer / Shokubutsu]

Poem: 白芥子や　時雨の花の　咲きつらん
Romaji:
Shira geshi ya
shigure no hana no
saki tsuran
My translation:
White poppies —
as though flowers of joy rain
have bloomed.
Kigo: 罌粟の花 Keshi no hana — Poppy Flowers [Summer / Shokubutsu]

Poem: あるとなきと　二本さしけり　けしの花
Romaji:
Aru to naki to
nihon sashi keri
keshi no hana
My translation:
One with petals,
one without — two were arranged,
poppy flowers.
Kigo: 罌粟の花 Keshi no hana — Poppy Flowers [Summer / Shokubutsu]

Poem: 僧となる　子のうつくしや　けしの花
Romaji:
So to naru
ko no utsukushi ya
keshi no hana
My translation:
The child who's
to be a monk, beautiful!
Poppy flowers.
Kigo: 罌粟の花 Keshi no hana — Poppy Flowers [Summer / Shokubutsu]

Poem: 杜若　べたりと　鳶のたれてける
Romaji:
Kakitsubate
betari to tobi no
tarete keru
My translation:
Flower de luce —
"plop", a kite dropped
his dung.
Kigo: 杜若 Kakitsubata — Flower De Luce [Summer / Shokubutsu]

Poem: ことぶきや　亀のひたいの　花あやめ
Romaji:
Kotobuki ya
kame no hitai no
hana ayame
My translation:
Auspicious!
By the turtle's forehead,
a blue flag.
Kigo: あやめ Ayame — Blue Flag [Summer / Shokubutsu]

Poem: あやめ草　足にむすばん　草靴の緒
Romaji:
Ayama gusa
ashi ni musuban
waraji no o
My translation:
Acorus grass,
I'll tie on my feet,
as sandal straps.
Kigo: 菖蒲 Shobu — Acorus [Summer / Shokubutsu]
Notes: He received two pairs of straw sandals on leaving on a walking tour of the northern provinces; acorus will help give him a safe journey.

Poem: 玉水の　菖蒲を走る　匂ひかな
Romaji:
Tama mizu no
shobu wo hashiru
nioi kana
My translation:
Pure water drops
rush through the acorus —
the perfume.
Kigo: 菖蒲 Shobu — Acorus [Summer / Shokubutsu]

Poem: 湯上りの　尻にべったり　菖蒲かな
Romaji:
Yu agari no
shiri ni bettari
shobu kana
My translation:
On the rump
just out of the bath,
an acorus leaf.
Kigo: 菖蒲 Shobu — Acorus [Summer / Shokubutsu]

Romaji:
hototogisu
koi ni nenu yo no
wakakarishi
Kigo: 時鳥 【ほととぎす】 hototogisu, little cuckoo [kanji literally "bird of time"] (all summer).
Keene Dawn:
The nightingales—
When I was young it was love
That kept me awake.

Romaji:
chi wo nagasu
ame ya orifushi
hototogisu
Kigo: 時鳥 【ほととぎす】 hototogisu, little cuckoo [kanji literally "bird of time"] (all summer).
Notes: 血が洗われる (chi ga arawareru) = blood washed away. The rain washes away blood. Hototogisu sings at a moment of violence.
Keene Dawn:
Rain washes away
The blood: just at that moment
A nightingale sings.

Poem: 糸瓜咲いて痰のつまりし仏かな
Romaji:
hechima saite
tan no tsumarishi
hotoke kana
Kigo: 糸瓜 【へちま】 hechima, sponge gourd / luffa (all autumn).
Notes: Shiki's famous deathbed poem. The sponge gourd blooms outside; he lies inside choking. Composed three days before his death, Sep 18, 1902.
Keene Dawn:
The sponge-gourd has flowered!
Look at the Buddha
Choked with phlegm.

Poem: 鶏頭の十四五本もありぬべし
Romaji:
keitō no
jūshigo hon mo
arinu beshi
My translation: test trans
Kigo: 鶏頭 【けいとう】 keitō, cockscomb(s) (all autumn).
Notes: One of Shiki's most debated poems. Obsessively precise realist count of 14 or 15 cockscomb stalks.
Keene Dawn:
Cockscomb—
I'm sure there are at least 
Fourteen or fifteen stalks.

Poem: 低く飛ぶ畦のいなごや日の弱り
Romaji:
hikuku tobu
aze no inago ya
hi no yowari
Kigo: locust
Notes: 日の弱り (hi no yowari) = the sun weakening. Locusts flying low; the autumn sun waning—precise observation of season's decline.
Keene Dawn:
See how low it flies.
That locust on the paddy walk—
The sunshine weakens.

Romaji:
akikane ni 
koborete akashi
hamigakiko"
Keene Dawn:
Spilling over 
In the spring breeze, how red—
My tooth powder!

Romaji:
ikutabi mo
yuki no fukasa wo
tazunekeri
Keene Dawn:
Again and again
I asked the others how much
Snow had fallen.

Romaji:
nagaki hi ya                                                                                         
roba wo oiyuku                                                                                    
muchi no kage
Keene Dawn:
The long days—
the shadow of a lash
Chases a donkey.

Romaji:
hatsuaki no
ishidan takashi
sugi kodachi
Kigo: early autumn
Keene Dawn:
The stone flight of steps
Looms high in early autumn 
Amidst the cedars.

Poem: 山の湯泉や裸の上の天の川
Romaji:
yama no yu ya
hadaka no ue no
ama-no-gawa
Kigo: 天の川 【あまのがわ】 ama-no-gawa, Milky Way (mid autumn).
Notes: Hot-spring bathers naked under the Milky Way—a boldly physical juxtaposition of the earthly and celestial.
Ueda Haiku:
Hot spring in the mountains:
high above the naked bathers
the River of Heaven.

Poem: 妹に群書よまする夜長かな
Romaji:
imotō ni
gunsho yomasuru
yonaga kana
Kigo: 夜長 【よなが】 yonaga, long night (all autumn).
Notes: 群書 (gunsho) = ancient war chronicles. Young sister reading aloud on the long autumn night—domestic intimacy of a sick man.
Ueda Haiku:
My young sister
reads me an ancient war epic
this endless night.

Poem: 秋寒し眼の光る鬼女の面
Romaji:
aki samushi
manako no hikaru
kijo no men
Kigo: 秋寒し 【あきさむし】 aki samushi, autumn chill (all autumn).
Notes: 鬼女の面 (kijo no men) = demon-woman Noh mask. In the autumn chill, the mask's glaring eyes seem terrifyingly alive.
Ueda Haiku:
Autumn chill:
with eyes glaring, there hangs
the mask of a demoness.

Poem: 蛇逃げて山静かなり百合の花
Romaji:
hebi nigete
yama shizuka-nari
yuri no hana
Kigo: 百合の花 【ゆりのはな】 yuri no hana, lily (all summer).
Notes: 蛇逃げて (hebi nigete) = after the snake flees. The forest suddenly silent after the snake vanishes; the lily presides.
Ueda Haiku:
After the snake flees,
how quiet the forest is!
A lily flower.

Poem: 絶えず人いこふ夏野の石一つ
Romaji:
taezu hito
ikou natsuno no
ishi hitotsu
Kigo: 夏野 【なつの】 natsuno, summer field(s) (all summer).
Notes: 絶えず (taezu) = ceaselessly. People rest on a single stone in the summer field—the stone as timeless witness.
Ueda Haiku:
Unceasingly 
this stone on the summer moor
rests people.

Romaji:
ganjitsu ya
karegiku nokoru
niwa nosaki
Kigo: 元日 【がんじつ】 ganjitsu, New Year's Day (New Year).
Notes: 枯菊 (karegiku) = withered chrysanthemum. New Year's Day: dead chrysanthemums from autumn linger at the garden's edge.
Ueda Haiku:
New Year’s Day:
dead chrysanthemums remain
at the garden’s edge.

Poem: 蜘殺すあとのさびしき夜寒かな
Romaji:
kumo korosu
ato no sabishiki
yosamu kana
Kigo: 夜寒 【よさむ】 yosamu, night chill (late autumn).
Notes: 蜘 (kumo) = spider. After killing a spider, loneliness descends—unexpected pathos of a small act of violence.
Ueda Haiku:
After killing
a spider how lonely I feel
in the cold of night!

Poem: 馬下りて川の名問へば秋の風
Romaji:
uma orite
kawa no na toeba
aki no kaze
Kigo: 秋風 【あきかぜ】 akikaze, autumn breeze / autumn wind [carries with it the sound of rustling leaves] (all autumn).
Notes: Getting off the horse to ask a river's name; an autumn wind blows—the query unanswered by the landscape.
Ueda Haiku:
I get down from my horse 
and ask the name of the river—
an autumnal wind.

Poem: 木の影や我が影動く冬の月
Romaji:
ki no kage ya
waga kage ugoku
fuyu no tsuki
Kigo: 冬の月 【ふゆのつき】 fuyu no tsuki, winter moon (all winter).
Notes: 木の影 (ki no kage) = shadows of trees. Tree shadows and the speaker's own shadow waver together in the winter moonlight.
Ueda Haiku:
Shadows of the trees:
my shadow wavers with them
in the winter moonlight.

Poem: 凩や鐘引きすてて道の端
Romaji:
The wintry gust:
they have left a temple bell
by the roadside.
Kigo: 木枯らし 【こがらし】 kogarashi, wintry gust (early winter).
Notes: A temple bell left abandoned by the roadside; the cold wind blows. Ref. to the Noh play Dōjōji.
Ueda Haiku:
The wintry gust:
they have left a temple bell
by the roadside.

Poem: 砂浜にきららの光る春日なか
Romaji:
sunahama ni
kirata no hikaru
haru hinaka
Kigo: 春日 【はるひ】 haruhi, a day in spring / spring day / spring sun [either or both meanings simultaneously, depending on context] (all spring).
Notes: 砂浜 (sunahama) = sandy beach. きらら (kirara) = glittering mica. Spring sunlight glittering on the sand.
Ueda Haiku:
On a sandy beach
glassy chips sparkle
in the spring sunshine.

Poem: 花散って水は南へ流れけり
Romaji:
hana chitte 
mizu wa minami e
nagare-keri
Kigo: 落花 【らっか】 rakka, （らくくわ）, falling (cherry) blossoms (late spring).
Notes: 水は南へ (mizu wa minami e) = the water flows south. Cherry petals fall; the water carries them southward.
Ueda Haiku:
Blossoms have fallen
and the water is flowing
towards the south.

Poem: 看護婦やうたた寝さめて蠅を打つ
Romaji:
kangofu ya
utatane samete
hae wo utsu
Kigo: 蠅 【はえ】 hae, fly / flies (all summer).
Notes: 看護婦 (kangofu) = nurse. A nurse dozing off, waking to swat a fly—wartime hospital reality, quiet irony.
Ueda Haiku:
My nurse,
awakening from a nap,
swats a fly.

Poem: 雲の峰硯に蟻の上りけり
Romaji:
kumo no mine
suzuri ni ari no 
nobori-keri
Kigo: 雲の峰 【くものみね】 kumo no mine, towering summer clouds (mid summer).
Notes: Thunderheads rising; an ant crawls up onto the inkstone—the monumental and the minute side by side.
Ueda Haiku:
A column of cloud—
onto my inkstone, an ant
has climbed.

Poem: 世をいとふ心薊を愛すかな
Romaji:
yo wo itou
kokoro azami wo
aisu kana
Kigo: 薊 【あざみ】 azami, thistle (late spring).
Notes: 世をいとふ (yo wo itou) = to loathe the world. The one who hates the world loves thistles—prickly beauty as consolation.
Ueda Haiku:
The heart that loathes 
this world thinks lovingly
of a thistle.

Poem: 雪解や竹はね返る日の表
Romaji:
yukidoke ya
take hanekaeru
hi no omote
Kigo: 雪解 【ゆきどけ】 yukidoke, snowmelt (mid spring).
Notes: 竹はね返る (take hanekuru) = bamboo snapping back. Snow melting; bamboo springs back into the sunlight.
Ueda Haiku:
The snow melts:
bamboos uncoil themselves
where the sunlight falls.

Poem: ある僧の月を待たずに帰りけり
Romaji:
aru sō no
tsuki wo matazu ni
kaeri-keri
Kigo: 月 【つき】 tsuki, moon (mid autumn).
Notes: ある僧 (aru sō) = a certain monk. The monk leaves without waiting for the moon to rise—enigmatic departure.
Ueda Haiku:
A Buddhist monk
without waiting  for the moonrise
takes his leave.

Poem: 愛憎は蠅打って蟻に与へけり
Romaji:
aizō wa
hae utte ari ni
atae-keri
Kigo: 蠅 【はえ】 hae, fly (all summer).
Notes: 愛憎 (aizō) = love and hate. Swatting a fly and giving it to an ant—the dialectic of love and hate enacted on insects.
Ueda Haiku:
For love and for hate
I swat a fly and offer it
to an ant.

Poem: 初暦五月の中に死ぬ日あり
Romaji:
hatsugoyomi
gogatsu no naka ni
shinu hi ari
Kigo: 初暦 【はつごよみ】 hatsugoyomi, new calendar [literally "first (use of the new) calendar"] (New Year).
Notes: Looking through the new year's calendar—finding a day in May marked for death. Shiki's premonition, written while ill.
Ueda Haiku:
New year’s calendar:
in the month of May there is 
a day for dying.

Poem: 棚の糸瓜思ふ所へぶら下がる
Romaji:
tana no hechima
omou tokoro e
burasagaru
Kigo: 糸瓜 【へちま】 hechima, sponge gourd / luffa (all autumn).
Notes: 棚の糸瓜 (tana no hechima) = the gourd on the shelf. The gourd dangles where it wants to—the sick man finds comfort in its self-determination.
Ueda Haiku:
From the trellis
sponge gourds dangle down, each one
where it pleases.

Poem: ある僧の月を待たずの帰りけり
Romaji:
aru sō no
tsuki wo matazu no
kaeri keri
Kigo: 月 【つき】 tsuki, moon (mid autumn).
Notes: Variant of Row 27. ある僧の月を待たずの帰りけり.
21 Century:
A certain monk
has gone without waiting
for the moon to rise

Poem: いくたびも雪の深さを尋ねけり
Romaji:
ikutabi mo
yuki no fukusa wo
tazune keri
Kigo: 雪 【ゆき】 yuki, snow (all winter).
Notes: いくたびも (iku tabi mo) = again and again. Shiki bedridden, repeatedly asking how deep the snow has fallen—yearning for the outside world.
21 Century:
How many times
I asked how deep
the snow was

Poem: 柿食えば鐘が鳴るなり法隆寺
Romaji:
kaki kueba   
kane ga naru nari  
hōryūji
My translation:
I bite the persimmon 
and the bell starts booming
Hōryūji Temple
Kigo: persimmon
Notes: 法隆寺 (Hōryūji). Eating a persimmon; the bell of Hōryūji tolls—one of Shiki's most celebrated poems.
Other translation:
As I eat a persimmon
I hear the temple bell toll:
Hōryūji. Keene Dawn

Romaji:
gantan ya
fudoshi tatande
makuragami
Keene Dawn:
It’s New Year’s morning!
A neatly folded loincloth
Above my pillow.

Romaji:
jirōshu no
you hodo mo naku
samenikeri
Keene Dawn:
Before I could get drunk
On that sake that cures deafness
I was sober again.

Romaji:
hyakushō ni
hibari agatte
yo aketari
Keene Dawn:
A skylark soars,
And for the farmers
The day has dawned.

Poem: 冬蜂の死にどころなく歩きけり
Romaji:
fuyu hachi no
shini dokoro naku
aruki keri
Kigo: cold bee
Notes: Kijo was deaf and struggled in life so he may have seen himself in the bee
Ueda Haiku:
A bee in winter
without anywhere to die
goes wandering on
Other translation:
The bee in winter
Walks around,nowhere for him
To lay  down and die. Keene,Dawn

Poem: 夏草を這ひ上りたる捨子かな
Romaji:
natsu kusa wo
haiagari-taru
sutego kana
Kigo: 夏草 【なつくさ】 natsukusa, summer grasses (all summer).
Notes: 捨子 (sutego) = abandoned child. A child crawling up through summer grass—Kijō's characteristic pathos for the helpless.
Ueda Haiku:
Crawling up and up
on a blade of summer grass
an abandoned silkworm.

Poem: 今朝秋や見入る鏡に親の顔
Romaji:
kesa aki ya
miiru kagami ni
oya no kao
Kigo: 今朝の秋 【けさのあき】 kesa no aki, first morning of autumn (early autumn).
Notes: 親の顔 (oya no kao) = parent's face. Looking in the mirror on the first autumn morning—seeing one's parent's aging face.
Ueda Haiku:
First autumn morning:
the mirror I stare into
shows my father’s face.

Poem: 小春日や石を嚙み居る赤蜻蛉
Romaji:
koharubi ya
ishi wo kami iru
akatonbo
Kigo: 小春 【こはる】 koharu, Indian summer / little spring (early winter).
Notes: 赤蜻蛉 (aka tombo) = red dragonfly. An autumn dragonfly biting a stone in the warm late-season sun.
Ueda Haiku:
Balmy autumn day:
on a stone, biting it,
a red dragonfly.

Poem: 冬の日や前に塞がる己が影
Romaji:
fuyu no hi ya
mae ni fusagaru 
ono ga kage
Kigo: 冬の日 【ふゆのひ】 fuyu no hi, winter sun (all winter).
Notes: 己が影 (onore ga kage) = one's own shadow. The winter sun casts the shadow directly in the path forward—inescapable self.
Ueda Haiku:
The winter sun:
blocking the way ahead of me,
my own shadow.

Poem: 己が影を慕ふて這へる地虫かな
Romaji:
ono ga kage wo
shitōte haeru
jimushi kana
Kigo: 地虫 【じむし】 jimushi, grub / earthworm (spring).
Notes: 己が影を慕ふて (onore ga kage wo shitaite) = yearning after one's own shadow. A grub following its own shadow—self-pursuit, loneliness.
Ueda Haiku:
Yearning towards
its own shadow, there creeps
a grab.

Poem: 世を恋うて人をおそるる余寒かな
Romaji:
yo wo kōte 
hito wo osoruru
jimushi kana
Kigo: 余寒 【よかん】 yokan, remaining cold (early spring).
Notes: 世を恋うて (yo wo koute) = loving the world. Loving the world yet fearing people—social anxiety in the lingering cold.
Ueda Haiku:
I long to go out,
yet I am fearful of people—
cold season lingers.

Poem: 春の夜や灯を囲み居る盲者達
Romaji:
haru no yo ya
hi wo kakomi iru 
mekura-tachi
Kigo: 春の夜 【はるのよ】 haru no yo, spring night (all spring).
Notes: 盲者達 (mōsha-tachi) = blind people. Blind people gathered around a lamp on a spring night—Kijō's sympathy for the handicapped (he was deaf).
Ueda Haiku:
Spring night:
sitting around a lamp, relax
blind men in a group.

Poem: さみだれや起き上がりたる根無し草
Romaji:
samidare ya 
okiagari-taru 
nenashi-gusa
Kigo: 五月雨 【さみだれ】 samidare, early summer rains (mid summer).
Notes: 根無し草 (ne-nashi-gusa) = rootless grass. Rising up in the summer rains—the uprooted person finds unexpected energy.
Ueda Haiku:
Long rainy days:
a weed. cut at the root,
raises its head.

Poem: しらしらと人踏まで暮るる落花かな
Romaji:
shira-shira to
hito fumade kururu
rakka kana
Kigo: 落花 【らっか】 rakka, （らくくわ）, falling (cherry) blossoms (late spring).
Notes: 人踏まで (hito fumade) = untrodden by people. Blossoms falling white and white in the evening, no one walking on them.
Ueda Haiku:
How white they are!
It darkens, no one trampling
the fallen blossoms.

Poem: 浮草や蜘蛛渡りゐて水平ら
Romaji:
ukikusa ya
kumo watari-ite
mizu taira
Kigo: 浮草 【うきくさ】 ukikusa, duckweed (all summer).
Notes: 蜘蛛渡りゐて (kumo watariite) = a spider crossing. A spider walking across duckweed, the water perfectly flat beneath.
Ueda Haiku:
Floating duckweed:
a spider passes over it
the water, calm.

Poem: 御仏のお顔しみや秋の雨
Romaji:
mihotoke no
okao no shimi ya
aki no ame
Kigo: 秋の雨 【あきのあめ】 aki no ame, autumn rain (all autumn).
Notes: 御仏のお顔 (mihotoke no okao) = the face of the Buddha. Stains on the Buddha's face in the autumn rain—pathos of aged devotional objects.
Ueda Haiku:
On the Buddha’s 
august face some pockmarks show:
autumnal rain.

Poem: 水泡の相依れば消ゆ蓮の花
Romaji:
suihō no 
aiyoreba kiyu
hasu no hana
Kigo: 蓮の花 【はすのはな】 hasu no hana, lotus flower (all summer).
Notes: 水泡 (suihō) = water bubbles. Water bubbles clinging together then dissolving—Buddhist impermanence at the lotus pond.
Ueda Haiku:
The moment two bubbles
are united, they both vanish.
A lotus blooms.

Poem: 冬蜂の死にどころなく歩きかり
Romaji:
fuyu-bachi no
shinidokoro naku
aruki-keri
Kigo: 冬蜂 【ふゆばち】 fuyubachi, winter bee (all winter).
Notes: Variant of Row 37. Winter bee with nowhere to die, still walking.
Ueda Haiku:
A winter hornet
without a place to die
staggers along.

Poem: 水すまし水に跳て水鉄の如し
Romaji:
mizu-samushi
mizu ni hanete mizu
tetsu no gotoshi
Kigo: 水馬 【あめんぼう】 amenbō, water strider(s) [family Gerridae], (all summer).
Notes: 水に跳て (mizu ni hane) = leaping on the water. The water strider skips across—quick as iron.
Ueda Haiku:
A water spider
bounces on the water, and
the water is like steel.

Poem: 冬川や小さき石に浪の花
Romaji:
fuyu kawa ya
chiisaki ishi ni
nami no kana
Kigo: 冬川 【ふゆかわ】 fuyukawa, winter river (all winter).
Notes: 浪の花 (nami no hana) = wave flowers. Small stones in the winter river catching the wave-foam.
Ueda Haiku:
A winter stream:
abloom on a little stone,
blossoms of water.

Poem: 春雨やたしかに見たる石の精
Romaji:
harusame ya
tashika ni mi-taru
ishi no sei
Kigo: 春雨 【はるさめ】 harusame, spring rain (all spring).
Notes: 石の精 (ishi no sei) = the spirit of the stone. In the spring rain, Kijō sees the stone's spirit clearly.
Ueda Haiku:
Spring rain:
I am certain I saw
the spirits of stones.

Poem: 春寒やぶつかり歩く盲犬
Romaji:
haru-samu ya
butsukari aruku
mekura inu
Kigo: 春寒 【はるさむ】 haruzamu, spring cold (early spring).
Notes: 盲犬 (mōken) = blind dog. A blind dog bumbling through the spring cold—Kijō's empathy for sightless creatures.
Ueda Haiku:
Cold day in spring:
bumping into this and that,
a blind dog walking.

Poem: 静かさに堪へでたにしの移りけり
Romaji:
shizukasa ni
taede tanishi no
utsuri-keri
Kigo: 田螺 【たにし】 tanishi, mud-snail(s)/paddy-snail(s) (all spring).
Notes: 静かさに堪へで (shizukasa ni taede) = unable to bear the quiet. The pond snail moves—unable to endure the stillness.
Ueda Haiku:
Not able to bear
the stillness, a mud snail
has moved!

Poem: 秋暑し草の実につくむら雀
Romaji:
aki atsushi 
kusa no mi ni tsuku
mura-suzume
Kigo: 秋暑し 【あきあつし】 aki atsushi, autumn heat (early autumn).
Notes: 草の実 (kusa no mi) = grass seeds. Sparrows clinging to grass seeds in the autumn heat.
Ueda Haiku:
Hot autumn day—
swarming to the grass seed,
a flock of sparrows.

Poem: 土くれをかかへて死ぬる螽かな
Romaji:
tsuchikure wo
kakaete shinuru
inago kana
Kigo: 螽 【きりぎりす】 kirigirisu, cricket (all autumn).
Notes: 土くれをかかへて (tsuchi kure wo kakaete) = clutching a clod of earth. A cricket dying while clasping a clod of earth—poignant final embrace.
Ueda Haiku:
Clutching a lump
of earth, it lies dying—
a grasshopper.

Poem: よき衣のつめたき裏や春浅き
Romaji:
yoki kinu no
tsumetaki ura ya
haru asashi
My translation:
a fine kimono    
how cool lining feels―    
spring is shallow
Kigo: Shallow spring

Romaji:
natsu asaki
kusa-bana mise ya
tane mo uru
My translation:
the arboretum
in shallow summerー
seed are also for sale
Kigo: 春浅し haru asashi

Romaji:
kiri ki naru
ichi ni ugoku ya
kagebōshi
Keene Dawn:
See how it hovers
In these streets of yellow fog,
A human shadow.

Poem: 雀来て障子にうごく花の影
Romaji:
susume kite
shōji ni ugoku
hana no kage
Kigo: 花の影 【はなのかげ】 hana no kage, blossom shadow (mid spring).
Notes: 雀来て (suzume kite) = a sparrow comes. A sparrow lands; its shadow trembles on the shoji screen—delicate visual poetry.
Ueda Haiku:
When a sparrow arrives
they move on the sliding screen,
shadows of the blossoms.

Poem: 炭竃に葛這ひ上る枯れながら
Romaji:
sumigama ni
kazura hai-agaru
kare nagara
Kigo: 炭竃 【すみがま】 sumigama, charcoal kiln (all winter).
Notes: 葛這ひ上る (kuzu hairagaru) = kudzu vines climbing. Kudzu climbing up an old charcoal kiln even as it withers—life in decay.
Ueda Haiku:
Onto a charcoal kiln
a vine keeps climbing, while
being burnt to death.

Poem: 時雨るるや泥猫眠る経の上
Romaji:
shigururu ya
doroneko nemuru
kyō no ue
Kigo: 時雨 【しぐれ】 shigure, winter drizzle (early winter).
Notes: 泥猫 (doro neko) = a muddy cat. A muddy cat sleeping on a sutra—comic juxtaposition of sacred and worldly.
Ueda Haiku:
Is it showering?
A muddy cat is asleep
on a Buddhist sutra.

Poem: 秋の空名もなき山の愈高し
Romaji:
aki no sora
na mo naki yama no
nao takashi
Kigo: 秋の空 【あきのそら】 aki no sora, autumn sky (all autumn).
Notes: In the autumn sky, a nameless mountain seems to grow ever taller—the anonymous sublime.
Ueda Haiku:
Against the autumn sky
a nameless mountain towers
higher than ever.

Poem: 凩や海夕日を吹き落す
Romaji:
kogarashi ya 
umi ni yūhi wo 
fuki-otosu
Kigo: wintery gust
Notes: wintery gust normally blow leaves off the trees. The metaphor is a bit much but it has a nice impact
Ueda Haiku:
The wintry gust:
it blows the evening sun down
into the ocean.

Poem: 烏飛んで夕日に動く冬木かな
Romaji:
karasu tonde
yūhi ni ugoku 
fuyuki kana
Kigo: 冬木 【ふゆき】 fuyuki, bare winter tree(s) (all winter).
Notes: 烏飛んで (karasu tonde) = a crow flies. A crow flies; in the sunset light, the winter trees seem to move.
Ueda Haiku:
The crow has flown away.
swaying in the evening sun,
a leafless tree.

Poem: 元旦に生まれぬ先の親恋し
Romaji:
ganjitsu ni
umarenu saki no
oya koishi
Kigo: 元旦 【がんたん】 gantan, New Year's morning (New Year).
Notes: 生まれぬ先の親 (umarenu mae no oya) = parents before one was born. New Year's morning brings longing for parents one never knew.
Ueda Haiku:
On New Year’s Day
I long to meet my parents
as they were before my birth.

Poem: 梅ちるや月夜に廻る水車
Romaji:
ume chiru ya
tsukiyo ni mawaru 
mizuguruma
Kigo: 梅 【うめ】 ume, （sometimes むめ mume）, plum (blossoms) [technically, the "Japanese apricot", Prunus mume; but this has almost always been translated "plum" for literary purposes] (early spring).
Notes: Plum blossoms scattering in the moonlit night; a water wheel turns—Sōseki's classical lyricism.
Ueda Haiku:
Plum blossoms fall:
turning in the moonlit night,
a water wheel.

Poem: 永き日や欠伸うつして別れ行く
Romaji:
nagaki hi ya
akubi utsushite
wakare-yuku
Kigo: 永き日 【ながきひ】 nagaki hi, long day(s) (all spring).
Notes: 欠伸うつして (akubi utsushite) = yawning contagiously. Parting with a yawn passed back and forth—the languid, endless spring day.
Ueda Haiku:
A long day:
I take over his yawning
when he leaves.

Poem: 寂として掾に鋏と牡丹哉
Romaji:
jaku toshite
en ni hasami to
botan kana
Kigo: 牡丹 【ぼたん】 botan, tree peony (early summer).
Notes: Scissors and peonies on the sill—stilled life in the quiet spring house.
Ueda Haiku:
It is quiet—
on the veranda, clippers
and peonies.

Poem: 落ちざまに蝱を伏せたる椿哉
Romaji:
ochi-zama ni
abu wo fuse-taru
tsubaki kana
Kigo: 椿 【つばき】 tsubaki, camellia(s) (all spring).
Notes: 蛱 (abu) = horsefly. A camellia falls and pins a horsefly beneath it—sudden, silent violence.
Ueda Haiku:
Falling to the ground 
it has trapped a gadfly,
a camellia flower.

Poem: 朧夜や顔に似合ぬ恋もあらん
Romaji:
oboroyo ni
kao ni niawanu 
koi mo aran
Kigo: 朧夜 【おぼろよ】 oboroyo, hazy spring night (all spring).
Notes: 顔に似合ぬ恋 (kao ni niau nu koi) = a love not suited to one's face. On this hazy night, even ill-suited love is possible.
Ueda Haiku:
Hazy moonlight night:
there must be love for
unlikely faces too.

Poem: 菫程小さき人に生れたし
Romaji:
sumire hodo
chiisaki hito ni
umare-tashi
Kigo: 菫 【すみれ】 sumire, violet(s) [Viola mandshurica] (all spring).
Notes: 小さき人 (chiisaki hito) = a small person. Wishing to be born as small as a violet—Sōseki's longing for insignificance.
Ueda Haiku:
Into a man
as tiny as a violet
may I be reborn!

Poem: 有耶無耶の柳近頃緑也
Romaji:
uyamuya no
yanagi chikagoro
midori nari
Kigo: 柳 【やなぎ】 yanagi, willow(s) / weeping willow(s) (late spring).
Notes: 有耶無耶 (uyamuya) = vague, uncertain. The willow's uncertain green has recently deepened—subtle arrival of spring.
Ueda Haiku:
That inconspicuous
willow tree—of late it has
become green!

Poem: 顔洗ふ盥に立つや秋の影
Romaji:
kao arau
tarai ni tatsu ya
aki no kage
Kigo: 秋の影 【あきのかげ】 aki no kage, autumn shadow (all autumn).
Notes: 盥 (tarai) = washbasin. Washing the face; the autumn shadow rising in the basin—surprising self-reflection.
Ueda Haiku:
In the basin, 
as I wash my face, there rises
autumn’s shadow.

Poem: 眠らざる僧の嚔や夜半の梅
Romaji:
nemurazaru
sō no kusame ya
yowa no ume
Kigo: 梅 【うめ】 ume, （sometimes むめ mume）, plum (blossoms) [technically, the "Japanese apricot", Prunus mume; but this has almost always been translated "plum" for literary purposes] (early spring).
Notes: 嚔 (kushami) = sneeze. A monk not sleeping, sneezing in the midnight plum-scented air.
Ueda Haiku:
Not yet asleep,
a Buddhist monk sneezes:
midnight plum blossoms.

Poem: 寒徹骨梅を娶ると夢みけり
Romaji:
kantekkotsu
ume wo metoru to
yumemi-keri
Kigo: 梅 【うめ】 ume, （sometimes むめ mume）, plum (blossoms) [technically, the "Japanese apricot", Prunus mume; but this has almost always been translated "plum" for literary purposes] (early spring).
Notes: 寒徹骨 (kan tessu kotsu) = cold piercing to the bone. Dreaming of marrying the plum—Sōseki's playful infatuation with the winter plum.
Ueda Haiku:
The piercing cold—
I marry a plum blossom
in a dream.

Poem: 肩に来て人なつかしや赤蜻蛉
Romaji:
kata ni kite
hito natsukakashi ya
aka-tonbo
Kigo: 赤蜻蛉 【あかとんぼ】 aka-tombo, red dragonfly (all autumn).
Notes: 人なつかしや (hito natsukashi ya) = longing for people. A red dragonfly lands on the shoulder—homesickness for people.
Ueda Haiku:
It comes to my shoulder
longing for human company:
a red dragonfly.

Poem: 別るるや夢一筋の天の川
Romaji:
wakaruru ya
yume hitosuji no
ama-no-gawa
Kigo: 天の川 【あまのがわ】 ama-no-gawa, Milky Way (mid autumn).
Notes: 別るる (wakaruru) = parting. A dream of parting; a single thread of the Milky Way—elegant grief.
Ueda Haiku:
I take my leave:
in my dream there stretches a streak—
the River of Heaven.

Poem: 芝草や陽炎ふひまを犬の夢
Romaji:
shibakusa ya
